value.text: Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:42 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. The victim's identity has not been released as police work through the family notification process. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

An explosion inside a Port St. Lucie home destroyed almost everything owned by a family of four. Lucie County Fire District, the initial call came in at 1:24 p.m. for a fire at a home in the 100 block of Carmelite Street Friday afternoon. Neighbors called 911 after noticing the home was on fire. "I looked, and there was all kinds of smoke going through the yard," said neighbor Rob Roadman. "I was outside in the backyard, and then I see very heavy smoke," said Marina Cheong, who lives a few doors down. Cheong said she ran toward the home to help but was stopped by the explosion. "And then there was explosion, very loud, loud explosion, and debris started flying everywhere," she said. "I heard a huge explosion. At first, I thought maybe it's a transformer or something, but it was much, much, much louder than that," Roadman said. Neighbors said the man who lives in the home told them he had been cooking when a grease fire started in the garage, where the propane tank was located. The explosion sent the propane tank flying out of the garage, across the street, and into the garage of a neighbor's home. "I thought it was an air raid. It was not a casual thing. My house shook," Roadman said. "I thought that the whole house had exploded. It was very loud," Cheong added. Roadman said he spoke to the man shortly after the explosion. "I asked the dad if he was OK, and he goes, 'Yeah.' But you could tell he wasn't. Who wouldn't be?" Roadman said. The man was briefly hospitalized but returned to the house a few hours later to join family and friends in going through the debris to see what could be salvaged. They said there wasn’t much left. However, a family member told WPBF 25 News that they consider themselves lucky that nobody was seriously injured. She said the family has a strong community and a strong church to help them persevere. The family has set up a GoFundMe account for donations. After years of infertility, pregnancy loss and unanswered questions, one Jupiter mother is turning her personal journey into a source of hope for others.The inaugural Hope Rising 5K and Fun Walk will take place Oct. 17 at Carlin Park, bringing together families, wellness providers and community partners with a shared goal: ensuring that no one facing infertility or pregnancy loss feels alone.WATCH: Jupiter woman creates Hope Rising after infertility journeyFor founder Kimberly Malik, the event grew from her own experience navigating five miscarriages and four years of infertility."When you get told unexplained infertility, that's not really what you want to hear and that's not an answer I can accept," Malik said.She spent years researching, advocating for herself and searching for answers before ultimately learning she had a blood-clotting condition that contributed to her losses.Despite the heartbreak, Malik said the experience eventually led her to a larger purpose."Welcomed our rainbow baby on Nov. 8 of 2024, my husband's birthday, and I just felt this calling of don't let others walk alone," she said.That mission became the foundation of Hope Rising.Malik says one of the most difficult parts of infertility and pregnancy loss is the isolation many families experience.The Hope Rising event is designed to change that.Organizers are bringing together local businesses, wellness providers and community partners to create a Support Village where attendees can connect with resources and others who understand the journey firsthand."We can have those that unfortunately are on a fertility journey feel seen and supported," Malik said.Among those helping organize the event is Jenny Frattaruolo, owner of Jupiter Fit Club, who became part of Malik's support system during her fertility journey."Just having resources and having someone along the journey with you is everything," Malik said during an earlier interview.While the event centers around a 5K and fun walk, organizers say the focus extends far beyond race day.Participants will be able to leave messages of encouragement on wooden hearts, honor loved ones through remembrance activities and celebrate children born after pregnancy loss on a Rainbow Baby Wall.The event will also raise money for the Hope Rising Grant, which aims to help Florida families facing the financial challenges often associated with infertility treatment."Fitness is a great way to bring people together, so this race is going to bring a lot of women together and hopefully we can help them find resources," Frattaruolo said.Pregnancy loss remains a topic many families struggle to discuss openly, even though countless people are affected by it.Frattaruolo believes connection can make a meaningful difference."It's one of those, if you know, you know," she said. "I think we will all experience death and grief in our lifetime, but miscarriage is the only death you will experience inside your own body."For Malik, that understanding is exactly why Hope Rising exists.What began as a search for answers has evolved into a movement focused on support, community and hope.The Hope Rising 5K and Fun Walk will take place Oct. 17 at Carlin Park in Jupiter.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

The West Palm Beach GreenMarket is more than a weekend destination. It’s also serving as a launching pad for local entrepreneurs, including several new vendors making their debut this season.For this week’s Saturday Small Business, WPTV’s Christy Waite visited Truffle Smiles, one of five new vendors joining the GreenMarket this year.Owner Robert Hurbanek specializes in artisan truffle products imported from Italy.“We import artisan truffle products from Italy. If you love to cook, this is the place to stop,” Hurbanek said.Visitors to the Truffle Smiles booth can find a variety of products, including oils, pasta, sauces, and truffle chips.Hurbanek recommends the truffle mayonnaise.“The mayonnaise! Oh my gosh, if you put that on a burger or a BLT sandwich, it changes everything,” he said.With so many options, Hurbanek said one product customers keep coming back for: Parmesan Reggiano.“People come back for the Parmesan Reggiano,” Hurbanek said. “You can put it on mashed potatoes, a burger. I have even made decadent grilled cheese sandwiches.”The business also fits into this year’s GreenMarket theme, “The World Right Here,” which celebrates the food traditions, people and cultures that make the community unique.Hurbanek said choosing the West Palm Beach GreenMarket was an easy decision because farmers markets give him the opportunity to connect directly with customers and hear how they use his products.“I mostly sell at farmers markets. I like interacting with people and listening to people’s recipes, and just being here at the GreenMarket, which is a nice place to be,” he said.Truffle Smiles is one of the new businesses shoppers can check out this season at the West Palm Beach GreenMarket in downtown West Palm Beach.

By: Brooke Chau Posted and last updated WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — West Palm Beach police are investigating a deadly shooting that left a man dead early Sunday morning. Police say officers responded to a 911 call reporting a shooting in the 1500 block of Presidential Way around 4:50 a.m. The victim, an adult male, died at the scene. According to police, the shooter has been identified and was also at the scene. Investigators say there is no danger or threat to the community. The investigation remains ongoing. Police have not released additional details. Stay with WPTV for breaking news updates.

A busy stretch of Haverhill Road across from Greenacres Elementary School will become a designated school zone after parents raised concerns about children crossing the road.WPTV reporter Christy Waite has been pressing the county, city and the Palm Beach County School District for answers. WATCH BELOW: School zone, crosswalk coming to Greenacres ElementaryBrandon and Lynn Pote reached out to Waite after growing increasingly concerned about student safety. The couple lives across from Greenacres Elementary School, where the speed limit along Haverhill Road is 40 mph, and there is currently no designated school zone or crosswalk."Right here on Haverhill Road there is no crosswalk and no school zone, and cars are going 40 mph," Brandon Pote said.The nearest guarded crosswalks are near Greenacres Christian Academy and another near 10th Avenue and Swain Boulevard.While reporting in the area, Waite witnessed some of the safety concerns families described, including children and families navigating traffic and students riding e-bikes and scooters. She also witnessed a crash along the roadway. Neighbors like Omar Trevino have lived in the area for about 20 years, and he says something needs to be done before someone gets hurt."Cars can't cross, much less kids," Trevino said.After WPTV began asking questions, Engineering and Public Works said a pedestrian safety study determined an additional crosswalk is needed along Haverhill Road to serve Greenacres Elementary School. EPW also says they are considering placing the crosswalk on Haverhill at the intersection of either Carver Street or Fourth Street. The new crosswalk will also be guarded.The City of Greenacres told WPTV it will allocate funding for the crossing guard(s) but the city will not be financially responsible for the rest of the project.But the guarded crosswalk is not the only safety change coming to the area.After Waite continued pressing the county about the lack of a designated school zone along Haverhill Road, EPW says the road will become a designated school zone.Greenacres Elementary already has a school zone along Jackson Avenue, where traffic speeds are limited to 20 mph during arrival and dismissal. However, the stretch of Haverhill Road bordering the school is not currently a designated school zone.The city also requested flashing signals or beacons to help improve visibility for students and crossing guards.For parents like Pote, the plans are welcome news after his family reached out to Waite asking for help."I watch you guys, and I see you guys do reports where you sit down and listen to the community," Pote said. "Thank you guys so much."Engineering and Public Works say they are now working to determine the location for the crosswalk and designated school zone. Once the location is determined, both are expected to be ready by early next year.The county has not said how much the project will cost.

A 54-year-old Jupiter woman is facing felony charges after she allegedly removed fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV infusion while working at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said Monday. On Thursday, Leslie Pope was arrested in Jupiter in conjunction with the Palm Beach Marshals Task Force and faces three felonies: grand theft of a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and fraudulently obtaining a controlled substance. Pope was booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on Thursday morning on an out-of-county warrant. She was released on Saturday morning after posting an original bond of $150,000. Pope is not an inmate at the St. "We take these allegations very seriously," Cleveland Clinic spokeswoman Rebecca Astorga told WPBF in a statement. "She individual no longer works with us, and we are fully cooperating with law enforcement. Because this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this time." https://www.facebook.com/PortStLuciePolice/posts/pfbid02W5HqPQihHo4JSGqHsePU1wjBMmTubGN5HyptojT8wtSJU5Pft8YBVYsKgckEN7mDl Port St. Lucie police arrested Pope after an investigation into the allegations. Investigators learned a family member reported witnessing Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient's fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket and leave the room. Pope was not assigned to the patient's care. The next evening, Pope allegedly returned to the patient's room and again approached the IV equipment, police said. The family member intervened. Detectives later reviewed video footage that shows Pope manipulating protective caps on the equipment. No additional medication was removed during the second incident, according to investigators. A 15-page arrest affidavit includes witness interviews, hospital video footage, medical and administrative records, medication transaction reviews and coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration. "PSLPD takes allegations of criminal misconduct seriously, particularly when they involve individuals entrusted with the safety and well-being of others," the police agency said in a news release. "We remain committed to thorough, evidence-based investigations and pursuing accountability when the evidence supports criminal charges." This remains an active criminal case. "Cleveland Clinic doesn’t comment on caregivers," spokeswoman Rebecca Astorga told WPBF. For many working families in Palm Beach County, having a job is no longer enough to guarantee they can afford a place to live.That was the message from faith leaders and community members with People Engaged in Active Community Efforts (PEACE), who gathered Monday at St. Ann Catholic Church to call attention to the county’s housing affordability crisis and urge local leaders to take action.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:“We are gathered today because across our congregations and our community, we continue to hear the same concern,” said the Rev. Latifah Griffin, a PEACE board of trustees member. “People who are working here are struggling to live here.”PEACE is a coalition of 31 congregations across Palm Beach County. Members say conversations within their congregations reveal a growing number of residents struggling with rising rents, stagnant wages and the possibility of being priced out of the communities where they work and raise their families.Palm Beach County data underscores those concerns. According to the county’s January 2025 affordable housing report, the average rent for a two-bedroom apartment increased from $1,899 in 2021 to $2,833 in 2024 — a 49.2% increase in three years. The cost of buying a home has also risen. The county report found the median price of a single-family home climbed from $425,000 in late 2020 to $600,000 in late 2024, an increase of 41.2%. Nationally, Redfin reported in August 2026 that households needed an annual income of nearly $110,000 to afford a typical U.S. For residents working in service and other modest-wage jobs, those costs can make independent living difficult even when they work consistently.Harry Wolin shared his family's experience at Monday’s gathering. He said he and his wife, who are retired and living on a fixed income, help support their adult daughter, a waitress who lives in Lake Worth.Woolen said his daughter has worked in the restaurant industry for more than 20 years, but her income is not enough to afford housing without help from her parents.“She’s doing everything that we’ve told people they’re supposed to do: get a job, work hard, help support your family,” Wolin said. “And it just doesn’t work given the price of housing.”He said he worries about workers in similar circumstances who do not have relatives able to help them financially.“What do they do if they don’t have a family who can help them?” Wolin asked.Wolin said his family is willing to make sacrifices to ensure his daughter has a safe place to live, but he worries about what will happen when he and his wife are no longer able to provide that support.Mamie Kisner, who represents Tabernacle Missionary Baptist Church, said the experiences Wolin described reflect what PEACE members hear from families across the county.She said residents have reported increasing rents, adult children unable to afford homes of their own and families doubling up in crowded living conditions. Some workers are moving farther away in search of more affordable housing, she said, while businesses struggle to retain employees who cannot afford to live nearby.“These aren’t just numbers; these are people that we know and love,” Kisner said. Faith leaders urged elected officials to listen to residents experiencing housing insecurity and consider solutions that help working people remain in Palm Beach County.PEACE members said raising awareness is only one part of their effort. The organization is also encouraging residents to hear directly from county commission candidates about their understanding of the housing crisis and the steps they would take to address it.The group announced a community kickoff and Palm Beach County Commission candidate forum focused on affordable housing.The event is scheduled for Monday, Oct. Juliana Catholic Church.For PEACE members, the issue comes down to whether people who contribute to the county every day can afford to remain part of the communities they help sustain.

South Florida utility crews and first responders are aiding recovery efforts in Florida's Panhandle following Hurricane Isaias. On Saturday, the Fort Pierce Utilities Authority sent seven crew members and five trucks to the area to help restore power. The crew is working with Choctawhatchee Electric Cooperative, also known as CHELCO, alongside other utility companies from across Florida. They are rebuilding power lines, removing damaged equipment, and installing new transformers and distribution lines. The American Public Power Association said nearly 67,000 CHELCO customers lost power during the storm, affecting about 90% of its system. Fort Pierce Utilities said a statewide mutual-aid agreement allows utilities to quickly send crews to areas where they are most needed. This agreement has also brought outside crews to South Florida following previous hurricanes. "Because of the collaboration and the help provided by the mutual aid agreements, we're able to help each other out. And we couldn't do it on our own. It's too much damage, and it gets our customers back up in a shorter amount of time when there's power loss," said Keith Stephens, director of gas and electric for Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. The Fort Pierce crew is expected to remain in the Panhandle throughout this week or as long as the crew's assistance is required. Florida Power Light has also sent thousands of lineworkers to the Gulf Coast to help restore power. Palm Beach County Fire Rescue and Delray Beach Fire Rescue have deployed crews as well, and they are expected to assist with recovery efforts for the next two weeks.

Dutch Bros Coffee is planning to open its first Fort Pierce location in early 2027, bringing the drive-thru beverage chain to the Treasure Coast. The shop will be located at 2050 S. Highway 1, according to a company announcement on Monday. It will be the company's 43rd location in Florida and its third on the state's east coast. Dutch Bros serves specialty coffee, cold brew, teas, smoothies, freezes, lemonade and energy drinks, including its Dutch Bros Rebel energy drink and Myst Energy Refresher. See also: Undercover buys, pound-level deals, coded texts: 6 arrested in Palm Beach County drug case The company was founded in 1992 in Grants Pass, Oregon, by brothers Dane and Travis Boersma. What began with a double-head espresso machine has grown into a chain with 1,225 locations as of June 30. Dutch Bros locations focus on drive-thru service and offer customizable drinks made to order.

"My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. The victim's identity has not been released as police work through the family notification process. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

Police are searching for a hit-and-run cargo van driver accused of fatally striking a man riding a gas scooter before he crashed into a nearby business and ran away in Fort Pierce. Police officers received multiple 911 calls just before 9 p.m. Sunday about a vehicle crash involving a motorcycle, which later was identified as a gas scooter, close to the intersection of Okeechobee Road and 25th Street, near HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. A white cargo van was behind the scooter, traveling east on Okeechobee Road, Maj. Michael Santiago told WPBF's Angela Rozier at a briefing Monday afternoon. The van driver fled the scene and made a U-turn to drive in the wrong direction across the median on Okeechobee Road, but he crashed into the side of a building, the Kings Queens Unisex Salon. The man then ran from the scene. A second vehicle, a Toyota pickup truck, was also struck, but no one was injured. Police were unable to locate the suspect despite aerial and K-9 units. They are in possession of the van. Anyone with information should call the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477. "We provide new sneakers, socks, underwear, and a toy for all of them."Because of the large number of children served, preparations begin months before the holiday season arrives. For nearly 40 years, The Golden Girls have entertained audiences with humor, friendship and unforgettable characters. Now, those beloved ladies are coming to South Florida through the touring stage production "Golden Girls: The Laughs Continue."The show arrives at the Raymond F. Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach on Oct. 25, bringing Dorothy, Blanche, Rose and Sophia back together in a new story that imagines the iconic friends still living under one roof decades after the original sitcom ended.Actor Vince Kelley, who portrays Blanche Devereaux, and Adam Graber, who plays Rose Nylund, say the comedy's enduring popularity comes from its ability to connect with people from all walks of life."It's a very multifaceted answer," Kelley said. "The generational appeal, the nostalgia and stuff like that."He said the sitcom remains a source of comfort for viewers who return to the familiar characters again and again."Women of a certain age who sometimes can feel forgotten or cast aside, this gives them a voice," Kelley said. "The LGBT community obviously has very strong ties. Everybody can kind of identify with one of the girls, so it's easy to see yourself in the show."Full Interview with CastAlthough the original sitcom was set in Miami, the cast believes its themes resonate throughout South Florida."The lifestyle is born from this area," Kelley said. "We're going to be in West Palm Beach. How many people in West Palm Beach are retirees of a certain age who are maybe living this life, living with friends? They have a timeshare; they're doing this."The actors said audiences across Florida often recognize elements of their own communities in the world created by the television series."It's all South Florida," Kelley said. "The alligators, the humidity, banana leaves."The performers also said Florida audiences have embraced the production since it first began touring in the state."We always look forward to coming to Florida because of how solid the fan base is," Kelley said.The production imagines a continuation of the television series rather than a simple tribute show.According to the cast, Sophia has been arrested for operating a drug ring at Shady Pines, while Blanche and Rose launch a dating app for seniors. Meanwhile, Dorothy is forced into the world of online dating and begins a relationship with the very attorney prosecuting Sophia.The result is a fast-paced comedy that blends modern humor with the personalities fans have loved for decades.The show also embraces some of the continuity quirks that longtime viewers know well.During the interview, the actors laughed about references in the original sitcom that seemingly placed Jupiter's Burt Reynolds Dinner Theatre just a short drive from Miami."None of it makes sense," Graber joked. "You just let it happen."For many fans, The Golden Girls represents more than comedy.The cast said audience members frequently share personal stories during meet-and-greet events, telling them how the show connected them with parents, grandparents and close friends.Others describe finding comfort in the sitcom during difficult periods of their lives.That emotional connection continues to help new generations discover Dorothy, Blanche, Rose and Sophia long after the series left the air.Whether viewers tune in for the one-liners, the friendships, or the nostalgia, the cast believes the secret is simple: everyone can find a little of themselves in one of the four friends.Golden Girls: The Laughs Continue comes to the Kravis Center on Sunday, Oct. 25, with performances at 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.Organizers recommend buying tickets directly through Kravis.org to avoid scams and third-party resellers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The award for funniest player on the Miami Dolphins goes to Ollie Gordon. Gordon is in his second year as a Dolphin, and the running back says the key to the team's potential this season comes down to what is happening inside the locker room.WATCH BELOW: Ollie Gordon sits down with WPTV sports reporter Eleanor SheahanGordon sat down with WPTV to talk about team chemistry, the competitive culture within the Dolphins' roster, his role as the locker room's self-proclaimed class clown — and why he believes this group is built to surprise people."I feel like it's going well. You know, it's getting to the basics, you know, the basics of football. I feel like we've built a good bond here. We got a new team, we got new coaches, and I feel like we're getting that brotherhood and that familyhood," Gordon said.When asked who the most competitive player in the locker room is, Gordon rattled off several names before making sure to include himself."I feel like we got a couple of people. I'm gonna say, Jordyn Brooks. He's one of the most competitive. Jacob (Rodriguez) also, Jordan Phillips, DJ Campbell. I'm gonna throw myself in there. I feel like I'm competitive too." Gordon said.Gordon said Aaron Brewer and Patrick Paul also raise the bar for the team's competitive attitude."I mean, everyone really. I feel like we just got a competitive locker room. You know, I feel like that's what makes the team. That's what makes us a good team and able to play for each other just because of stuff like that," Gordon said.Off the field, Gordon wears another title with equal pride — funniest guy on the team."I think you're looking at him. I think I can go with that. I think I can agree with that one." Gordon said.Asked why he deserves to wear that crown, Gordon was direct."Because I think that's just me. I feel like I'm always goofing around with everybody. I feel like no matter who it is, offense, defense, best teams, we're just here to have a good time," Gordon said.During practice, Gordon is uplifting his teammates and even dialing up a few handshakes with the Dolphins staff."You got to mix it up with everybody. You know, you got to get everybody ready to get everybody juice for work," Gordon said.That upbeat energy, Gordon explained, does not conflict with his competitive side; it is all about knowing when to flip the switch."I really just got to have that switch. You know, when you're in between those white lines, I feel like it's game mode. It's us versus them, you know? And then when we get outside of that, we can play around. But you know, I feel like once we're in between those white lines, those 100 yards, you know, I feel like it's go mode. We got to be ready for whatever, honestly," Gordon said.Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley said Gordon is upbeat and has grown in practice and maturity on the field."I appreciate that, Coach Hafley," Gordon said. "This is a young team, and I feel like some of us all got to lead by example, even if it's not being the oldest on the team, but it's still just showing the young guys how to go. I feel like Coach Hafley has instilled that in us. Like he doesn't just talk to the vets; he talks to all of us. He tells all of us we're leaders in some way. So I feel like with him being like that, I feel like that's turned me that way."Hafley has preached all season long about growth and development. When he was asked to finish the sentence: "The Dolphins team is going to surprise people this year because...," Gordon kept the focus on unity."We stick together, and we play for each other. You know, we come out here every day. I feel like we spend so much time together that we are willing to do anything for each other. You know, and I just feel like when you go back and look, we took a bunch of games down to the wire, and in the NFL, everybody's good. Some teams get in that they hit a wall, but I feel like that's not going to be us. I feel like we're going to push through this moment and stick together as we do," Gordon said.Fans should keep an eye on the No. 0 jersey; that's Ollie Gordon.

A 54-year-old Jupiter woman is facing felony charges after she allegedly removed fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV infusion while working at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said Monday. On Thursday, Leslie Pope was arrested in Jupiter in conjunction with the Palm Beach Marshals Task Force and faces three felonies: grand theft of a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and fraudulently obtaining a controlled substance. Pope was booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on Thursday morning on an out-of-county warrant. She was released on Saturday morning after posting an original bond of $150,000. Pope is not an inmate at the St. "We take these allegations very seriously," Cleveland Clinic spokeswoman Rebecca Astorga told WPBF in a statement. "She individual no longer works with us, and we are fully cooperating with law enforcement. Because this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this time." https://www.facebook.com/PortStLuciePolice/posts/pfbid02W5HqPQihHo4JSGqHsePU1wjBMmTubGN5HyptojT8wtSJU5Pft8YBVYsKgckEN7mDl Port St. Lucie police arrested Pope after an investigation into the allegations. Investigators learned a family member reported witnessing Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient's fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket and leave the room. Pope was not assigned to the patient's care. The next evening, Pope allegedly returned to the patient's room and again approached the IV equipment, police said. The family member intervened. Detectives later reviewed video footage that shows Pope manipulating protective caps on the equipment. No additional medication was removed during the second incident, according to investigators. A 15-page arrest affidavit includes witness interviews, hospital video footage, medical and administrative records, medication transaction reviews and coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration. "PSLPD takes allegations of criminal misconduct seriously, particularly when they involve individuals entrusted with the safety and well-being of others," the agency said in a news release. "We remain committed to thorough, evidence-based investigations and pursuing accountability when the evidence supports criminal charges." This remains an active criminal case. "Cleveland Clinic doesn’t comment on caregivers," spokeswoman Rebecca Astorga told WPBF. A federal judge on Sunday evening ordered the Trump administration to cancel any further airings of the controversial taxpayer-funded ads that promote President Donald Trump’s agenda.Judge Jennifer Rochon granted a temporary restraining order requested by a coalition led by the nonprofit government watchdog group Common Cause, which had challenged the ad buys in a New York federal court.RELATED STORY | Taxpayers have funded nearly $1.5M in pro-Trump ads. Criticism is mounting, including from the GOPThe Justice Department told Rochon, an appointee of Joe Biden, late Saturday that the ad push was set to end Sunday night. But Rochon said that timing didn’t render the lawsuit moot and ordered the government to halt any further airings as of 6:45 p.m. ET.Earlier, the government said in a filing to the court that it has already spent $19 million in taxpayer money on the ads.The administration allocated $20 million for the ads, which were classified as “public service announcements,” from US Customs and Border Protection, CNN previously reported. An advertising company, LMD Agency Inc., “purchased media buys under the terms of the Order through Sunday, October 11, 2026, at an approximate cost of $19,000,000,” senior Department of Homeland Security official Holly Mehringer said in a sworn declaration in the case.The Department of Homeland Security, which includes CBP, directed LMD “to not make any additional media buys past October 11,” she added. Mehringer noted there are “no plans” to purchase any additional ads.Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressed concerns about the unprecedented ad campaign when it began late last month.On October 5, Trump acknowledged the backlash and said “I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” his super PAC.But six days later, the taxpayer-funded ads were still airing.The Trump administration created at least 13 campaign-style ads, some of which have aired on TV networks including CBS, CNN, MS NOW, Fox News and Fox. Watchdog groups, including the nonprofit, nonpartisan Common Cause, said the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications. Common Cause and the Democratic National Committee separately sued the Trump administration over the ads.In a response to the Common Cause lawsuit, the Justice Department said in a filing late Saturday that an effort to halt the spending should be denied because the ads “will not continue past tomorrow.”The judge’s order Sunday would block any further ad buys for two weeks, so if the administration does consider resuming the ad campaign at taxpayer expense, DOJ lawyers would need to get the court order lifted.The coalition that brought the suit praised the judge’s order, writing, “We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda.”CNN previously reported that Trump has personally driven the video ads, including helping select the imagery and videos used, according to a source familiar with the matter. Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging — though at least one of them was produced by a pro-Trump meme group.RELATED STORY | Trump defends ad, says MAGA Inc. will cover cost instead of taxpayersMehringer, in the court filing, described the ads as “depicting the President of the United States and his administration’s various efforts related to protecting America’s borders, including enhancements of border security by combating drug trafficking,” though that is not the exact substance of many of the ads obtained by CNN.And while the Justice Department conceded the ads “(attack) a generic list of ‘villains,’” it emphasized they did not “address any specific race, electoral candidate, or party.”A White House spokesperson said Monday that Trump did not plan to reimburse the government for the money already spent on the ad buys, and Mehringer and other officials did not indicate any plans for a refund.The White House Office of Management and Budget last month allocated $20 million in taxpayer money from CBP for what it called “OBBBA commemorative events.” (OBBBA is an abbreviation for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in 2025.)Mehringer emphasized in her declaration that that money “did not fund the creation or production of any videos or media” and “only funded the airing of preexisting media.”Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was pressed during an appearance Sunday on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on whether the taxpayer dollars would be refunded.“Anytime we can do a public service announcement and brag about America, I’m all about it,” Mullin said, taking aim at negative coverage of the Trump administration as he pointed to success in securing the border and lowering fentanyl-related deaths.“We should be bragging about what’s happening inside America,” he said, adding, “I commend the opportunity of President Trump to give us the opportunity to brag about America.”The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

A legal battle has erupted in Martin County as the developer behind a massive data center project files a sprawling lawsuit against the Village of Indiantown, its village council, planning board, and local residents. Silver Fox 606 LLC filed the complaint and verified petition for a writ of prohibition, claiming local officials are illegally derailing its $25 million project. Silver Fox purchased the over 600-acre property at 13820 SW Silver Fox Lane in 2025 following zoning verifications confirming that computer and data processing facilities were permitted as an as-of-right use in Heavy Industrial districts. Following the 2026 municipal elections, a newly sworn-in village council attempted to stall or ban data center developments despite what the lawsuit alleges were prior municipal marketing efforts that actively recruited similar tech infrastructure. See also: ICU nurse accused of taking fentanyl from critically ill patient at PSL hospital Indiantown's Community and Economic Development Director administratively approved the Silver Fox plat on September 17. The lawsuit highlights a turbulent political climate, pointing to a September 1 emergency council meeting where the village manager and long-serving village attorney were ousted. Shortly after, an administrative appeal was filed by a local resident seeking to overturn the director's approvals. Silver Fox's legal team argues that the planning, zoning, and appeals board lacks the legal jurisdiction to review the plat approval, citing state statutes rendering recorded plats unassailable without landowner consent. Furthermore, the suit alleges that the Village Council violated Florida's Sunshine Law during the abrupt personnel changes. The developer is seeking emergency injunctive relief, a preliminary injunction halting any stop-work orders or retroactive reviews, and declaratory judgments affirming its vested development rights.

Lynora's Italian restaurant, a South Florida staple that started as an 800-square-foot pizzeria in Lake Worth in 1976, is marking 50 years in business — and the family behind it is planning to grow beyond Palm Beach County.Angelo Abbenante, son of founders Raffaele and Maria Abbenante, now leads the restaurant brand, which currently has 6 locations spanning Palm Beach County from Jupiter to Boca Raton."From a little hole in the wall in Lake Worth to now we've gotten to the point where we have six locations we have about five more in the pipeline," he said.The expansion will reach beyond Palm Beach County, with Melbourne set to be next."Our next location is going to be Melbourne, Florida and then from there we're going to hit Fort Lauderdale, and then we have Wellington, Royal Palm Beach coming and then Delray," Abbenante said.The Lynora's story begins with Abbenante's parents, who emigrated from Italy and chose South Florida after his mother found the cold weather in New York unbearable."They came to Italy first and stopped in New York and my mom didn't like the cold weather so she decided to go back to Italy or move to a warmer area, so they had the opportunity to come to South Florida and they landed in Lake Worth," he said.Growing up in the family business meant no traditional weekends off."We didn't have the luxury of the typical American weekends off, this was 7 days a week, 24 hours a day, it was really just putting their feet in the ground. Working 7 days a week and really trying to build a great life for the family," Abbenante said.He worked his way through every job in the restaurant."Dishwashing, washing tables, bartending, making pizzas, working with my mom in the line, just doing whatever had to be done," Abbenante said.I reviewed an original menu, a reminder of how it all began. A large pizza was priced at $3.65 to $4.70. Many of those early dishes are still on the menu today."Yeah, we have all the same dishes from our hoagies where we use the same bread to our eggplant parmesan to our chicken and veal parmesan," Abbenante said.Reflecting on 50 years, Abbenante said family unity and commitment to quality are what have set Lynora's apart."We didn't go out on weekends you know me and my brother it was like we were working and helping mom and helping Dad and when you get to that point you think about the business a little differently - we are really united and I think that is what has made Lynora's so special for the last 50 years. Is when you walk into these restaurants…you get that energy and you get that homemade food. And everything is made with love so it's been a great run and we're looking forward to the next 50 years," Abbenante said.The recipes have remained true to their origins, with bread, pasta, and sauces still made in-house."It really brings us back to how it all started right and the food has been the same, we still make our own bread we still make our own pasta and all the dishes we have created have really been from our mom the sauces," Abbenante said.Among Lynora's most distinctive preparations is its signature sauce."One of the things that is really true to us is how our sauces are made our sauces still take 8 hours to make," Abbenante said.The restaurant's famous meatballs carry the same recipes as when Lynora's first opened."These are actually the same recipes that my mom started 50 years ago, you can kind of see our sauce is a little different than most restaurants... our flavors are basically built into the sauce and our meatballs you know they really speak for themselves," Abbenante said.Quality and consistency, Abbenante says, are the foundation of the restaurant's longevity."It's about making sure that we have the quality ingredients, highest quality, and when you make the food - you have to make sure it's done consistent year in and year out, day in and day out, and when you do that, that's the secret sauce," Abbenante said.Each Lynora's location is designed to reflect the personality of its community."So, when you're Jupiter you get that little feel of Jupiter and when you're in Boca you get that feel of Boca," Abbenante said.Lynora's pizza is made in a wood-burning oven using a hybrid style that blends New York and classic Italian techniques."So we do a mixture of New York style and classic Napoletano pizza and so it's a hybrid and the reason we do that is, because of our oven - our oven is not a gas oven it's a wood burning oven," Abbenante said. "We cook our pizzas typically between 700 to 800 degrees."During a demonstration, Abbenante chose his personal favorite to make."So, we're going to make my favorite which is a classic it's Margherita," he said.Community support, Abbenante says, has been a key ingredient in the restaurant's success."Without the community giving us the support we have we wouldn't be where we're at," he said.As Lynora's enters its next chapter, Abbenante says what it takes has never changed."At the end of the day it's a lot of work a lot of sacrifice it's all the little things it's very meticulous and you have to love it. At the end of the day," he said.Watch "Finding Florida" each Sunday at 10 a.m. on WPTV!This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Jupiter woman who worked as an intensive care unit nurse at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital has been arrested after police say she stole fentanyl from a critically ill patient while on shift.The Port St. Lucie Police Department say 54-year-old Leslie Pope unlawfully removed fentanyl from a patient's IV infusion while working in the hospital's ICU.According to investigators, a family member of the patient reported seeing Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient's fentanyl infusion line, place the syringe in her pocket and leave the room. Police said Pope was not assigned to care for the patient.Detectives said Pope allegedly returned to the patient's room the following evening and again approached the IV equipment. The family member intervened during the encounter.Investigators later reviewed surveillance footage that they say showed Pope manipulating protective caps on the IV equipment. Authorities said they were unable to determine whether any additional medication was removed during the second incident.On Oct. 8, Pope was arrested in Jupiter and now faces felony charges of grand theft of a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and fraudulently obtaining a controlled substance.

A 54-year-old Jupiter woman is facing felony charges after she allegedly removed fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV infusion while working at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said Monday. On Thursday, Leslie Pope was arrested in Jupiter in conjunction with the Palm Beach Marshals Task Force and faces three felonies: grand theft of a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and fraudulently obtaining a controlled substance. Pope was booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on Thursday morning on an out-of-county warrant. She was released on Saturday morning after posting an original bond of $150,000. Pope is not an inmate at the St. https://www.facebook.com/PortStLuciePolice/posts/pfbid02W5HqPQihHo4JSGqHsePU1wjBMmTubGN5HyptojT8wtSJU5Pft8YBVYsKgckEN7mDl Port St. Lucie police arrested Pope after an investigation into the allegations. Investigators learned a family member reported witnessing Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient's fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket and leave the room. Pope was not assigned to the patient's care. The next evening, Pope allegedly returned to the patient's room and again approached the IV equipment, police said. The family member intervened. Detectives later reviewed video footage that shows Pope manipulating protective caps on the equipment. No additional medication was removed during the second incident, according to investigators. A 15-page arrest affidavit includes witness interviews, hospital video footage, medical and administrative records, medication transaction reviews and coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration. "PSLPD takes allegations of criminal misconduct seriously, particularly when they involve individuals entrusted with the safety and well-being of others," the agency said in a news release. "We remain committed to thorough, evidence-based investigations and pursuing accountability when the evidence supports criminal charges." This remains an active criminal case. Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico returned to the campaign trail over the weekend after a 12-day absence that fueled speculation about his whereabouts.His opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, and other Republicans questioned Talarico's explanation that he had been home with the flu.At one point, Paxton called for "proof of life" in a social media post questioning Talarico's whereabouts.The speculation included unsubstantiated claims circulating online that Talarico had been receiving treatment at a mental health facility in Ohio.“I had the flu," Talarico insisted in an interview with MS Now on Sunday. "This is the craziest thing I’ve ever heard. It’s wild that someone can just post something on the internet and then the media just runs with it."The rumors prompted the Lindner Center of HOPE to publicly deny that Talarico had been a patient."Representative James Talarico has never received treatment from Lindner Center of Hope," Lindner Center HOPE posted on X. Talarico responded to the post by saying, "I’ve never even been to Ohio 😂"Over the weekend, Talarico was seen meeting with potential voters at the Austin City Limits Music Festival. He also attended a Kacey Musgraves concert in Dallas on Saturday, where he met with the country singer.The Texas Senate contest is among the most closely watched races in the country as Democrats seek their first statewide election victory in more than 30 years.

A fire that spread through the garage of a Port St. Lucie home Friday afternoon left a father injured and displaced a family, while neighbors and church members rallied to help them begin the cleanup process. The fire happened on Carmelite Street in the Northport Village neighborhood near St. According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading through the garage. They say a propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and impacting a neighbor's garage doors across the street. Lucie County Fire District responded to the home around 1:30 p.m. Crews arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage. When firefighters extinguished the flames, significant damage was left behind, including a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot. Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire broke out. He suffered burns to his legs and was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this." By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, Laidlow said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

For the first time, the family of a man set to be executed for the 1986 murder of an Indian River County sheriff's deputy is speaking publicly about their effort to save his life.William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for shooting and killing 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves' execution is scheduled for Oct. 20.WATCH BELOW: As execution nears, Reaves' family asks DeSantis to spare his lifeNow, with less than two weeks remaining, Reaves' family is asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant him clemency and commute his death sentence to life in prison."I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him," Reaves' nephew, Meredith Farrington, told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey.Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of Reaves' crime or the pain Raczkowski's family has endured."I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," Farrington said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life."But Farrington added, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."That story stretches back to Sept. 23, 1986.According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County after he was unable to get a taxi.Raczkowski responded and was attempting to help Reaves call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name — a memorial to a life taken and a crime that continues to reverberate through two families four decades later."The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said.DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22, scheduling his execution for Oct. 20.Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison. Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," Farrington said.For the Raczkowski family, the case is about a life taken nearly 40 years ago.For Reaves' family, it is now about whether another life should end."But we're praying," Farrington said.Reaves has already lost his latest attempt to stop the execution in Indian River County court. He has appealed that decision to the Florida Supreme Court.For now, his execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency.If carried out, Reaves' execution will mark the 18th in Florida in 2026.

A Martin County woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she buried several cats alive in her yard at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office arrested 37-year-old Alba Luz Chavez on four counts of aggravated animal cruelty after investigators said they discovered two live kittens and two dead kittens buried on a property in Hobe Sound. Deputies were called to the home Thursday night for what family members described as a mental health crisis. Family members told deputies Chavez believed the cats were demons and had killed several animals earlier in the week. According to the affidavit, deputies learned that Chavez had allegedly told residents of the home she killed two kittens on Monday, Oct. Three juveniles living at the residence told deputies Chavez had appeared to be experiencing a mental health episode for most of the week. The juveniles said they locked three surviving kittens inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday evening. When they returned around 6 p.m., they discovered Chavez had forced her way into the room and the kittens were gone. Investigators said Chavez initially refused to tell family members where the animals were. However, while speaking with deputies, Chavez allegedly said, “If you want the cats, you will need gloves, a red bag and a shovel,” and directed them to an area on the property. Deputies began digging and found two live kittens buried underground inside plastic Publix bags, according to the affidavit. Investigators later uncovered two deceased kittens that appeared to be in the early stages of decomposition. Detectives searched for a third missing kitten but were unable to locate it. During an interview, Chavez told investigators she had been cleaning her house and referred to the cats as “very ugly,” according to the affidavit. Investigators wrote that Chavez also made statements indicating she did not want black cats and suggested kittens of different colors “had different fates.” The affidavit states Chavez later began singing instead of answering additional questions. The two surviving kittens were taken to a pet emergency center for treatment. A veterinarian told investigators the kittens were about three weeks old and very weak. The veterinarian said it was too early to determine whether a lack of oxygen while confined inside the plastic bags had caused brain damage or other medical complications. The two deceased kittens are expected to undergo necropsies to determine their exact causes of death. Chavez was arrested and booked into the Martin County Jail on four felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty and is being held without bond.

At a Let’s Hear It event in Okeechobee last month,, WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim spoke with a local veteran dedicated to serving fellow vets.Gregg Maynard, an Army veteran and founder of the nonprofit Thank You For Your Service, helps disabled veterans through projects such as building wheelchair ramps and providing other assistance.WATCH:Now, Maynard is working to bring the Traveling Vietnam Memorial Wall to Okeechobee. He hopes the display will give local Vietnam veterans, especially those unable to travel to Washington, D.C., the opportunity to experience the memorial and reflect on their service.“Not only does it help those veterans who may never make the trip to D.C., but I think these stories and what these guys went through can also be an educational experience for kids,” Maynard told Trim. “It gives them a chance to learn.”Maynard said it costs thousands of dollars to bring the wall to the area and is raising funds through his nonprofit. Those interested in supporting the effort can contact him at thankyouforyourservice34972@gmail.com .Ultimately, Maynard hopes the memorial will have a meaningful impact on the local Vietnam veteran community.“I want them to feel appreciated,” Maynard said. “But most importantly, if it helps just one Vietnam veteran, then all the work and effort that goes into making this happen will be worth it.”

Palm Beach Atlantic University wrapped up its three-day Hispanic Heritage Festival on Saturday, celebrating Hispanic art, culture and music during Hispanic Heritage Month in South Florida.The annual festival featured a contemporary art exhibition and a series of musical performances designed to showcase the cultural contributions and artistic traditions of the Hispanic world. Organizers say the event continues to grow as it enters its 17th year.In a region with a large Hispanic population, organizers say the festival provides an opportunity for students and community members to engage with artists and musicians while learning more about the diversity of Hispanic cultures.The festival began Thursday with an art exhibition featuring artists representing more than 10 countries.Visitors viewed a wide range of artistic styles and mediums, including oil paintings, photography and metalwork.Among the featured artists was Franco Sotillo, a visual artist originally from Lima, Peru, who said his work combines mixed media and reflects both his heritage and personal experiences."I'm a visual artist and came from Lima, Peru," Sotillo said. "I moved to this country 12 years ago."Sotillo said his work incorporates materials including oils, paper and other raw elements. He said sharing his art allows him to introduce audiences to Peruvian artistic expression."I'm an immigrant, but also bringing my culture to the states to show people how Peruvian art is expressed," Sotillo said.Festival Director Michael O'Connor said the event continues to evolve each year."We're expanding every year," O'Connor said.O'Connor said this year's festival marked the first time organizers expanded programming beyond art and classical music to also include popular music from Hispanic cultures."What we want to do is we want to celebrate the Hispanic artistic heritage, because here in South Florida, especially, we have a very, very large Hispanic population," O'Connor said.Organizers said they hope attendees leave with a deeper appreciation for Hispanic artistic traditions and the people behind them."We hope they'll be inspired too to see the artworks here at the exhibition and to see how the Hispanic world makes itself known through visual arts," O'Connor said. "Not just the art is Hispanic, but also the artists are Hispanic."The festival concluded Saturday with performances featuring both classical and popular Hispanic music.Organizers say they hope the festival continues for many years to come as it celebrates the art, music and cultural heritage that help shape South Florida's diverse communities.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A recent change to a flight out of Vero Beach is sparking a bigger conversation about travel options on the Treasure Coast.Travelers tell WPTV limited flight schedules and a lack of convenient transportation alternatives can make getting in and out of the area difficult, sometimes forcing them to drive to larger airports or rearrange their plans.WATCH: At the Vero Beach Regional Airport, travelers shared their frustrations with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the challenges of getting where they need to go.“In the Treasure Coast area, Vero Beach specifically, it is difficult to get around,” said Peter Masella. He pointed to the lack of a Brightline station in Vero Beach, saying people often have to travel to other cities to access additional transportation options.A recent schedule change to Breeze Airways' route between Vero Beach and the New York area has added to those concerns. The flight, which previously departed Vero Beach in the evening, now leaves in the morning.A New York City physician told WPTV the change has affected his work schedule.“I’m a physician working in New York City and because of the change of flight for Vero Beach, I have had to rearrange my patients schedule two days in a row,” he said.Another traveler from Westchester, New York said the change can mean a longer trip.“Then I have to take a taxi all the way down and around to Vero Beach. It’s very inconvenient,” she said.However, Breeze Airways has also been adding destinations from Vero Beach. Yes, the Florida Panthers are already seeing injuries piling up.And yes, the Panthers know things could be much, much worse.Florida forward Brad Marchand will need six weeks to recover from his left leg injury and should be able to resume play with the Panthers sometime in November, coach Paul Maurice confirmed Friday. But Maurice sees the silver lining."Nobody said 'months' yet," Maurice said.That's the difference between the injuries this season and what was happening to Florida at this point last season. By then, Barkov was already expected to be sidelined at least seven months with torn ligaments in his right knee and Matthew Tkachuk was also going to be out for multiple months while recovering from surgery to repair a sports hernia and torn adductor.Barkov wound up missing the entire season. Tkachuk didn't start his season until mid-January. The Panthers saw players miss a combined 544 games with injuries last season and missed the playoffs, an unceremonious end to their run as back-to-back Stanley Cup champions.So, yes, losing Barkov (who could be back by the end of November) and Marchand (who'll be back on the ice in three weeks, then is expected to need three more weeks to rehab and condition) for a few weeks now isn't ideal. But Florida has been there before."We're no stranger to guys going down the last few years and guys have done a great job of stepping up," Tkachuk said. "Worst case, you just got to win 1-0, 2-1."There have been clear sighs of relief with the knowledge that Barkov and Marchand will both return in a few weeks. Florida was short-handed in all four games of its season-opening road trip — Marchand missed the first two, Barkov missed the next two, and defenseman Aaron Ekblad also missed two because he and his wife were welcoming a baby — and the Panthers went 2-0-2 anyway.Ekblad is expected to be in the lineup when Florida plays its home opener Saturday against Minnesota."There's a threshold to this," Maurice said. "You can only survive so many (injuries) and we proved that. But you get two or three guys out, it's standard operating procedure in the National Hockey League. You prefer it's not your No. 1 at any one position because those guys hurt to lose. Everybody's got two or three. And then, you know, you get to five, it starts to get a little tight. Anything over five, you start to really feel it."

Martin County's contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders.Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution."Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," Martin County officials said in the statement.Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans," Argudo said.George Stokus, Martin County's Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service."We're doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can," George Stokus said.In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services.The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need.Carol G. Crews are making "steady" progress power restoration, and 24 parks have reopened after Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, Gov. Hundreds of thousands of people lost power in the wake of the storm, and 430,000 customers remained without power Saturday morning. As of Sunday afternoon, more than 200,000 customers had power restored, DeSantis said. FLP is expected to be largely finished with power restoration efforts by Monday. CHELCO, which had about 46,000 customers without power as of the press conference, is targeting to have power restored by Tuesday, DeSantis said. "I know it’s frustrating to lose power and some of you have been without it for a couple of days now... DeSantis held the press conference Sunday evening from Grayton Beach State Park in Santa Rosa Beach. The state park was closed after a bridge washout, but DeSantis said the park was expected to reopen Sunday night after substantial recovery efforts. WATCH HERE The bridge was "totally washed out" after the storm, and FDOT reported the 50-foot-long and 15-foot-deep washout was cutting off access and could "potentially cause harm to the to the beloved Western Lake here in Grayton Beach," DeSantis said. Recovery efforts at the Walton County park involved crews working overnight and bringing in 600 cubic yards of sand to restore the bridge in less than 18 hours, DeSantis said.
