Residents complained they were unaware of the stricter enforcement and said they received costly citations without warning.The change comes after concerns raised by residents. Luis Carvajal, a Lake Worth Beach resident since 2009, contacted WPTV after receiving a bill that included a $335 violation charge.Carvajal said landscapers working on his property had trimmed palm fronds and placed them near the street for pickup."They're still continuing to work in the backyard or whatever. And there are trucks out here, and then the city solid waste comes by and they scoop it up and they leave. Okay, I didn't think nothing of it," Carvajal told WPTV's Michael Hoffman.Days later, he received a bill in the mail."Make it make sense to me. It didn't make sense," Carvajal said. "They're Palm Beach prices."Carvajal said he had never previously received a city violation notice.Concerns about the fines quickly spread among residents and eventually reached the Lake Worth Beach City Commission.According to city officials, though the changes went into effect in October 2025, more than 1,200 violations were issued after enforcement began in August, generating widespread criticism from residents who said they were not adequately informed about the rules.Vice Mayor Mimi May acknowledged residents frustrations during recent commission discussions."As somebody who's sitting here all the time, I'm like, how do you not know that?" May said. "But if I was just a non-informed resident, I would be upset about that."May is one of the officials who helped spearhead the changes when the ordinance took effect in October 2025.At the time, she recommended fines as high as $500 and opposed sending notification letters to residents before enforcement began.Now, she has changed her position."$300 is way too much money for people on a fixed income," May said.The vice mayor also issued a public apology on social media."I sincerely apologize for any confusion or frustration this situation has caused. I understand that a $335 fine can be a significant financial burden, especially when someone may not have fully understood the rules," May wrote.City leaders have now approved changes to the penalty structure.The city has reduced the violation fine from $335 to $135. Officials also plan to reimburse affected residents $200 for each violation issued under the previous rate.For residents like Carvajal, the city's decision comes as welcome news."That's great news, and I thank Channel 5 for looking into this matter," he told WPTV's Michael Hoffman.City officials say the reduced fines are now in effect, and eligible residents will receive reimbursements related to previous violations on their next bill.

A former surgeon turned Wall Street analyst is taking on his city, its mayor and surveillance technology company Flock Safety in federal court. He has no lawyer and wants the city's license plate cameras gone for good. Steven Greer filed the lawsuit in August against Port St. Lucie, Mayor Shannon Martin and Flock Safety, arguing the technology police use to track criminals also threatens Americans' constitutional rights from privacy to gun ownership. "I was appalled at what I learned," Greer told the CBS12 News I-Team. Greer said he spent much of August researching Flock's technology and preparing the federal lawsuit himself. While he has no formal legal training, he says his years working as a surgeon and later on Wall Street prepared him for the technical research and writing involved in representing himself. Flock's automated license plate readers photograph passing vehicles, recording identifying information along with the time and location. Police can search those records to help identify vehicles connected to crimes, but Greer argues the technology also allows officers to reconstruct someone's movements without obtaining a warrant. His amended complaint alleges Port St. Lucie operated 53 Flock cameras and another 73 Axon license plate readers, for a combined network of 126 devices. See also: Brevard County sheriff’s agent killed in wrong-way crash while responding to shooting Greer argues the collection and sharing of that information violates the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. The CBS12 News I-Team has been reporting on Flock cameras since last year, examining how the technology is used by law enforcement and more recently, allegations of misuse. In Fort Pierce, Officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested after investigators accused him of searching his ex-girlfriend's vehicle 382 times. In another case, a woman was arrested and jailed after investigators mistakenly linked her vehicle to a deadly hit-and-run crash. The charges against her were later dropped. Greer cites both cases in his complaint, but argues the larger problem is the surveillance system itself. During their interview, CBS12 I-Team reporter Katie Bente asked Greer about people who aren't concerned about surveillance because they have nothing to hide. "A lot of people say, you know, 'I'm not doing anything wrong. So what does it really matter?'" Bente asked. "Those are the people who don't deserve freedoms. It's just sheer ignorance. They don't even understand why we have a Fourth Amendment," Greer responded. Law enforcement agencies, however, defend license plate readers as valuable investigative tools, crediting the technology with helping identify suspects, recover stolen vehicles and solve crimes. "I know that police have always argued these Flock cameras really help solve crimes. What would be your response to that?" Bente asked. "That's their number one defense. It's not true," Greer said. His assertion is disputed by law enforcement agencies that have documented cases in which license plate reader information helped investigators. Whether the technology is useful in solving crimes is a separate question from whether particular searches are constitutional. Greer's lawsuit also raises an argument not typically associated with traffic cameras: the right to bear arms. He points to Flock cameras reportedly installed at the entrance to the Ocala Shooting Range, a public gun range in Marion County. Greer argues that recording who visits a shooting range could discourage people from exercising their Second Amendment rights. "When I saw that case where they have Flock cameras in gun ranges, I said, 'Whoa, that's a Second Amendment violation,'" Greer told the I-Team. The key buzzword is chilling. You know, if they scare you away from using your gun rights that's a violation." The complaint also challenges the city's handling of public records requests, alleging officials withheld information about camera locations and system audit logs. It includes claims under Florida's constitutional privacy protections and questions the legality of public spending on the network. Greer has also raised First Amendment concerns following a Sept. Lucie City Council meeting. He told the I-Team that the number of police officers present made him feel intimidated and could discourage residents from speaking out. I'm looking around, I see police officers all over the place," Greer said. Meanwhile, the legal debate over Flock is playing out across the country. In Oklahoma, a federal judge ruled Oct. 1 that a warrantless search of approximately a month of license plate location records violated the Fourth Amendment, suppressing evidence obtained following the search. The ruling concerned the specific circumstances of that case and did not establish that all Flock searches are unconstitutional. Law enforcement agencies have continued to defend the technology, while privacy advocates argue that large networks of searchable cameras allow police to monitor ordinary drivers on a scale that wasn't previously possible. Florida is already seeing changes. The Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for automated license plate readers on state highway rights-of-way, requiring their removal from those locations. Lucie also voted to remove 18 of its 53 Flock cameras. But for Greer, taking down some cameras isn't enough. When Bente pointed out that Port St. Lucie was already removing cameras, Greer argued that voluntary decisions can be reversed by future administrations. "The end result is to get a consent decree, where the city and Flock agrees to pull the cameras forever," he said. His amended lawsuit seeks a declaration that the city's surveillance program violates constitutional protections and an injunction restricting operation of the network or national data sharing without a warrant supported by probable cause. It also seeks disputed public records, statutory damages under federal privacy law and litigation costs. Greer told the I-Team that his primary goal is a binding court order, not a financial payout. "I'm not running for office. I'm not seeking attention," he said. "It's my way of doing something." The lawsuit still faces significant legal hurdles, including potential motions to dismiss. A federal judge has not ruled that Port St. Lucie's camera program violates the Constitution. Greer says he's willing to accept help from an attorney, but for now, he's prepared to continue the fight himself. "You cannot have this technology and not violate the Fourth Amendment. There's no way around it," he said. "You've got to get rid of it.

A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student who was hit by a vehicle while walking to school last week has died from his injuries, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.Police said the crash happened the morning of Oct. 7 near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue.According to police, the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man.The teen suffered critical injuries and was transported to a local hospital. Jupiter Fire Rescue began its first day of municipal service Thursday by responding to four calls after midnight and unveiling Jupiter's first ladder truck, which carries a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10 and the six members who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.Fire Chief Darrel Donatto said the department's first calls unfolded as its members had prepared."They went perfectly, exactly as planned," Donatto said. "We've been planning for this moment for three years, and everything is perfect."The launch marks a new chapter for public safety in Jupiter, with locally controlled fire rescue and emergency medical services operating from stations serving the town's eastern, central and western communities.Jupiter's new ladder truck is based at Station 10, located at 500 N. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park. It is the first ladder truck based in Jupiter, according to Donatto.Donatto said the equipment is important because of the town's oceanfront high-rises and multi-story residential developments."Jupiter has a lot of high-rise buildings all along the oceanfront here, plus a lot of three-story type townhomes all through the Abacoa community," Donatto said. "And so a ladder truck is vital to protecting those, those type of occupancies."Palm Beach County Fire Rescue continues to serve nearby unincorporated areas, including county pockets near the Jupiter Inlet, DuBois Park and Jonathan's Landing, Donatto said.Jupiter's first ladder truck features an American flag design and imagery of the Jupiter Lighthouse. The truck carries the number 10 as a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10, whose firehouse sits across from the World Trade Center site in New York City.Following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, FDNY Ladder 10's replacement truck was wrapped in an American flag design honoring the firefighters who responded that day. Before adopting the tribute, Town of Jupiter officials contacted FDNY Ladder 10 to seek their blessing.Rodman Leas, a firefighter with Jupiter Fire Rescue, explained the significance behind the tribute."Today marks a brand new chapter in Jupiter fire history as we roll out 10 Truck, our community is, like you said, our community's very first ladder truck ever," Leas said. "It carries the number 10 badge ... as we honor FDNY Truck 10, whose firehouse stands directly across from the Sept. 11th World Trade Center site." Leas said six members of FDNY Ladder 10 made the ultimate sacrifice on Sept. 11."I took an inspiration from their American flag design as well ... as a constant reminder of the bravery, courage, brotherhood that defined the fire service," Leas said.Battalion Chief Jason Bohan said Jupiter Fire Rescue worked with Palm Beach Gardens as crews prepared for the new department's launch."We've had an incredible partnership with Palm Beach Gardens," Bohan said. "We've been using their training facility, and because of that partnership over the last couple of months, they and us have been training, getting ready for today."That preparation includes learning to put on approximately 60 pounds of protective equipment quickly when an emergency call comes in.Bohan said the most exciting part of launch day was bringing the new department together around its public service mission."Getting us all together, knowing what we're called to do, which is to protect and save people," Bohan said. "So now that it finally came today, we're all really excited."For Lt. Christian Lainhart, joining Jupiter Fire Rescue also represents a personal homecoming. Lainhart previously worked for Martin County Fire Rescue and described himself as a sixth-generation Jupiter pioneer."I'm super excited, very blessed to be here," Lainhart said.Lainhart said his family's roots in the Jupiter area extend to the 1890s. He grew up and attended school in Jupiter and is now raising his family there."It's just truly remarkable," Lainhart said. "Growing up here, I'm a sixth-generation pioneer, so that really means something here. Grew up here, went to school here, currently raising my family, and now I'm here serving the community that I know and love."While Jupiter's new stations, apparatus and equipment are central to the launch, Donatto said the department's personnel are what make the milestone meaningful."The most exciting thing is the people in it," Donatto said. "We've just been so incredibly blessed to hire some of the best people in the world. They're excited to serve the town of Jupiter."By 5 a.m. Thursday, Jupiter Fire Rescue's firefighters and paramedics had already answered four calls while introducing the community to the people and equipment behind the new department.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. As Hurricane Isaias heads toward the Florida Panhandle, homeowners across the state will see hurricane deductibles go into effect on their insurance policies."The trigger in this case for most policies is a (hurricane) watch or (hurricane) warning anywhere in the state of Florida," Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said.WATCH BELOW: Isaias triggers Florida insurance deductibles that could cost homeowners thousandsHurricane deductibles are common in Florida and are used for hurricane-related claims. They also have a much higher deductible than the usual deductibles on insurance policies."Typically, it's 2 to 3 percent of the property's insured value — not 2 to 3 percent of the claim — so it can be pretty extensive; some people even have 5 or 10 percent deductibles," Norberg said.A 2 percent deductible on a $300,000 home can run about $6,000.And that deductible applies anywhere in the state as long as a hurricane is posted somewhere in Florida."Any type of wind damage that causes a claim — say you're in Palm Beach County, those people will be subject to the wind deductible," Norberg saidThe hurricane deductible, according to state statute, expires 72 hours after the last hurricane warning is lifted.RELATED COVERAGE:

The detention center Florida dubbed "Alligator Alcatraz" may have shut down, but questions remain about who will ultimately pay for it.Last year, the federal government awarded Florida more than $600 million through FEMA to help fund operations at the immigration detention facility built in the Everglades. WATCH ALLIGATOR ALCATRAZ, IS FEDERAL FUNDING AT RISK?While state leaders touted the project and President Donald Trump praised it shortly after opening, only a portion of the promised funding has been distributed so far.Now, two federal reports are putting renewed attention on whether that money could be withheld and Florida could face additional scrutiny before receiving the rest of the funds."I think what these reports and the findings in them do is create a potential basis for scrutiny," said Stetson University law professor Anthony Palermo, who specializes in contracts.The questions stem from two separate federal reviews examining the facility's operations.A report from the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General found the detention center failed to meet several basic standards related to environmental health, safety, medical care, food service and hygiene.According to the report, some detainees reported lacking access to clean drinking water. Inspectors also documented detainees being confined in what were described as "small metal enclosures."A separate Government Accountability Office report highlighted concerns about spending and potential waste. The report found Immigration and Customs Enforcement had not finalized a contract or formal agreement with Florida before immigrants began arriving at the facility.Without pre-negotiated rates in place, the state sought reimbursement at significantly higher costs. The GAO found Florida's approved reimbursement rate was $249 per detainee per day, compared with ICE's reported median detention bed rate of $92 per day, a difference of 171%.So far, neither report concludes Florida violated the terms of its FEMA grant. That distinction could prove important.Palermo says federal agencies typically look first at whether grant recipients complied with the specific requirements attached to funding."Just because there is some sort of deviation from the anticipated standard doesn't necessarily mean that any funding will be withheld," Palermo explained.While the grant excludes typical termination language, it requires Florida to provide a detailed cost breakdown and justification for each reimbursement request.He noted that FEMA retains the authority to review spending, conduct audits and potentially challenge reimbursements if costs are deemed unreasonable. "There is always a chance that there could be an audit or even an investigation into reimbursement that was granted that could potentially lead to a reversal," Palermo said.Federal regulations also give agencies avenues to revisit previously issued payments."There is usually a chance under federal regulations for the government to potentially audit, investigate, review funds that have been paid out and make sure that they were reasonable and could potentially claw them back," he said.Gov. Ron DeSantis dismissed the findings in the federal reports and defended the state's handling of the facility.He also told us last month that additional federal funding continues to flow to the state. To date, just over $134 million has been dispersed from the grant according to USAspending.gov.Neither the Governor's office nor Florida's Department of Emergency Management responded to our inquiries about how the federal reports could impact funding for the facility.The detention center is closed. The federal money is still in question. And until federal officials determine whether all reimbursement requests meet grant requirements, Florida taxpayers have no guarantee they won't end up responsible for part of the final bill.

Amy Offenbach said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore holding onto the same surfboard. Watch report: Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department and is an avid surfer, said something about the situation immediately caught her attention. "The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she became concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed. "That kind of struck me as strange," she said. "The other one seemed a little agitated." Moments later, a girl on the beach told Offenbach she believed her friends needed help. "By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said. Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls. When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress. "I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'" Offenbach hopes the rescue serves as a reminder for beachgoers to understand ocean conditions before entering the water. She encourages people to swim at guarded beaches when possible, check rip current forecasts and use flotation devices or boards when appropriate. "I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl she rescued or learn more about her condition. While she enjoys spending time in the ocean, Offenbach said it is important to remember the dangers it can present. "It can be very treacherous. A proposed 150-unit assisted-living facility in Port St. Lucie is moving through the development process as nearby residents question whether enough is known about the environmental history of a neighboring property with petroleum contamination. The project, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF , is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development, along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard. The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component. Lucie City Council approved the project’s major site plan on Sept. Construction has not begun, and the developer must still submit construction plans for technical review and additional agency reviews. A group of residents opposes the project, citing concerns about the neighboring property’s contamination history and the potential implications for people who could eventually live at the facility. A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls who were struggling in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach. Amy Offenbach said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore holding onto the same surfboard. Watch report: Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department and is an avid surfer, said something about the situation immediately caught her attention. "The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she became concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed. "That kind of struck me as strange," she said. "The other one seemed a little agitated." Moments later, a girl on the beach told Offenbach she believed her friends needed help. "By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said. Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls. When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress. "I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'" Offenbach said she gave the surfboard she was riding to two of the girls and instructed them to hold on and kick toward shore. She then placed the third girl on her soft-top surfboard and paddled her back to the beach. Offenbach said she has some lifeguard training and quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention after they returned to shore. "The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache." Because Bob Graham Beach is unguarded, Offenbach said she drove the girl to a nearby lifeguard station, where an ambulance was called. Offenbach hopes the rescue serves as a reminder for beachgoers to understand ocean conditions before entering the water. She encourages people to swim at guarded beaches when possible, check rip current forecasts and use flotation devices or boards when appropriate. "I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl she rescued or learn more about her condition. While she enjoys spending time in the ocean, Offenbach said it is important to remember the dangers it can present. "It can be very treacherous. Crews are making "steady" progress power restoration, and 24 parks have reopened after Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, Gov. Hundreds of thousands of people lost power in the wake of the storm, and 430,000 customers remained without power Saturday morning. As of Sunday afternoon, more than 200,000 customers had power restored, DeSantis said. FLP is expected to be largely finished with power restoration efforts by Monday. CHELCO, which had about 46,000 customers without power as of the press conference, is targeting to have power restored by Tuesday, DeSantis said. "I know it’s frustrating to lose power and some of you have been without it for a couple of days now... Be assured we’re working around the clock to recover from this devastating hurricane," CHELCO CEO Steve Rhodes said. DeSantis held the press conference Sunday evening from Grayton Beach State Park in Santa Rosa Beach. The state park was closed after a bridge washout, but DeSantis said the park was expected to reopen Sunday night after substantial recovery efforts. WATCH HERE The bridge was "totally washed out" after the storm, and FDOT reported the 50-foot-long and 15-foot-deep washout was cutting off access and could "potentially cause harm to the to the beloved Western Lake here in Grayton Beach," DeSantis said. Recovery efforts at the Walton County park involved crews working overnight and bringing in 600 cubic yards of sand to restore the bridge in less than 18 hours, DeSantis said. DeSantis said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida. That damage came primarily from falling trees, debris and other wind damage, as opposed to storm surge, he said. The state plans to submit a major disaster declaration to the federal government, DeSantis said. "There's a certain damage threshold that has to be reached," he said. "I think clearly, just given the amount of trees that fell down on different things, there's going to be more than enough."The disaster declaration, which must be approved by the president, "provides a wide range of federal assistance programs for individuals and public infrastructure, including funds for both emergency and permanent work," according to FEMA. Isaias made landfall in the panhandle Friday night as a Category 2 hurricane. DeSantis has confirmed there were two storm-related deaths in Escambia County.Some of the hardest-hit counties included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers were without power, Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%, according to the governor.Despite the storm's impacts, state emergency officials said Saturday they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.RELATED LINKS:Who to contact during power outagesLeon County deputies deploy to Santa Rosa Co.Firefighters battle house fire amid Hurricane IsaiasWakulla County escapes major damageWant to see more local news?

The WPTV Town Hall on Amendment 3 has led to more questions about the referendum facing voters on raising the homestead exemption to lower property taxes and reduce revenue for cities and counties.One question attendees posed was: Why are our property taxes increasing every year?WATCH BELOW: Florida property tax increases explained ahead of Amendment 3 votePalm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo talked about it at the town hall, saying inflation is a big factor."This is a national problem, not even a Florida problem; it's not a Palm Beach County problem," Abruzzo said. "What it cost for traffic arms where our lights go: $700,000 five years ago. Now, they're at 1.5 million. The cost of labor, asphalt, concrete, the things we actually use in government is just skyrocketing, so we have to budget appropriately to be able to afford the things we need to buy." Another email asked why municipal workers get raises every three years."They're not coming in and saying we want to take a pay cut," said West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James, talking about negotiating with police, fire and labor unions. "Every three years we're looking at increases, and we also want to pay our employees so they’re competitive with the market; otherwise we lose them to the private sector and other cities, and they're living in a city where affordability is an issue."Another question asked about the impact on apartment living."Over 50% of the occupied housing units in West Palm Beach are renters," James said. "There is no dispute that the rents are going to increase, because those are not homesteaders and so the taxes will go up on those units and the landlords will pass those expenses on to the renters."

Palm Beach Atlantic University wrapped up its three-day Hispanic Heritage Festival on Saturday, celebrating Hispanic art, culture and music during Hispanic Heritage Month in South Florida.The annual festival featured a contemporary art exhibition and a series of musical performances designed to showcase the cultural contributions and artistic traditions of the Hispanic world. Organizers say the event continues to grow as it enters its 17th year.In a region with a large Hispanic population, organizers say the festival provides an opportunity for students and community members to engage with artists and musicians while learning more about the diversity of Hispanic cultures.The festival began Thursday with an art exhibition featuring artists representing more than 10 countries.Visitors viewed a wide range of artistic styles and mediums, including oil paintings, photography and metalwork.Among the featured artists was Franco Sotillo, a visual artist originally from Lima, Peru, who said his work combines mixed media and reflects both his heritage and personal experiences."I'm a visual artist and came from Lima, Peru," Sotillo said. "I moved to this country 12 years ago."Sotillo said his work incorporates materials including oils, paper and other raw elements. He said sharing his art allows him to introduce audiences to Peruvian artistic expression."I'm an immigrant, but also bringing my culture to the states to show people how Peruvian art is expressed," Sotillo said.Festival Director Michael O'Connor said the event continues to evolve each year."We're expanding every year," O'Connor said.O'Connor said this year's festival marked the first time organizers expanded programming beyond art and classical music to also include popular music from Hispanic cultures."What we want to do is we want to celebrate the Hispanic artistic heritage, because here in South Florida, especially, we have a very, very large Hispanic population," O'Connor said.Organizers said they hope attendees leave with a deeper appreciation for Hispanic artistic traditions and the people behind them."We hope they'll be inspired too to see the artworks here at the exhibition and to see how the Hispanic world makes itself known through visual arts," O'Connor said. "Not just the art is Hispanic, but also the artists are Hispanic."The festival concluded Saturday with performances featuring both classical and popular Hispanic music.Organizers say they hope the festival continues for many years to come as it celebrates the art, music and cultural heritage that help shape South Florida's diverse communities.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Palm Beach County Fire Rescue and Animal Care and Control are joining forces once again to help homeless animals find loving homes through a one-of-a-kind fundraiser.The annual Palm Beach County Fire Rescue calendar brings together firefighters, EMTs and adoptable animals for a photo shoot designed to raise money and awareness for animals in need. Organizers say the calendar has become much more than a collection of photos, helping support local animal welfare efforts while connecting pets with potential adopters.WATCH BELOW: Firefighters team up with adoptable pets for popular charity calendar fundraiserWhile posing for the camera may be outside their usual line of work, firefighters say they are happy to step out of their comfort zones for a good cause."I am excited but a little nervous, but it's for a great cause," firefighter Jose Besosa said.The fundraiser began last year and quickly gained momentum."Last year we started it, and it kind of took off from there, and it's become a huge event," said Bryan Brather, Second Legislative Vice President of Local 2928.According to organizers, proceeds from the calendar benefit Palm Beach County Public Safety Animal Care and Control. Last year, the fundraiser raised $10,000, and all of the dogs featured in the calendar were adopted."Last year we raised $10,000, and we would like to double that and do what we can to help out all the animals in Palm Beach County," Bryan Brather, Second Legislative Vice President of Local 2928. said.This year's kickoff event will give the public a chance to help decide which firefighter and dog duo is featured in each month of the calendar.Some of the firefighters are already campaigning for their preferred spots."I would like a summer month because that explains why I am so hot," firefighter and EMT Trey Gilbert joked.The event is about more than fundraising. It is also an opportunity to shine a spotlight on animals looking for a second chance."There are so many dogs and cats that go through unfortunate situations. Not only because people don't want them, but because people die, and they deserve to have second chances," said Palm Beach County Fire Rescue Capt. Janice Vassalotti.The calendar kickoff event is scheduled for Sunday from 6 p.m. at Renegades in West Palm Beach. Attendees can meet firefighters, learn about adoptable animals and help determine which firefighter-and-pet pairs will represent each month of the upcoming calendar.WPTV reporter Christy Waite will be emceeing the event and announcing which firefighter and animal duo were selected for which months.

A Hobe Sound woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she killed and buried several kittens because she believed they were possessed by demons.The Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) arrested 36-year-old Alba Chavez on Thursday after responding to reports of animal cruelty at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayAccording to MCSO Sheriff John Budensiek, three youths living in the home called 911 after they discovered several of their kittens had disappeared. The children told deputies they believed Chavez had killed two kittens earlier in the week and were worried about the remaining animals.Budensiek said the children had attempted to protect three kittens by locking them inside a bedroom before going out to dinner Thursday evening. When they returned, they found the door had been forced open, and the kittens were gone."When deputies arrived, she admitted she thought the kittens had demons and said she didn't want black cats or brown cats in her residence," Budensiek said during a Friday news conference.Investigators said Chavez told deputies she had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them into the trash, later removed them and buried them in the backyard.Deputies said she then led them to a burial site behind the home and told them to bring gloves, shovels and bags if they wanted to find the missing kittens.Despite heavy rain and lightning, deputies began digging in the backyard."As they were digging, they could hear cries from the kittens," Budensiek said.Deputies rescued two kittens that were buried alive inside a plastic Publix bag. The two kittens killed earlier in the week were also recovered deceased from the burial site.A fifth kitten remains missing. Budensiek said deputies and investigators extensively searched the backyard and mobile home but have not located the animal.The two surviving kittens were rushed to a veterinary emergency clinic, where they are being treated for dehydration and monitored for potential long-term effects from being buried underground."If they survive, they'll eventually be taken to the Humane Society and go through the adoption process," Budensiek said.Chavez was arrested on four counts of animal cruelty involving torture, inflicting pain, serious injury or death to an animal. Authorities said additional charges could follow if the missing kitten is found dead.The arrest marks at least the third animal cruelty or neglect case in Martin County since late July. Asked whether the trend surprised him, Budensiek said reports of violence against animals often mirror broader societal problems."We've seen society kind of going downward and we see more violence with interactions with humans, and then that translates into animals," Budensiek said. "In fact, a lot of times it starts with animals and then moves over to humans. So unfortunately, based on the trends and societal trends that we're seeing, it does not surprise me, but when we see it, it's extremely alarming.Budensiek said Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and is also subject to an immigration hold. The sheriff identified her as a Venezuelan national who he said is in the United States illegally.According to the sheriff, deputies had previously responded to the home for incidents involving Chavez's mental health but had never received complaints related to animal cruelty.When asked about Chavez's motive, Budensiek said investigators still aren't certain whether mental health issues played a role."She said they were demonic. She said she didn't want those cats in her house," Budensiek said. "I don't know whether it was a mental health issue or she just didn't like the cats."Budensiek said the three youths who reported the incident were emotional but showed courage by contacting law enforcement."I applaud them for reaching out, calling 911 and letting us save the two kittens," he said.The children were taken into the custody of the Florida Department of Children and Families before being turned over to their father, who lives locally, according to investigators.Other adult cats found at the home were examined by animal services and determined to be healthy.Budensiek called the case "extremely alarming" and praised the responding deputies for their efforts to rescue the buried animals."We're going to aggressively pursue criminal charges on her to make sure she pays for the damage that she did to these animals," he said.

Brandee Anthony, known as the Vero Beach Mermaid, is an elite level PADI dive instructor, who teaches people of all ages to become mermaids — offering experiences that range from glamorous mermaid makeovers and beach photoshoots to poolside swimming lessons."I was a professional live streamer a long time ago, so I thought it would be really cool to take all my viewers underwater, but how can I make that interesting and magical?" Anthony said.That curiosity grew into a deep and lasting passion."That was 10 years ago and I'm a little in love with mermaiding for sure," Anthony said.The experience begins with a mermaid makeover, starting inside Anthony's custom fantasy closet — brimming with tropical-inspired tails, tops and accessories created just for mermaid gear."We're going to start with a mermaid makeover, which is one of my favorite parts," Anthony said. "Kate, so this is your magical closet."The closet features silicone tails that each weigh about 30 to 35 pounds. Accessories are on hand to complete every look."Mermaid crowns and armbands and embellishments, kind of the final touches to help people really feel like they have a full ensemble," Anthony said.Armbands come in a variety of styles, including options with a vibrant teal accent."We have a few options if you want to go with armbands. We have these, these are super cute and they have that nice teal," Anthony said.Anthony even offered a personalized recommendation while I was browsing through the options."I think with what you are wearing I would probably wear this one," she said.Browsing the closet felt like being a kid in a candy store — wanting more of everything. Anthony said that reaction is exactly the goal."That is exactly what you should feel like," she said. "So, we'll pick out a tail, a top, some accessories, and a crown, and then we'll head over to the beach."After settling on a look — including a tail Anthony called a "wind trader" and a stunning leafy sea dragon design — I was feeling the mermaid vibe and ready for the beach.Anthony, a professional photographer for 15 years, combines breathtaking backdrops and elaborate costumes to create magic where whimsy meets the water. Once suited up, I made my way toward the water, making my mermaid marks in the sand along the way."Like a sea turtle you are going to migrate towards the ocean," she said. "And then your going to turn toward me put your fin over here — we call it a fluke."Anthony walked me through the first poses on the shoreline."The seated is the easiest first pose — you can kind of just look at the ocean and relax and let the wind take your hair," she said. "Look out towards the beach — a little water love."Next, I headed poolside for a basic mermaiding class.Anthony caters to every client's ability, even those who are a little cautious about the experience."Once people get in a tail and they find their groove, it turns into a bunch of people just playing in a pool," she said.People come to the experience for all kinds of reasons."I've had people come to me for fun and some for deeper reasons," Anthony said."Coming on a retreat or take a course really did change their lives — or changed the trajectory of their lives. I've turned a few people into pro mermaids," Anthony said.In the pool, Anthony was ready to teach me how to mermaid — stripping back the glam and focusing on the fundamentals."So now you've had the photoshoot and the glam and now we are going to strip it back and just have some fun swimming as a mermaid," Anthony said.She walked me through every step of the movement."So you can flex your foot up towards the top of the water and then push it down…and just do that a few times….you can feel the resistance of the water and that's what propels you," Anthony said. "I'm going to have you back float in the tail — I'll kind of help you float there."The lesson even included a dive completely underwater."3.2.1. breathe out — we dive down and then pop up," Anthony said. "That was so good — that was fun — and that's how we shoot video underwater."For Anthony, the joy of mermaiding as an adult goes far beyond the water itself. "I think that's what mermaiding as an adult feels like is you don't have to act like a kid but you can be an adult that plays," she said. "And that's where it can be fun or it can be more — some people just want to feel empowered. Or good in their skin and they do a photo shoot or a bucket list thing."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student remains in critical condition after police say he was struck by an SUV while walking to school along a construction zone in Port St. Lucie Police, the crash happened around 6 a.m. Wednesday on Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue. Investigators say the freshman was walking along the roadway, which does not have sidewalks, when a 72-year-old driver hit him from behind with an SUV. The area is currently under construction as crews work to widen a portion of Port St. Police say the driver initially believed he had struck a construction barrel. After turning around and returning to the scene, officers say he found the teen unconscious on the side of the road and called 911. Neighbors who live near the crash site say the lack of sidewalks has long been a concern, especially for students who walk or bike to school. "It's not safe to walk around here," said neighbor Kendry Portal. "We need those sidewalks." Neighbors told CBS12 News they have seen multiple crashes involving pedestrians along the busy stretch of road since construction began a few years ago. See also: Jury convicts former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct The Florida Department of Transportation is widening the southern portion of Port St. Lucie Boulevard into a four-lane road and adding sidewalks as part of the ongoing project. Neighbors say the safety improvements cannot come soon enough. "I want to see this street finished as soon as possible," Portal said. Police do not believe the driver was impaired, and it remains unclear whether any charges will be filed. Authorities are asking anyone with dashcam or surveillance video from the area around the time of the crash to contact Port St. As of Thursday morning, the 14-year-old remains hospitalized in critical condition. "I just hope that he gets well soon and hope for the family in this situation," said Portal.

Lucie police confirmed that a man found unconscious in the roadway with severe head injuries early Friday morning was the victim of a hit-and-run crash.WATCH BELOW:The victim has been identified as a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, police said. The incident occurred at about 12:56 a.m. near the intersection of NW University Boulevard and NW California Boulevard.The 63-year-old man was unconscious and suffering from severe head trauma and significant bleeding, police said. He was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for medical treatment and remains in critical condition.Police said detectives obtained surveillance video from a nearby business that captured the incident and are continuing to collect and evaluate additional video footage as they work to determine the circumstances surrounding the crash and identify the vehicle and driver involved.Authorities are asking anyone who was driving in the area around the time of the crash, may have witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or other video footage from the area to come forward.Even information that may seem insignificant could assist investigators in identifying the driver and bringing this investigation to a resolution. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000. The investigation remains active and ongoing.

WPTV is continuing to follow flooding issues at the intersection of California and Savona boulevards in Port St. The water has receded, but earlier this week, the intersection looked like a lake.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie flooding hits pizza shop hard as city works on fixWPTV is pressing city leaders about any solution to keep the water levels down.Neighbors shared video of the roadways, looking like a river."We were actually calling it the California River, as a joke," said Joe Dascoli, who works at Estella Pizzaria right of the intersection. "It becomes like an island around here."That island is a shopping plaza where the pizza shop is located. Due to the flooding on Thursday, Dascoli said they had to close early."It's an ongoing thing that you know should be resolved," said Dascoli.Dascoli told WPTV customers couldn't go in and orders couldn't go out during this week’s flooding."We've lost thousands of dollars just in revenue and people not being able to come in," said Dascoli. "Some of our drivers, their cars aren't capable of going through the floods, so we have to stop deliveries."WPTV pressed the city of Port St. Lucie about any solutions to the flooding.Scott Samples with the city said it's starting a pilot program for water level sensors at flood-prone areas in the city."There'll be alerts that'll be able to go to Public Works and the police to say, 'Hey, this area is seeing rapid flooding,' so they might be able to respond quicker," said Samples.Samples said long-term solutions include a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood.The project includes two new retention ponds, baffle boxes to collect runoff, and even raising sections of the roadway at California and Savona boulevards.Right now, Samples said the project is in the data collection phase before moving on to design."This is one of the highest priorities that we have in terms of capital investment projects, and so it's going to take time," said Samples.

Ron DeSantis said two people have died and more than 430,000 customers remain without power as state and local officials begin recovery efforts following Hurricane Isaias' landfall in the Florida Panhandle.Speaking Saturday in Okaloosa County, where the Category 2 hurricane came ashore Friday night, DeSantis said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida, primarily from falling trees and debris.WATCH BELOW: DeSantis confirms 2 storm-related deaths in Florida Speaking from Destin, Florida, the governor said both people died in Escambia County, highlighting ongoing safety concerns as residents cope with power outages.Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons said in a video posted to Facebook that one woman died after a tree fell on her home. In a second video, Simmons said the other victim, a man, died from a generator that was not properly ventilated. The sheriff said that four other people were inside the same home and had to be hospitalized. "What I saw was both from the structural perspective, I think our structures handled the storm very well," DeSantis said. "The problem is that the storm knocked over a lot of trees."State officials confirmed two storm-related deaths. One person in Escambia County was killed when a tree fell on a home. Another person died after operating a generator inside a garage, highlighting ongoing safety concerns as residents cope with power outages.Emergency crews have completed roughly 180 missions through the Florida Division of Emergency Management, according to the governor. State officials said nearly 10,000 power accounts have already been restored, but approximately 430,000 customers remained without electricity Saturday morning. About 325,000 of those outages are within Florida Power & Light's service area.Officials said debris removal remains one of the biggest challenges slowing restoration efforts."The folks have been out since daylight," DeSantis said. "Some of it is that you've got to get the debris out of the way before the linemen can connect it."The Florida Department of Transportation began clearing roads and bridges before sunrise, while the Florida Highway Patrol has completed dozens of debris-clearing missions. State officials said 85 traffic signals have been restored using generators.Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport has reopened to commercial air traffic, while airports in Pensacola and Fort Walton Beach remained closed Saturday but were expected to resume operations soon.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said more than 16,000 utility workers have been mobilized to restore power throughout the region.Perdue also warned residents that flooding risks remain even after the storm's passage. Several rivers, including the Shoal River in Okaloosa County, are still rising and are not expected to crest for several days."We want to make sure we keep enough resources on hand in case search and rescue is needed," Perdue said.State leaders urged residents to avoid flooded roads and standing water, warning that even shallow water can quickly become dangerous.Meanwhile, Attorney General James Uthmeier said a small number of price-gouging complaints had already been reported. Residents who believe businesses are overcharging for essentials such as fuel, food or other emergency supplies are encouraged to file complaints through the attorney general's office.Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia also warned residents about post-storm scams, including unlicensed contractors and fraudulent roofers targeting homeowners.Officials urged residents not to sign contracts or provide deposits before verifying a contractor's credentials. The state also plans to establish insurance assistance hubs in impacted areas within the next 48 hours to help residents file claims and meet with insurance representatives.Businesses affected by the storm can report damage through the state's business damage assessment survey at FloridaDisaster.biz. State officials said the information will help expedite recovery assistance and assess losses.DeSantis said recovery efforts will continue across the Panhandle, where damage stretches from the Alabama state line to the eastern Panhandle.The governor cautioned that additional flooding could develop in the coming days as rivers continue rising but said Florida has water rescue teams and emergency assets positioned throughout the region."We're going to get through this," DeSantis said. "There's damage, and that's going to be difficult for people whose property was damaged, but I also feel like this is very surmountable for us if we all just work together and get the job done."

Martin County’s contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution. “Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders,” Martin County officials said in the statement. Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, “we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.” Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown. “We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system,” Martin County Transit said. In an afternoon press conference, county leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday, according to the county. Jim Gordon, Martin County’s Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming. “We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today,” Gordon said. For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily. “[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food,” Joe said. Joe said he received no notice before service was cut. “No warning at all, nothing, zero.” Joe said. Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe. “I’ve had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can’t feel my feet, so I’m not getting anywhere,” Joe said. Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company’s handling of the shutdown lacked transparency. “I don’t think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans,” Argudo said. George Stokus, Martin County’s Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service. “We’re doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can,” George Stokus said. In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services. The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it. “Transportation isn’t a luxury for the people who depend on it. It’s how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn’t disappear with it,” Houwaart-Diez said. Region Martin County Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption. “This is important for people to be able to get to the doctor’s, to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there,” Houwaart-Diez said. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program’s response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY’s fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county’s transit website . Offenbach, who has years of lifeguard training, said her instincts kicked in when she saw three girls struggling in the water. "I took off my clothes, grabbed the board, and started paddling," she said. "I immediately went into rescue mode." Authorities said one of the girls was choking on water, and the beach had no lifeguards on duty. Offenbach rushed in to help, using a surfboard to stabilize the girl. "Once she was on the board, she was kind of limp. Her body wasn't doing anything else," Offenbach said. Offenbach said the girl's forehead felt cold, prompting her to rush the child to the nearest lifeguard stand down the road. The girl was then taken to the hospital with minor drowning injuries. Deputies digging through a rain-soaked backyard in Martin County heard the cries of kittens buried up to 3 feet underground, leading to the rescue of two animals while two others were found dead, the sheriff revealed Friday. During a news conference, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek provided new details about the arrest of 36-year-old Alba Chavez, who is accused of killing two kittens and burying two others alive at a mobile home park in Hobe Sound. According to the sheriff's office, deputies responded to the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park on Thursday night after several minors inside the home called 911 to report that Chavez had allegedly killed two kittens Monday, placed them in the trash and later buried them in the backyard. The children, who feared for the safety of three remaining kittens, attempted to protect them by locking them inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday night. Budensiek said that when the children returned home, they discovered the bedroom door had been forced open and the kittens were missing. The children then called law enforcement to report the incident. When deputies arrived, Chavez was standing in the roadway and reportedly admitted to killing the two kittens. While speaking with deputies, Chavez said she believed the kittens had demons, described them as ugly and said she did not want black or brown cats inside the home. Chavez then led deputies to the backyard, where the kittens had allegedly been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. See also: Hurricane Isaias strengthens into major Category 3 storm near Florida Panhandle As deputies dug through the backyard, they heard cries coming from underground. Two kittens were recovered alive, while the two kittens Chavez allegedly killed Monday were found dead. A fifth kitten remains missing despite repeated searches of the property. Budensiek said the two surviving kittens were immediately taken to an emergency veterinary facility, where they were being treated for dehydration. The sheriff said veterinarians were also concerned about possible injuries caused by a lack of oxygen while the kittens were buried. Despite being rescued, the kittens could still die from their injuries. Chavez was arrested and charged with four counts of animal torture involving pain, serious injury or death, according to the sheriff's office. The four charges correspond to the two kittens found dead and the two rescued alive. The sheriff said Chavez was being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and also had an immigration hold. Investigators have not determined exactly how the first two kittens died. The sheriff said Chavez initially cooperated with deputies and led them to the burial site but later stopped answering questions about how the animals were killed. Authorities also have not determined her motive. Budensiek said deputies had previously responded to calls involving Chavez's mental health but had received no prior animal cruelty complaints at the residence. Additional charges could be filed if the fifth kitten is found dead, according to the sheriff. Following the incident, the Florida Department of Children and Families became involved, and the children were later released to their father, who lives locally. Officials said resources were available to help the children cope with what happened.

A proposed 150-unit assisted-living facility in Port St. Lucie is moving through the development process as nearby residents question whether enough is known about the environmental history of a neighboring property with petroleum contamination. The project, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF , is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development, along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard. The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component. Lucie City Council approved the project’s major site plan on Sept. Construction has not begun, and the developer must still submit construction plans for technical review and additional agency reviews. A group of residents opposes the project, citing concerns about the neighboring property’s contamination history and the potential implications for people who could eventually live at the facility. See also: 'It's not safe': Treasure Coast neighbors raise concerns after teen hit walking to school It’s not about what is being built there, resident David Lipps said, arguing that nearby businesses and other facilities could also be affected by environmental concerns. Resident Charlie D’Agata said residents have raised objections at City Council meetings for about two years. He questioned why a developer would be allowed to build near a property he described as contaminated. Residents say they have contacted outside organizations, including the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Health , in an effort to get answers about the site. An engineering letter provides some context for their concerns. In a letter discussing a March 2026 meeting with environmental officials about the neighboring property, BTEX Engineering said the proposed remediation approach should be changed because of concerns about surrounding properties, including the planned assisted-living facility. The letter said vapors would need to be captured during remediation. The environmental history of the neighboring property and the extent of any potential impact on surrounding land remain central questions for residents seeking more information. The city has approved the major site plan, but the project must clear additional steps before construction can begin. The developer is expected to submit construction plans for technical review, followed by reviews involving the South Florida Water Management District and other agencies. Residents say they want clearer answers about the neighboring property’s environmental history and how any potential risks would be addressed as the project advances

Martin County’s contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution. “Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders,” Martin County officials said in the statement. Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, “we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.” Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown. “We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system,” Martin County Transit said. In an afternoon press conference, county leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday, according to the county. Jim Gordon, Martin County’s Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming. “We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today,” Gordon said. For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily. “[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food,” Joe said. Joe said he received no notice before service was cut. “No warning at all, nothing, zero.” Joe said. Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe. “I’ve had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can’t feel my feet, so I’m not getting anywhere,” Joe said. Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company’s handling of the shutdown lacked transparency. “I don’t think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans,” Argudo said. George Stokus, Martin County’s Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service. “We’re doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can,” George Stokus said. In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services. The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it. “Transportation isn’t a luxury for the people who depend on it. It’s how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn’t disappear with it,” Houwaart-Diez said. Region Martin County Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption. “This is important for people to be able to get to the doctor’s, to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there,” Houwaart-Diez said. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program’s response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY’s fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county’s transit website . Residents seeking transportation assistance can call the United Way of Martin County at 772-283-4800 or click here to visit their website. Residents seeking paratransit transportation assistance can call 772-463-2822. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

WPTV is continuing to follow flooding issues at the intersection of California and Savona boulevards in Port St. The water has receded, but earlier this week, the intersection looked like a lake.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie flooding hits pizza shop hard as city works on fixWPTV is pressing city leaders about any solution to keep the water levels down.Neighbors shared video of the roadways, looking like a river."We were actually calling it the California River, as a joke," said Joe Dascoli, who works at Estella Pizzaria right of the intersection. "It becomes like an island around here."That island is a shopping plaza where the pizza shop is located. Due to the flooding on Thursday, Dascoli said they had to close early."It's an ongoing thing that you know should be resolved," said Dascoli.Dascoli told WPTV customers couldn't go in and orders couldn't go out during this week’s flooding."We've lost thousands of dollars just in revenue and people not being able to come in," said Dascoli. "Some of our drivers, their cars aren't capable of going through the floods, so we have to stop deliveries."WPTV pressed the city of Port St. Lucie about any solutions to the flooding.Scott Samples with the city said it's starting a pilot program for water level sensors at flood-prone areas in the city."There'll be alerts that'll be able to go to Public Works and the police to say, 'Hey, this area is seeing rapid flooding,' so they might be able to respond quicker," said Samples.Samples said long-term solutions include a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood.The project includes two new retention ponds, baffle boxes to collect runoff, and even raising sections of the roadway at California and Savona boulevards.Right now, Samples said the project is in the data collection phase before moving on to design."This is one of the highest priorities that we have in terms of capital investment projects, and so it's going to take time," said Samples.
