Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room. As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life. Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said. Bah’s close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him. Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said. Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff’s office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense . No arrests have been made. Bah’s mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened. “I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.” During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives. Angela Sanders, one of Bah’s former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said. Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.” Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person. The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years. “He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration. Bah’s funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

A Hobe Sound woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she killed and buried several kittens because she believed they were possessed by demons.The Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) arrested 36-year-old Alba Chavez on Thursday after responding to reports of animal cruelty at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayAccording to MCSO Sheriff John Budensiek, three youths living in the home called 911 after they discovered several of their kittens had disappeared. The children told deputies they believed Chavez had killed two kittens earlier in the week and were worried about the remaining animals.Budensiek said the children had attempted to protect three kittens by locking them inside a bedroom before going out to dinner Thursday evening. When they returned, they found the door had been forced open, and the kittens were gone."When deputies arrived, she admitted she thought the kittens had demons and said she didn't want black cats or brown cats in her residence," Budensiek said during a Friday news conference.Investigators said Chavez told deputies she had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them into the trash, later removed them and buried them in the backyard.Deputies said she then led them to a burial site behind the home and told them to bring gloves, shovels and bags if they wanted to find the missing kittens.Despite heavy rain and lightning, deputies began digging in the backyard."As they were digging, they could hear cries from the kittens," Budensiek said.Deputies rescued two kittens that were buried alive inside a plastic Publix bag. The two kittens killed earlier in the week were also recovered deceased from the burial site.A fifth kitten remains missing. Budensiek said deputies and investigators extensively searched the backyard and mobile home but have not located the animal.The two surviving kittens were rushed to a veterinary emergency clinic, where they are being treated for dehydration and monitored for potential long-term effects from being buried underground."If they survive, they'll eventually be taken to the Humane Society and go through the adoption process," Budensiek said.Chavez was arrested on four counts of animal cruelty involving torture, inflicting pain, serious injury or death to an animal. Authorities said additional charges could follow if the missing kitten is found dead.The arrest marks at least the third animal cruelty or neglect case in Martin County since late July. Asked whether the trend surprised him, Budensiek said reports of violence against animals often mirror broader societal problems."We've seen society kind of going downward and we see more violence with interactions with humans, and then that translates into animals," Budensiek said. "In fact, a lot of times it starts with animals and then moves over to humans. So unfortunately, based on the trends and societal trends that we're seeing, it does not surprise me, but when we see it, it's extremely alarming.Budensiek said Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and is also subject to an immigration hold. The sheriff identified her as a Venezuelan national who he said is in the United States illegally.According to the sheriff, deputies had previously responded to the home for incidents involving Chavez's mental health but had never received complaints related to animal cruelty.When asked about Chavez's motive, Budensiek said investigators still aren't certain whether mental health issues played a role."She said they were demonic. She said she didn't want those cats in her house," Budensiek said. "I don't know whether it was a mental health issue or she just didn't like the cats."Budensiek said the three youths who reported the incident were emotional but showed courage by contacting law enforcement."I applaud them for reaching out, calling 911 and letting us save the two kittens," he said.The children were taken into the custody of the Florida Department of Children and Families before being turned over to their father, who lives locally, according to investigators.Other adult cats found at the home were examined by animal services and determined to be healthy.Budensiek called the case "extremely alarming" and praised the responding deputies for their efforts to rescue the buried animals."We're going to aggressively pursue criminal charges on her to make sure she pays for the damage that she did to these animals," he said.

Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls who were struggling in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach. "By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said. Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls. When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress. "I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'" Offenbach said she gave the surfboard she was riding to two of the girls and instructed them to hold on and kick toward shore. She then placed the third girl on her soft-top surfboard and paddled her back to the beach. Offenbach said she has some lifeguard training and quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention after they returned to shore. "The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache." Hurricane Isaias became the first hurricane to make direct landfall in the United States in more than two years when it came ashore late Friday as a Category 2 storm.By Saturday morning, Isaias had weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved across Alabama. While no longer a hurricane, its remnants were expected to bring heavy rain and gusty winds across parts of the South on Saturday before spreading into the Great Lakes and Northeast on Sunday.As of 2 p.m. CT Saturday, more than 700,000 customers were without power. More than 400,000 outages were reported in Florida's Panhandle, while Alabama reported more than 180,000 outages and Georgia reported about 40,000.At its peak, nearly 900,000 customers were without power. The storm also caused significant wind damage in the Pensacola area, where a hotel lost its roof as Isaias made landfall.RELATED STORY | Study: Super-sized El Niño could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by FebruaryThe hurricane pushed storm surge onto coastal roadways across the Florida Panhandle.Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons confirmed one person died during the storm. He added that some roads were impassable due to downed trees and power lines. Away from the coast, a death was reported in Birmingham, Alabama, due to a fallen tree limb. Isaias marked a departure from what had been one of the quietest Atlantic hurricane seasons in recent years. It was also the first hurricane to form in the Atlantic basin in 2026.Forecasters had predicted a below-normal season because of a strong El Niño, which typically creates upper-level winds that can disrupt tropical cyclone development.Although Isaias was the ninth named storm of the season, all previous systems had peaked at tropical-storm strength.The same upper-level winds that limited hurricane activity this year also contributed to Isaias weakening before landfall. The storm maintained Category 3 strength for much of Friday before being downgraded to a Category 2 hurricane just hours before reaching the coast.RELATED STORY | El Nino keeps Atlantic hurricane season historically calmBehind Isaias, the National Hurricane Center said it was not tracking any additional systems. The Atlantic hurricane season typically peaks around Sept. 10 and begins to wind down by mid-October before ending Nov. 30.Since 2013, only two hurricanes have made U.S. The most recent was Hurricane Nicole in 2022.

Ron DeSantis said Saturday morning that nearly 450,000 utility customers remained without power across Northwest Florida after Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Panhandle. Speaking from Destin later in the day, he confirmed there were two storm-related deaths in Escambia County.The governor said Isaias came ashore near Destin at 9:30 p.m. Friday as a Category 2 hurricane with sustained winds of about 105 mph. Wind gusts reached as high as 116 mph near Santa Rosa Sound, while storm surge pushed water levels approximately 5.5 feet above normal in some areas.WATCH BELOW: Santa Rosa County among hardest hit counties, DeSantis saysAlthough the storm has since weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and moved out of Florida, DeSantis warned that flooding remains a concern, particularly in parts of the Panhandle and Big Bend expected to receive 4 to 8 inches of rain through the weekend."As of now there have been no confirmed fatalities," DeSantis said, noting reports of a possible death in Escambia County linked to a fallen tree had not yet been confirmed by the state.State officials said more than 16,000 linemen were staged ahead of the storm and began restoration efforts as early as 3 a.m. Saturday.By 7 a.m., approximately 448,000 customer accounts were without electricity statewide, including about 323,000 Florida Power & Light customers and roughly 110,000 customers served by electric cooperatives.Some of the hardest-hit counties included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers were without power, Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%, according to the governor.The Florida Department of Transportation and Florida Highway Patrol launched overnight "cut and toss" operations to clear roads of fallen trees and debris. Officials said all state-owned bridges had been inspected and reopened by 6 a.m. 98, two major transportation corridors in the region, were also reopened.Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport resumed commercial operations Saturday morning, while Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport and Pensacola International Airport remained closed.Despite the storm's impacts, state emergency officials said they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said state teams remain on standby as flood risks continue."We are going to keep search and rescue teams ready to go," Perdue said. "There could be continued flooding from all of the rainfall."Officials urged residents to avoid driving through flooded roadways, stay clear of downed power lines and limit unnecessary travel while utility crews and emergency workers continue recovery efforts.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned residents to watch for scams in the aftermath of the storm, including reports of fraudulent text messages offering tree-removal services and unlicensed contractors seeking repair work.State officials said damage assessments are underway and will help determine whether Florida qualifies for additional federal disaster aid beyond the pre-landfall emergency declaration already approved by FEMA.DeSantis said he planned to visit storm-damaged areas in the Panhandle later Saturday, including parts of Okaloosa County, to assess conditions and meet with local officials."We were ready for the worst," DeSantis said. "We'll get everything back up and running and let people go on with their lives as soon as possible."

Julie Wallace Thomas of Delray Beach has been part of the WPTV First Alert Weather Spotters program since it began and a recent visit to the WPTV newsroom gave her a new appreciation for the role she plays.WATCH BELOW:I connected with Thomas and gave her a tour of the station to learn more about what brought her to the team.During the visit, Thomas learned that Weather Spotters have direct communication with the weather service and that their observations actively help the weather service do its job. Her passion for weather stretches back to her childhood."I've always loved the weather ever since a kid in science class when they're teaching us about the different kinds of clouds," Thomas said. Deputies digging through a rain-soaked backyard in Martin County heard the cries of kittens buried up to 3 feet underground, leading to the rescue of two animals while two others were found dead, the sheriff revealed Friday. During a news conference, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek provided new details about the arrest of 36-year-old Alba Chavez, who is accused of killing two kittens and burying two others alive at a mobile home park in Hobe Sound. According to the sheriff's office, deputies responded to the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park on Thursday night after several minors inside the home called 911 to report that Chavez had allegedly killed two kittens Monday, placed them in the trash and later buried them in the backyard. The children, who feared for the safety of three remaining kittens, attempted to protect them by locking them inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday night. Budensiek said that when the children returned home, they discovered the bedroom door had been forced open and the kittens were missing. The children then called law enforcement to report the incident. When deputies arrived, Chavez was standing in the roadway and reportedly admitted to killing the two kittens. While speaking with deputies, Chavez said she believed the kittens had demons, described them as ugly and said she did not want black or brown cats inside the home. Chavez then led deputies to the backyard, where the kittens had allegedly been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. See also: Hurricane Isaias strengthens into major Category 3 storm near Florida Panhandle As deputies dug through the backyard, they heard cries coming from underground. Two kittens were recovered alive, while the two kittens Chavez allegedly killed Monday were found dead. A fifth kitten remains missing despite repeated searches of the property. Budensiek said the two surviving kittens were immediately taken to an emergency veterinary facility, where they were being treated for dehydration. The sheriff said veterinarians were also concerned about possible injuries caused by a lack of oxygen while the kittens were buried. Despite being rescued, the kittens could still die from their injuries. Chavez was arrested and charged with four counts of animal torture involving pain, serious injury or death, according to the sheriff's office. The four charges correspond to the two kittens found dead and the two rescued alive. The sheriff said Chavez was being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and also had an immigration hold. Investigators have not determined exactly how the first two kittens died. The sheriff said Chavez initially cooperated with deputies and led them to the burial site but later stopped answering questions about how the animals were killed. Authorities also have not determined her motive. Budensiek said deputies had previously responded to calls involving Chavez's mental health but had received no prior animal cruelty complaints at the residence. Additional charges could be filed if the fifth kitten is found dead, according to the sheriff. Following the incident, the Florida Department of Children and Families became involved, and the children were later released to their father, who lives locally. Officials said resources were available to help the children cope with what happened.

The Soup Kitchen in Boynton Beach is seeing a surge in demand, with need up about 25% as residents struggle with rising gas prices, medical bills, and other monthly expenses.Marlene Mejia, CEO and executive director of The Soup Kitchen, said the need is increasing."I would say it's about 25% higher need," she said.People are telling the kitchen that tough times are getting tougher."They're telling us that the gas prices are killing them, that medication and the bills that they have to pay at the end of the month, it's not enough," Mejia said. Yolanda Marcellus was among the dozens of people standing in a long line and walking through The Soup Kitchen for food."I just come here. They have good food every day. James Talarico has been absent from the campaign trail over the past 12 days as the Texas Senate race enters a critical stretch, prompting Republicans to open a new line of attack on the Democratic nominee.At a campaign rally in San Antonio Wednesday, Texas attorney general and GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton led the crowd in a chant about his opponent’s whereabouts.“Where is James Talarico?” Paxton prompted the crowd to ask.Paxton’s campaign has also drawn attention to the topic in social media posts in recent days, and President Donald Trump has jumped into the debate on Truth Social, describing Talarico as “MISSING IN ACTION.”Talarico’s campaign said the Texas Democrat has been getting over being sick.“James looks forward to being back out this weekend after recovering from the flu,” said JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico’s campaign, on Thursday. “It’s been 83 days since James challenged Ken Paxton to come out of hiding and answer Texans’ question in a debate, which even President Trump called on him to do last night. Ball is in Paxton’s court.”RELATED STORY | Trump faces hecklers while making high-profile Texas campaign pushTalarico revealed his flu diagnosis September 30 when he spoke virtually with the United States Hispanic Business Council, an event he was supposed to attend in person.“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico told the crowd gathered in Edinburg, Texas, over video conference. “I’m running a fever, and I’m at my most contagious right now, and I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail and so I want to keep everybody safe.”Talarico’s last public appearance in Texas took place on September 26 when he held a press conference on suspending the federal gas and diesel tax and ending the war with Iran.“This is the kind of immediate action we need to provide Texans some relief at the pump in the middle of this affordability crisis,” Talarico said at a gas station in Carrollton, Texas.After publication of this story, a Talarico campaign source noted the candidate attended a private fundraiser in New York City featuring actor Robert De Niro on September 28.During this time stretch, Paxton has made several campaign trail stops, including speaking at Trump’s rally in San Antonio on Wednesday. Paxton has spoken at four other campaign events, including a conversation with the USHBC, and was on hand at the president’s event in Denton. At that stop, Trump said he didn’t even know Paxton was there and jokingly called him a “pain in the ass.”In a Truth Social post Wednesday night, Trump questioned Talarico’s whereabouts and called for a debate between the two Senate candidates.“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able,” Trump wrote.The Paxton campaign did not respond to a request for comment about Trump’s proposed debate between the two candidates. Talarico has challenged Paxton to several debates, including one on Fox News, but the window for debates is narrowing with Election Day less than four weeks away.Talarico will appear at a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media on Wednesday, October 14 in Fort Worth, Texas. The media outlets have also extended a town hall invitation to Paxton.The two candidates are locked in a tight battle for the US Senate seat currently occupied by GOP Sen. John Cornyn, who Paxton defeated in a bruising Republican primary in May.RELATED STORY | Republicans fret as Talarico bombards airwaves and Paxton awaits Trump team’s cashA recent New York Times/Siena University poll showed Talarico with a six-point lead over Paxton.The close nature of the race in a state Trump won by double digits in 2024 is causing anxiety for Republicans, who are flooding the Texas airwaves in the final stretch. (CBS12) The American Red Cross assisted five people, including two children, following two house fires in Palm Beach and St. According to a news release issued Friday, Oct. 9, Red Cross Disaster Action Team volunteers responded to both fires within a 12-hour period. The fires occurred at two locations: ● Riviera Beach: A home on West 28th Street, where one adult received assistance. Lucie: A home on Northwest Carmelite Street, where four people, including two adults and two children, received assistance. Red Cross volunteers provided emergency financial assistance, health and mental health services, and recovery support to those affected. The organization’s Disaster Action Team consists of specially trained volunteers who respond to emergencies 24 hours a day, seven days a week, providing resources and support to families impacted by disasters. All Red Cross disaster assistance is provided free of charge through donations. The Red Cross did not release information about what caused either fire or the extent of the damage. Residents interested in supporting disaster relief efforts can donate at redcross.org/donate. Information about home fire safety and preparedness is available at redcross.org/homefires.

Lucie County courtroom found former Fort Pierce city manager Nicholas Mimms not guilty of bid tampering and guilty of official misconduct on Thursday, Oct. Sentencing is scheduled for December 11. Jurors deliberated in the trial of former Fort Pierce city manager Nicholas Mimms, who is accused of bid tampering and official misconduct involving city-owned properties and a nonprofit linked to his niece. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position as city manager to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit co-founded by his niece, secure a lease to develop two city-owned properties. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The defense denied Mimms did anything wrong, arguing that he and his niece, Caleta Scott, have a distant relationship. The prosecution argued there was a conflict of interest, saying Scott was granted special treatment because of her relationship with Mimms. Deliberations began late yesterday after closing arguments from both sides and resumed at 9 a.m. Jurors have broken for lunch but have not yet reached a verdict. An explosion inside a Port St. Lucie home destroyed almost everything owned by a family of four. Lucie County Fire District, the initial call came in at 1:24 p.m. for a fire at a home in the 100 block of Carmelite Street Friday afternoon. Neighbors called 911 after noticing the home was on fire. "I looked, and there was all kinds of smoke going through the yard," said neighbor Rob Roadman. "I was outside in the backyard, and then I see very heavy smoke," said Marina Cheong, who lives a few doors down. Cheong said she ran toward the home to help but was stopped by the explosion. "And then there was explosion, very loud, loud explosion, and debris started flying everywhere," she said. "I heard a huge explosion. At first, I thought maybe it's a transformer or something, but it was much, much, much louder than that," Roadman said. Neighbors said the man who lives in the home told them he had been cooking when a grease fire started in the garage, where the propane tank was located. The explosion sent the propane tank flying out of the garage, across the street, and into the garage of a neighbor's home. "I thought it was an air raid. It was not a casual thing. My house shook," Roadman said. "I thought that the whole house had exploded. It was very loud," Cheong added. Roadman said he spoke to the man shortly after the explosion. "I asked the dad if he was OK, and he goes, 'Yeah.' But you could tell he wasn't. Who wouldn't be?" Roadman said. The man was briefly hospitalized but returned to the house a few hours later to join family and friends in going through the debris to see what could be salvaged. They said there wasn’t much left. However, a family member told WPBF 25 News that they consider themselves lucky that nobody was seriously injured. She said the family has a strong community and a strong church to help them persevere. MARTY public transit service in Martin County came to an abrupt halt Thursday, leaving residents who depend on the transit system without regular transportation as county officials scramble to find a solution. Martin County officials told WPBF's Caleb Califano they were given no advance warning that service would stop Thursday. According to the county, MARTY’s operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract. The company says rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs have led to significant financial losses since it began operating the service in July 2025. Despite negotiations with the county, the two sides were unable to reach an agreement. County officials said the company provided a 180-day notice to terminate its contract approximately two weeks ago. However, Thursday morning, Martin County Transit LLC notified the county that it was immediately discontinuing service. The sudden shutdown has left residents who rely on MARTY to get around the county without their regular transportation option. George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said officials are now exploring both short-term and long-term solutions to restore service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It’s just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It’s going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." In the meantime, county officials say they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents impacted by the shutdown. The county has not provided a timeline for when MARTY operations could resume. Officials say they will continue posting updates on social media and will notify residents as soon as a solution is reached. Riders react Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for the bus in Stuart on Thursday, but it never came. She was unaware that the MARTY bus had been suspended until WPBF's Jasimine Yasmine Julmisse informed her. Chaclain says she's been riding the bus for years and that it's a staple for many members of the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don’t have a driver’s license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It’s very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don’t drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don’t drive, and we go everywhere to shop." The sudden suspension of service impacted riders including Steven Godell, who said he was on his bicycle Thursday because he didn't see the MARTY bus come Thursday morning. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Hurricane Isaias became the first hurricane to make direct landfall in the United States in more than two years when it came ashore late Friday as a Category 2 storm.By Saturday morning, Isaias had weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved across Alabama. While no longer a hurricane, its remnants were expected to bring heavy rain and gusty winds across parts of the South on Saturday before spreading into the Great Lakes and Northeast on Sunday.As of 6 a.m. CT Saturday, more than 900,000 customers were without power. More than 400,000 outages were reported in Florida's Panhandle, while Alabama reported more than 320,000 outages and Georgia reported about 120,000.The storm also caused significant wind damage in the Pensacola area, where a hotel lost its roof as Isaias made landfall.RELATED STORY | Study: Super-sized El Niño could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by FebruaryThe hurricane pushed storm surge onto coastal roadways across the Florida Panhandle.No deaths or injuries associated with the storm had been reported as of early Saturday morning.Isaias marked a departure from what had been one of the quietest Atlantic hurricane seasons in recent years. It was also the first hurricane to form in the Atlantic basin in 2026.Forecasters had predicted a below-normal season because of a strong El Niño, which typically creates upper-level winds that can disrupt tropical cyclone development.Although Isaias was the ninth named storm of the season, all previous systems had peaked at tropical-storm strength.The same upper-level winds that limited hurricane activity this year also contributed to Isaias weakening before landfall. The storm maintained Category 3 strength for much of Friday before being downgraded to a Category 2 hurricane just hours before reaching the coast.RELATED STORY | El Nino keeps Atlantic hurricane season historically calmBehind Isaias, the National Hurricane Center said it was not tracking any additional systems. The Atlantic hurricane season typically peaks around Sept. 10 and begins to wind down by mid-October before ending Nov. 30.Since 2013, only two hurricanes have made U.S. The most recent was Hurricane Nicole in 2022.

Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Florida Panhandle near Destin on Friday night with 105 mph winds.Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a news conference a short time later that power outages spanned from Pensacola to Panama City to Tallahassee.Watch update from Governor DeSantis:"(Power) crews will be mobilizing once the storm passes, and they will be hard at work as soon as it's safe to do so and they have the light to be able to operate," DeSantis said Friday night.Ahead of the storm, the governor on Friday warned that storm surge would impact a large stretch of the Gulf Coast, extending well beyond the immediate landfall area.While residents in areas such as Destin and neighboring communities faced the greatest surge threat, officials said coastal flooding could reach as far east as Apalachicola and potentially affect portions of the Tampa Bay region because of the storm's large size."You're going to see water across the entire region of the Florida Panhandle," DeSantis said.Officials cautioned that hazards will not be limited to communities near the eye of the storm. Tornadoes could develop far from the center, including in Tallahassee and other parts of North Florida, while heavy rain bands are expected to continue through Saturday."There will be impacts from this far, far outside the National Hurricane Center's cone," DeSantis said.State Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said dangerous conditions had already begun for some communities."The time to prepare has passed," Perdue said. "For many of you, if you're there, it's time to shelter in place and stay safe."Evacuation orders remain in effect across multiple Panhandle counties, particularly for barrier islands, low-lying areas and RV parks. Officials urged residents who are still able to leave evacuation zones to do so immediately.State crews have staged significant resources ahead of the storm, including more than 1,400 generators, fuel, food and water supplies and thousands of emergency responders.The state has also positioned 16,000 utility workers to begin restoring power once conditions are safe."We do anticipate extensive power outages here," DeSantis said.The Florida National Guard has mobilized 5,000 service members and more than 1,300 high-water vehicles. Search-and-rescue teams, helicopters, boats and other specialized equipment have been pre-positioned throughout the region.More than 6,000 linemen and restoration personnel are standing by to support power restoration efforts following Hurricane Isaias.The Florida State Guard has deployed nearly 400 soldiers to assist with pre-landfall and post-landfall efforts, including preliminary damage assessments, route clearance, points of distribution operations, and air, ground, and maritime search and rescue support.Transportation disruptions are also expected. Officials said Florida Highway Patrol may close portions of Interstate 10 and other major roadways and bridges once winds exceed 39 mph. Multiple airports, including Pensacola International Airport and airports in Destin and Fort Walton Beach, have announced closures.State officials also warned residents not to drive through flooded roadways and to stay away from downed power lines after the storm passes.Attorney General James Uthmeier warned that looting and price gouging during the emergency will be aggressively prosecuted."Don't even try it," Uthmeier said. "During emergencies, there's heightened penalties."Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia encouraged residents to document their homes and belongings before the storm by taking photos and videos and storing records digitally for insurance purposes.Officials emphasized that residents should be prepared to be self-sufficient for at least 72 hours after the storm and reminded generator users never to operate generators inside homes because of the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.As Isaias approaches, emergency managers are asking Floridians to follow local evacuation orders, monitor weather alerts and avoid travel once conditions deteriorate."We're ready for it," DeSantis said. "We just got to get through it."Currently, 27 Florida counties are under a state of emergency.RELATED LINKS:Who to contact during power outagesList of shelter locationsSchool Closures around the Big BendLatest list on sandbag locationsWant to see more local news?

Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

Two women in Fort Pierce are accused of animal neglect after a dog died on their watch, according to arrest reports from the Fort Pierce Police Department . FPPD says that Samya Shanice Bryant, 25, and Danielle Amanda Potts, 28, were arrested on Oct. 2 in connection with the neglect and death of a dog at Pine Creek Apartments. Officers found the dog days before on Sept. 29 lying outside an apartment. The dog was severely underweight with visible ribs, infected sores on his paws, and no food or water. Bryant told the officers that the dog was hers, and that he had been sick for weeks after another man allegedly poured boiling water on him. FPPD says that both women who each lived in the apartment had control of the dog but did not get him veterinary treatment. See also: Trump touts West Palm golf club as possible Camp David-style retreat for future presidents Animal Control took the dog for emergency care, but the dog had to be euthanized on Oct. 2 because of injuries, infections and organ failure. Both Bryant and Potts were arrested and are being charged with aggravated animal cruelty and confining/impounding an animal without sufficient food or water.

The Florida Department of Health in Indian River County has issued a 60-day rabies alert after a bat captured near the Sonrise Apartments tested positive for the virus.Health officials said the bat was captured in the Sonrise Apartments area off Sonrise Place in Fellsmere on Sept. Anyone who may have had contact with or touched the bat is urged to contact the Department of Health in Indian River County at 772-794-7472.WATCH BELOW: Rabid bat prompts alert in Indian River CountyThe alert comes as health officials monitor rabies activity among wild animals in the area and warn residents that the disease is present in the local wildlife population.Rabies is a viral disease that affects the nervous system of mammals, including humans. Health officials say people who are exposed to rabies can protect themselves by seeking prompt medical treatment after exposure.The Department of Health is reminding residents and visitors to avoid contact with wild animals such as raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats and coyotes, which are more likely to carry the disease.Officials also recommend taking several precautions to reduce the risk of exposure, including:Keeping pets vaccinated against rabiesSupervising pets and keeping them on a leashSecuring livestock on private propertyAvoiding contact with wild or stray animals, including catsNot feeding or handling wildlifePreventing bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildingsAnyone bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Indian River County at 772-794-7472.If a pet or livestock animal is bitten by another animal, owners should contact a veterinarian immediately and notify Indian River County Animal Control at 772-226-4799.Visit the Florida Department of Health website for more information on rabies.

A 17-year-old died after being shot near a boat ramp in Indian River County late Friday night, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.Deputies responded to reports of a juvenile shot in the 3700 block of County Road 512, near Garcia's Boat Ramp, at approximately 11:24 p.m.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampThe sheriff's office said deputies found the 17-year-old and began lifesaving measures until Indian River County Fire Rescue arrived.The teen was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center before being flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center, where he died from his injuries.Detectives with the sheriff's office's Criminal Investigations Division and crime scene personnel are processing the scene and interviewing multiple witnesses.Investigators said the shooting appears to be an isolated incident and there is no threat to the public.No information about a possible suspect or what led up to the shooting has been released.Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.The investigation remains active.

No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen"We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said.The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp."The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case."The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries.The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampFlowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed."There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene.During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School.The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance."When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there."Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger."Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead."The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention."The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups."With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office."Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said.He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place.The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward."I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that."Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

Governor Ron DeSantis was in Indian River County on Monday to celebrate the completion of a new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road, a $100 million project state officials say will improve traffic flow, emergency response times and freight movement.The interchange, which opened about a year ahead of schedule, marks the first new I-95 interchange built in Indian River County in nearly 50 years.DeSantis said the project will provide a new direct connection to I-95 while easing congestion at nearby interchanges at Indrio Road and State Road 60."This is going to bring a new critical connection to I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit," DeSantis said.According to the governor, drivers using Oslo Road to access I-95 can expect travel times to be cut roughly in half. State transportation officials also project traffic along the corridor will continue growing through 2045.DeSantis said the project is expected to have significant public safety benefits as well. The state estimates emergency response times in the area could be reduced by as much as 56%, allowing first responders to reach crashes and other emergencies more quickly."This will ultimately save some lives because time is of the essence in some of these situations," DeSantis said.Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue said improved access to I-95 for first responders was one of the project's most important features."Every single second counts when it comes to saving lives, and this is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially," Perdue said.The new interchange is also expected to improve freight movement for businesses in southern Indian River County by providing a more direct route to the interstate for trucks and commercial traffic.State officials said the project was accelerated through Florida's Moving Florida Forward initiative, a transportation funding program launched by the DeSantis administration to speed up major road projects across the state.Perdue said FDOT worked with contractors through a "voluntary acceleration" program that rewarded construction teams for finding ways to complete projects more quickly. As a result, the Oslo Road interchange was finished approximately 400 days ahead of schedule.In addition to transportation improvements, FDOT acquired land near the interchange to establish a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. State officials said the site will serve as the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida, allowing protected tortoises to be moved while infrastructure projects continue.The Oslo Road interchange is part of nearly $1 billion in planned transportation investments across Florida's Treasure Coast region."This interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future," DeSantis said.

Parking in Vero Beach is free, but overstaying your welcome is about to cost significantly more.Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to double most parking fines starting Oct. WATCH BELOW: Vero Beach doubling parking fines Fines for timed parking violations will increase from $20 to $40, while other miscellaneous infractions will rise from $30 to $60.Handicap violations will remain the same at $200 per violation.The city said the increases are the first since 2011.Vero Beach police sent a letter to the City Council in August requesting the rate increase, saying it would "encourage motorists to abide by the regulations."Lt. Brian Kerensky said the goal is to keep parking spaces moving and bring more foot traffic to the city."We have to kind of sometimes give them an incentive to move," Kerensky said. "It creates turnover and can benefit from that."For residents like Wendy Gage, who regularly parks along Beachland Boulevard, the change hits close to home."The free parking is great...when it's free," Gage said. "We've been tagged multiple times for not moving it after two hours." Neighbor Corey Wapnick said the increase is not fair because there are not enough spaces available to move to."There's only so much parking, and it's usually on a beach day here, it's very [full] there's enough cars here that it's almost impossible," Wapnick said.Eugene Billero, who parks outside his real estate office, said a permit system could offer a better long-term solution for business owners and employees who need to park close to work."You could do a permit for the month and charge X amount of dollars, and they're going to get their money anyway," Billero said.With property taxes on the ballot this November, Mayor John Cotugno said the timing of the fine increase was deliberate."I think we did it at the opportune time," Cotugno said. "Some of those courtesies that you paid, especially from a fee standpoint, we had to readdress." Cotugno left the door open to exploring permit options and other long-term parking solutions."I think that's something that possibly should come up for discussion," Cotugno said.The new fines take effect Oct.

Lucie teenager has earned the highest honor awarded by the Boys & Girls Clubs of America.Enrique Rosario Liz has been named the organization’s 2026-27 National Youth of the Year, a recognition that celebrates outstanding leadership, academic achievement and service to others.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie teen named National Youth of the YearThe honor marks the latest milestone in a remarkable year for Rosario Liz. In April, he was named Florida Youth of the Year. WPTV reporter Tyler Hatfield helped deliver the exciting news during a special presentation.Now, Rosario Liz is being recognized on the national stage as a standout young leader who exemplifies dedication in the classroom, strong personal values and a commitment to serving his community.The National Youth of the Year program honors exceptional teens from Boys & Girls Clubs across the country who inspire others through their leadership, character and achievements.Rosario Liz's journey from local club member to national honoree highlights the impact of mentorship, perseverance and community involvement.

Fort Pierce City Clerk Linda Cox took the stand Wednesday as the trial of former city manager Nick Mimms entered its third day.Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct.WATCH BELOW: Fort Pierce city clerk takes the stand in Nick Mimms trialThe jury heard first from Cox, who testified about a series of city meetings shown in video evidence by the state. One meeting, held in October 2019, showed a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presenting a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for two vacant lots along Avenue D.The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Among the organization's board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee.According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared as surplus, even though it had been designated for use as parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater.Prosecutors questioned Cox about whether the city board relied on Mimms for accurate information."Does the board also expect the defendant to give them correct information?" Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said."Yes," Cox said."Do they rely on the defendant to give correct information?" Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said."Yes," Cox said.Attorneys also showed footage from future meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, where the board voted to declare the lots surplus and later announced that the Lincoln Park Young Professionals had won the bid.WATCH BELOW: Opening statements begin in trial of former city managerUnder cross-examination, the defense argued it was no secret that Mimms' niece was among those seeking to obtain the property. Defense attorney Donald Murrell questioned Cox about whether she had raised any concerns at the time."You knew they were city employees," Murrell said."I did," Cox said."And it bothered you that they were doing this?" Murrell said."I thought it was a little odd," Cox said."You didn't raise any objections," Murrell said."I did not," Cox said.Murrell also questioned Cox about the city attorney's presence at the meetings."He saw the same slideshow you saw, the same PowerPoint?" Murrell said."Yes," Cox said."He didn't raise any objections or concerns, did he?" Murrell said."Not at the meeting," Cox said."Ever?" Murrell said."I wouldn't know. Not that I know of," Cox said.The trial is expected to last at least a week.

WPTV learned there are 13 license plate reader cameras in St. Lucie County that don't have permits, according to county staff.Wednesday, Sept. 30, was the deadline the Florida Department of Transportation gave municipalities to remove the license plate readers from state-controlled roads.WATCH BELOW: Unpermitted license plate readers found in St. Lucie CountyNow WPTV is pressing city leaders about why the cameras are there, who they belong to, and what is happening to the cameras now.On Thursday, WPTV spoke to Ricky Mathura, who works at a gas station off Orange Avenue and 25th Street in Fort Pierce, where one of the unpermitted license plate readers was found."I don't know why it's there," said Mathura. Lucie County Communications Director Erick Gill said they're trying to find that out."We don't know who they belong to," Gill said. "They were just put in our right-of-way."The county says there's 53 permitted license plate readers on their right-of-ways and gave WPTV a list with all the locations of the unpermitted license plate readers staff found.RELATED: FDOT revokes permits for automated license plate readers"We were surprised, you know, that were that many out there,” said Gill.The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office told WPTV they claimed three of them but are working to find out why they weren't permitted.Gill said county staff is actively working to identify the owners of the other readers and taped notices on the cameras for the owners to take them down within 30 days.Once the 30 days are up, Gill said staff will remove the readers safely."We'll begin the process of either removing them if we feel like we can safely remove them without damaging the equipment and endangering our staff, or at least covering up so the cameras can't capture any surveillance," Gill said.

Lucie County Fire District's attorney resigned minutes after a heated special fire board meeting Wednesday, as fallout from an alleged hazing investigation continues to threaten district leadership.Attorney Kim Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. She is the subject of several complaints stemming from allegations that she and Fire Chief Jeff Lee improperly handled internal investigations.WATCH BELOW: St. Lucie County fire district attorney resigns amid hazing falloutNearly a dozen people spoke at the special meeting, which was called to address what board members described as a major gap in district policy: who investigates complaints against the district's own leaders."Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said. "They — being those positions— have essentially been able to investigate themselves." Those contract positions include the Fire Chief, District Attorney, Clerk Treasurer and Medical Director.The issue stems from an alleged hazing incident we reported on earlier this year. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent." Months before the incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson then filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation — and their subsequent termination — were part of a broader pattern of retaliation."That's not a good process," Fowler said. The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy. Meanwhile, firefighters are casting ballots in a no-confidence vote regarding Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message." Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process. He told Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey: "I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," adding he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Per Sabol's resignation, Lee said it's a "sad day." "She's been a tremendous attorney for the district," Lee said of Sabol. As for the vote of no confidence, Lee said he didn't have much to say until it's over with "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee told Hussey. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line." Tension inside district headquarters was evident throughout Wednesday's meeting."This system is so broken," one attendee said."Everybody is fed up. They want action," said retired fire captain Mike Jenkins.As the union's legal fight to reinstate the three firefighters continues, calls are growing for the fire board to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work. When asked whether the board has that authority, Fowler said, "I think we might actually," adding, "The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back. I'm going to ask the board in a week from now — what do we want to do? What's the process?" Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote. There is no word yet on when results will be released.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. But hey, change comes, and you got to go with the change,” Smith said.The organization said seniors will continue to have access to meals, activities, social opportunities and transportation once services move to the Port St.

Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie property tax rate going downSince 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services."Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," said Mayor Shannon M. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

By: Scott Sutton Posted and last updated MARTIN COUNTY, Fla. — A barn that caught fire in Martin County on Thursday caused large flames and sent black smoke into the air that could be seen for miles. The fire occurred on a ranch in the 13000 block of Southwest Allapattah Road near Indiantown at about 5:30 p.m., according to a social media post by Martin County Fire Rescue. No horses or residents were injured. One firefighter was taken to the hospital with minor overexertion symptoms but was released Friday morning, Fire Rescue said. Officials said the barn and about six vehicles were a "total loss," including a side-by-side and a small front-loader tractor. Southwest Allapattah Road is back open after earlier closures. The State Fire Marshal is investigating the cause of the blaze.

By: Samantha Roesler Posted and last updated MARTIN COUNTY, Fla. — A deadly crash Monday morning shut down lanes of Interstate 95 North in Martin County, with closures lasting over seven hours. The crash occurred at around 3:40 a.m. at mile marker 91, involving a Honda Civic and a Hino box truck. According to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP), both vehicles were traveling northbound when the Honda Civic collided with the rear of the box truck in the outside lane. The sedan lodged underneath the back of the tractor-trailer and engulfed in flames. Despite lifesaving efforts, the Honda driver was pronounced deceased on scene. The driver of the box truck was not injured in the crash. FHP has not identified the deceased driver. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed until just before 11 a.m.

Despite regulations requiring it, an air traffic controller failed to tell the pilots of an Amazon cargo plane about the potential for strong tail winds as they landed in Miami, careening off the runway and killing five people last month, according to a preliminary report Thursday from the National Transportation Safety Board.Just four minutes before clearing the plane for landing, an air traffic controller had provided a wind advisory to a different flight, noting gusts of up to 25 mph from the south. But the controller “did not issue information about the wind” to the pilots of the Amazon cargo plane, the report said.According to federal regulations, “both wind direction and velocity were required to be stated when authorizing use of a runway when a tail wind component exists,” the NTSB report said.The preliminary report did not list a cause of the crash. The ongoing investigation could take more than a year to complete.The airplane, carrying packages of contact lenses for Amazon, came in fast after a flight from Puerto Rico and barreled roughly 1,200 feet past the end of the runway at Miami International Airport on Sept. It smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes. Five people who were in the van died. Two others in the van sustained serious injuries, as did the driver of a car that was hit by the plane. The two pilots had minor injuries.RELATED STORY | 5 dead after Amazon cargo aircraft overruns runway in Miami, striking multiple vehiclesTail winds can make landing a plane harderExperts said it appears the weather played at least some role in the accident. Tail winds can make it harder to slow a plane and push it past an ideal landing spot on a runway.“When you’ve got winds like that, it is your responsibility as a controller to issue that to a pilot, especially on landing and especially when you have gusts,” said Tony Mello, a former Federal Aviation Administration official who oversaw air traffic control services in the central U.S.Landing with a gusting tail wind “requires more concentration on the part of the pilot” but is not impossible, said former NTSB member John Goglia.Failing to share the wind conditions “was a significant omission but, in and of itself, would not have caused a crash,” Goglia said. “Every crash is a chain of events. That’s just one event.”The plane had little runway left when it touched downA summary of cockpit voice recordings previously released by the NTSB said one of the pilots repeatedly warned his counterpart that they were going too fast as they approached for landing and after touchdown. But the fellow pilot never gave “a consistent verbal response” to the warnings, the NTSB said. The two pilots had flown together for the first time just earlier that day, according to the preliminary NTSB report.The cockpit audio recordings also captured a series of automated warnings from the plane about the speed of descent and the approaching terrain.When it touched down, the plane was traveling at 184 mph and was already about three-quarters of a mile past the start of the runway, the NTSB report said.The pilots may have tried too late to abort the landing. Data from the plane show its wheel brakes were applied, then released as the engines throttled to “go-around” thrust values before the brakes again were applied with about 415 feet of runway remaining.The plane ran off the pavement while still traveling at 130 mph, then struck some airport equipment and the cleaning crew’s van before crashing through a perimeter fence, hitting a car on a public road and coming to rest with its nose in a parking lot fence, the preliminary report said.RELATED STORY | Amazon suspends use of 21 Air, the cargo carrier whose plane careened off Miami runway and killed 5Plane's operator says it is focused on safetyAfter the crash, Amazon suspended its partnership with 21 Air, which operated the plane. The North Carolina carrier had flown packages for Amazon since 2024. The Boeing 767 that crashed was 32 years old and originally built to carry passengers. It was converted to a cargo plane in June 2016, the preliminary NTSB report said.The plane’s operator, 21 Air, said in a written statement Thursday that safety is “a core focus” of its organization.“We are reviewing the information in the NTSB preliminary report closely, alongside our own internal safety and operational protocols, and we will take all appropriate action to improve our safety based on the facts as they are established,” the company said.The Miami crash came less than a year after a UPS cargo plane crashed at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway. That crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.

A 10th-grade student and another person were killed after a multi-vehicle crash involving a school bus happened Monday morning in Central Florida. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news conference that the crash happened around 6 a.m., when a Chevrolet Malibu veered over the center line of a road and hit a Winter Haven High School bus traveling in the opposite direction. There were 37 students on board. The impact of the collision ripped the tire off the bus and caused it to crash head-on into an oncoming Jeep before rolling over off the side of Winter Haven Road. The sheriff said the driver of the Jeep had died. At least five other people involved in the crash were hospitalized, according to authorities. "It was a horrible crash," Judd said. "It was a terrible, tragic morning. We had a beautiful 10th grade girl lose her life."The city of Winter Haven is located about 51 miles east of Tampa and 47 miles southwest of Orlando.This story was originally published by Leilyn Torres and Anthony Romano with the Scripps News Group in Tampa.

Florida's minimum wage increased on Sept. This is the fourth and last of the annual scheduled hikes from a 2020 approved referendum. The minimum wage for tipped workers also rose to $11.98.WATCH BELOW: Florida minimum wage hits $15/hour "Minimum wage is going up but so is everything going up," a young man named Neff told me Wednesday on Clematis Street. "You have to have another hustle, or another job so that way you can create more revenue and income for your family; $15 an hour is not enough." Starting in 2027, the state minimum wage will be adjusted for inflation annually. In South Florida, where the cost of living is high, a $25-an-hour wage is considered "livable," according to a Massachusetts Institute of Technology report. The higher wage can also mean more pressure on small businesses. "I have to pass that cost on to the consumer; I cannot absorb a 7% increase in labor," John Ries, owner of Hot Pie Pizza in West Palm Beach, said. Ries says that, as a policy, he pays his employees above the minimum wage, and he admits inflation on all aspects of his business make it tough to keep prices down.

Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Florida Panhandle near Destin on Friday night with 105 mph winds.Gov. Tornadoes could develop far from the center, including in Tallahassee and other parts of North Florida, while heavy rain bands are expected to continue through Saturday."There will be impacts from this far, far outside the National Hurricane Center's cone," DeSantis said.State Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said dangerous conditions had already begun for some communities."The time to prepare has passed," Perdue said. "For many of you, if you're there, it's time to shelter in place and stay safe."Evacuation orders remain in effect across multiple Panhandle counties, particularly for barrier islands, low-lying areas and RV parks. Officials urged residents who are still able to leave evacuation zones to do so immediately.State crews have staged significant resources ahead of the storm, including more than 1,400 generators, fuel, food and water supplies and thousands of emergency responders.The state has also positioned 16,000 utility workers to begin restoring power once conditions are safe."We do anticipate extensive power outages here," DeSantis said.The Florida National Guard has mobilized 5,000 service members and more than 1,300 high-water vehicles. Search-and-rescue teams, helicopters, boats and other specialized equipment have been pre-positioned throughout the region.More than 6,000 linemen and restoration personnel are standing by to support power restoration efforts following Hurricane Isaias.The Florida State Guard has deployed nearly 400 soldiers to assist with pre-landfall and post-landfall efforts, including preliminary damage assessments, route clearance, points of distribution operations, and air, ground, and maritime search and rescue support.Transportation disruptions are also expected. Officials said Florida Highway Patrol may close portions of Interstate 10 and other major roadways and bridges once winds exceed 39 mph. Multiple airports, including Pensacola International Airport and airports in Destin and Fort Walton Beach, have announced closures.State officials also warned residents not to drive through flooded roadways and to stay away from downed power lines after the storm passes.Attorney General James Uthmeier warned that looting and price gouging during the emergency will be aggressively prosecuted."Don't even try it," Uthmeier said. "During emergencies, there's heightened penalties."Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia encouraged residents to document their homes and belongings before the storm by taking photos and videos and storing records digitally for insurance purposes.Officials emphasized that residents should be prepared to be self-sufficient for at least 72 hours after the storm and reminded generator users never to operate generators inside homes because of the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.As Isaias approaches, emergency managers are asking Floridians to follow local evacuation orders, monitor weather alerts and avoid travel once conditions deteriorate."We're ready for it," DeSantis said. "We just got to get through it."Currently, 27 Florida counties are under a state of emergency.RELATED LINKS:Who to contact during power outagesList of shelter locationsSchool Closures around the Big BendLatest list on sandbag locationsWant to see more local news?

Ron DeSantis signed an executive order Tuesday issuing a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of Hurricane Isaias.The counties included are: Baker, Bay, Calhoun, Columbia, Dixie, Escambia, Franklin, Gadsden, Gilchrist, Gulf, Hamilton, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Lafayette, Leon, Liberty, Madison, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Suwannee, Taylor, Walton, Wakulla, and Washington.TRACKING THE TROPICS: Hurricane Center | Hurricane Guide“Today, I signed an Executive Order issuing a state of emergency ahead of potential impacts from Tropical Depression 9.
