President Donald Trump, facing protesters and a poor political climate, fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday night in a bid to stave off sweeping Democratic victories in the nation's most populous red state.But Trump's remarks were not focused solely on Paxton.Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump also pledged to award retired baseball star Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, restated his support for the death penalty for drug dealers and clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are “a small price to pay” for the war.“You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles,” Trump said. “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our country.”The president's message was interrupted repeatedly by protesters, including by one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police.Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.“He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”Texas has become an unexpected battleground for RepublicansThe Republican Party did not plan to devote so much money and manpower to Texas this midterm season.Texas is the nation’s most populous reliably Republican state, where Trump won in 2024 by almost 14 percentage points. But with Election Day less than a month away, Trump’s poor approval ratings, the Iran war and soaring gas prices have threatened Republicans in virtually every state.Wednesday’s appearance marked Trump’s third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far.RELATED STORY | Obama is set to get more involved in the midterms, starting with an appearance alongside Abdul El-SayedIn a sign of Trump’s poor standing, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott did not attend the evening rally. A three-term Republican governor who won reelection in 2022 by roughly 11 percentage points, even Abbott has been caught in the turbulent national currents.He’s locked in a competitive reelection race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.Instead of appearing with Trump, Abbott was scheduled to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on the governor’s absence.“For years, Greg Abbott has never been shy about embracing Donald Trump, calling Trump a ‘great friend’ and championing his agenda every step of the way,” said Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long. “But now, as Texas families get crushed by record-high prices driven by Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran, suddenly Greg Abbott has somewhere else to be.”Trump focuses on helping the Senate candidate he endorsed in GOP primaryWhile the race for governor has drawn a sudden influx of cash from Democrats, the state’s U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention as Democrats fight for the chamber’s majority. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, but candidate James Talarico’s fundraising, Trump’s low approval rating and nagging concerns about Paxton’s character have put the race squarely in play.Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tour“He was tough and he was with us all the way,” Trump said of Paxton, whom he endorsed in the state's GOP primary over incumbent Sen. “He’s a fantastic man.”Trump made no mention of the recently leaked recording of Paxton lamenting the war in Iran and rising fuel prices, while also complaining his campaign was being run by operatives in Washington.He repeatedly criticized Talarico, including on the death penalty, a point that would appeal to many conservatives in the state that leads the nation in executions.Trump restated his support for the death penalty for “large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer,” while acknowledging that Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad.The president approved the method of execution earlier this week and suggested that Talarico opposes it.The Talarico campaign did not immediately respond when asked about the candidate’s position on Hasan’s scheduled execution.Paxton, invited onstage near the end of the rally, heaped praise on Trump, who stood behind him: “I am so grateful that you’re here."Trump makes a big announcement, but not about the Senate raceWhile Trump promoted Paxton briefly at the beginning of his remarks, he spent almost as much time later talking up Clemens, the retired Red Sox and Yankees pitcher who has been denied a spot in Major League Baseball's Hall of Fame due to his alleged involvement with performance-enhancing drugs.Trump brought him onstage and said he'd be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, which is the highest civilian honor — and, Trump said, “a step up” from the Hall of Fame.Clemens said he was stunned by the honor.“This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” he said, standing alongside Trump. “And to get it from this man, this president. You talking about a winner? That’s a winner right there.”

A group of potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates is heading to Denver days after the midterms to discuss the party’s future, in one of the party’s first major gatherings following the election.Attendees will include former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former US Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel, as well as Sens. A deadly school bus crash in Polk County is raising new questions about how students are protected inside Florida school buses and why state law still falls short of federal safety recommendations.One student, a 10th grader on her way to Winter Haven High School, was killed Monday morning when a school bus carrying 39 people was involved in a crash. The circumstances surrounding the crash remain under investigation, including what happened outside the bus and what took place inside it.Watch report from Katie Lagrone"We have one fatality of a beautiful high school girl. It's just heartbreaking," Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news briefing.Investigators have not released details about how many students were wearing seat belts, what type of restraints were in use, or whether the belts played a role in the outcome of the crash.Florida law requires school buses built since 2001 to be equipped with seat belts. However, students are not required to wear them, and state law does not require the more protective lap-and-shoulder belts recommended by federal safety investigators. Instead, many Florida school buses continue to use standard lap belts.The federal recommendation followed an investigation by investigative reporter Katie LaGrone more than a decade ago.In 2012, a St. Lucie County school bus collided with a semi-truck, killing 9-year-old Aaron Beauchamp. Aaron was wearing the bus's standard lap belt at the time of the crash.Several years later, investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) examined that crash and studied how different types of seat belts affect student safety.The agency's testing showed significant differences between standard lap belts and lap-and-shoulder restraints. Simulations demonstrated that lap-and-shoulder belts provide greater protection by better controlling a passenger's movement during a crash.As a result, the NTSB recommended that all school buses nationwide be equipped with lap-and-shoulder belts.The NTSB specifically urged Florida to change state law to require lap-and-shoulder belts on new large school buses.That recommendation was never adopted.Today, it remains unclear how many Florida school districts have voluntarily upgraded their fleets to meet the federal recommendation.In St. Lucie County, nearly 15 years after Aaron's death, about 20% of district school buses still use only standard lap belts.In Polk County, a district spokesperson confirmed on Monday that all the district’s school buses are equipped with just lap belts.The latest crash has renewed questions about whether stronger seat belt requirements could better protect students who are traveling to and from school on a school bus.Despite the concerns raised by this tragedy, transportation safety experts continue to emphasize that deadly school bus crashes are extremely rare, and that school buses remain the safest form of transportation for students traveling to and from school.For families in Polk County and across Florida, the crash could prompt renewed scrutiny of whether the state's school bus safety standards should be updated to reflect federal recommendations."No one will ever understand how heavy this weighs on our hearts," Polk County Schools Superintendent Fred Heid said following the crash.

An explosion inside a Port St. Lucie home destroyed almost everything owned by a family of four. Lucie County Fire District, the initial call came in at 1:24 p.m. for a fire at a home in the 100 block of Carmelite Street Friday afternoon. Neighbors called 911 after noticing the home was on fire. "I looked, and there was all kinds of smoke going through the yard," said neighbor Rob Roadman. "I was outside in the backyard, and then I see very heavy smoke," said Marina Cheong, who lives a few doors down. Cheong said she ran toward the home to help but was stopped by the explosion. "And then there was explosion, very loud, loud explosion, and debris started flying everywhere," she said. "I heard a huge explosion. At first, I thought maybe it's a transformer or something, but it was much, much, much louder than that," Roadman said. Neighbors said the man who lives in the home told them he had been cooking when a grease fire started in the garage, where the propane tank was located. The explosion sent the propane tank flying out of the garage, across the street, and into the garage of a neighbor's home. "I thought it was an air raid. It was not a casual thing. "I asked the dad if he was OK, and he goes, 'Yeah.' But you could tell he wasn't. Who wouldn't be?" Roadman said. The man was briefly hospitalized but returned to the house a few hours later to join family and friends in going through the debris to see what could be salvaged. They said there wasn’t much left. A Martin County employee is being praised for her quick actions after rescuing a girl from drowning at Bob Graham Beach in Stuart on Thursday afternoon. Offenbach, who has years of lifeguard training, said her instincts kicked in when she saw three girls struggling in the water. "I took off my clothes, grabbed the board, and started paddling," she said. "I immediately went into rescue mode." Authorities said one of the girls was choking on water, and the beach had no lifeguards on duty. Offenbach rushed in to help, using a surfboard to stabilize the girl. "Once she was on the board, she was kind of limp. Her body wasn't doing anything else," Offenbach said. Offenbach said the girl's forehead felt cold, prompting her to rush the child to the nearest lifeguard stand down the road. The girl was then taken to the hospital with minor drowning injuries. Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

Martin County's contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders.Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution."Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," Martin County officials said in the statement.Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, "we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.”Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown."We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system," Martin County Transit said.In an afternoon press conference, county leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday, according to the county.Jim Gordon, Martin County's Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming."We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today," Gordon said.For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily."[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food," Joe said.Joe said he received no notice before service was cut."No warning at all, nothing, zero." Joe said.Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe."I've had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can't feel my feet, so I'm not getting anywhere," Joe said.Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company's handling of the shutdown lacked transparency."I don't think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans," Argudo said.George Stokus, Martin County's Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service."We're doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can," George Stokus said.In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services.The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need.Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it."Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it," Houwaart-Diez said.Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption."This is important for people to be able to get to the doctor's, to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there," Houwaart-Diez said.Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program's response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding.Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. A Martin County woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she buried several cats alive in her yard at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office arrested 37-year-old Alba Luz Chavez on four counts of aggravated animal cruelty after investigators said they discovered two live kittens and two dead kittens buried on a property in Hobe Sound. Deputies were called to the home Thursday night for what family members described as a mental health crisis. Family members told deputies Chavez believed the cats were demons and had killed several animals earlier in the week. According to the affidavit, deputies learned that Chavez had allegedly told residents of the home she killed two kittens on Monday, Oct. Three juveniles living at the residence told deputies Chavez had appeared to be experiencing a mental health episode for most of the week. The juveniles said they locked three surviving kittens inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday evening. When they returned around 6 p.m., they discovered Chavez had forced her way into the room and the kittens were gone. Investigators said Chavez initially refused to tell family members where the animals were. However, while speaking with deputies, Chavez allegedly said, “If you want the cats, you will need gloves, a red bag and a shovel,” and directed them to an area on the property. Deputies began digging and found two live kittens buried underground inside plastic Publix bags, according to the affidavit. Investigators later uncovered two deceased kittens that appeared to be in the early stages of decomposition. Detectives searched for a third missing kitten but were unable to locate it. During an interview, Chavez told investigators she had been cleaning her house and referred to the cats as “very ugly,” according to the affidavit. Investigators wrote that Chavez also made statements indicating she did not want black cats and suggested kittens of different colors “had different fates.” The affidavit states Chavez later began singing instead of answering additional questions. The two surviving kittens were taken to a pet emergency center for treatment. A veterinarian told investigators the kittens were about three weeks old and very weak. The veterinarian said it was too early to determine whether a lack of oxygen while confined inside the plastic bags had caused brain damage or other medical complications. The two deceased kittens are expected to undergo necropsies to determine their exact causes of death. Chavez was arrested and booked into the Martin County Jail on four felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty and is being held without bond.

The WPTV Town Hall on Amendment 3 has led to some more questions about the referendum facing voters on raising the Homestead Exemption to lower property taxes and reduce revenue for cities and counties.One question attendees posed was why are our property taxes increasing every year.Palm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo talked about it at the town hall, saying inflation is a big factor.“This is a national problem not even a Florida problem, its not a Palm Beach County problem," Abruzzo said. "What it costs for traffic arms where our lights go: 700 thousand five years ago. Now, they’re at 1.5 million. The cost of labor, asphalt, concrete, the things we actually use in government is just skyrocketing, so we have to budget appropriately to be able to afford the things we need to buy," Another email asked why municipal workers get raises every three years."They’re not coming in and saying we want to take a pay cut," said West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James, talking about negotiating with police, fire and labor unions."Every three years we’re looking at increases, and we also want to pay our employees so they’re competitive with the market otherwise we lose them to the private sector and other cities and they’re living in a city where affordability is an issue," James said.Another question asked about the impact on apartment living.“Over 50% of the occupied housing units in West Palm Beach are renters," the mayor said."There is no dispute that the rents are going to increase, because those are not homesteaders and so the taxes will go up on those units and the landlords will pass those expenses on to the renters," he said.

Brandee Anthony, known as the Vero Beach Mermaid, is an elite level PADI dive instructor, who teaches people of all ages to become mermaids — offering experiences that range from glamorous mermaid makeovers and beach photoshoots to poolside swimming lessons."I was a professional live streamer a long time ago, so I thought it would be really cool to take all my viewers underwater, but how can I make that interesting and magical?" Anthony said.That curiosity grew into a deep and lasting passion."That was 10 years ago and I'm a little in love with mermaiding for sure," Anthony said.The experience begins with a mermaid makeover, starting inside Anthony's custom fantasy closet — brimming with tropical-inspired tails, tops and accessories created just for mermaid gear."We're going to start with a mermaid makeover, which is one of my favorite parts," Anthony said. "Kate, so this is your magical closet."The closet features silicone tails that each weigh about 30 to 35 pounds. Accessories are on hand to complete every look."Mermaid crowns and armbands and embellishments, kind of the final touches to help people really feel like they have a full ensemble," Anthony said.Armbands come in a variety of styles, including options with a vibrant teal accent."We have a few options if you want to go with armbands. We have these, these are super cute and they have that nice teal," Anthony said.Anthony even offered a personalized recommendation while I was browsing through the options."I think with what you are wearing I would probably wear this one," she said.Browsing the closet felt like being a kid in a candy store — wanting more of everything. Anthony said that reaction is exactly the goal."That is exactly what you should feel like," she said. "So, we'll pick out a tail, a top, some accessories, and a crown, and then we'll head over to the beach."After settling on a look — including a tail Anthony called a "wind trader" and a stunning leafy sea dragon design — I was feeling the mermaid vibe and ready for the beach.Anthony, a professional photographer for 15 years, combines breathtaking backdrops and elaborate costumes to create magic where whimsy meets the water. Once suited up, I made my way toward the water, making my mermaid marks in the sand along the way."Like a sea turtle you are going to migrate towards the ocean," she said. "And then your going to turn toward me put your fin over here — we call it a fluke."Anthony walked me through the first poses on the shoreline."The seated is the easiest first pose — you can kind of just look at the ocean and relax and let the wind take your hair," she said. "Look out towards the beach — a little water love."Next, I headed poolside for a basic mermaiding class.Anthony caters to every client's ability, even those who are a little cautious about the experience."Once people get in a tail and they find their groove, it turns into a bunch of people just playing in a pool," she said.People come to the experience for all kinds of reasons."I've had people come to me for fun and some for deeper reasons," Anthony said."Coming on a retreat or take a course really did change their lives — or changed the trajectory of their lives. I've turned a few people into pro mermaids," Anthony said.In the pool, Anthony was ready to teach me how to mermaid — stripping back the glam and focusing on the fundamentals."So now you've had the photoshoot and the glam and now we are going to strip it back and just have some fun swimming as a mermaid," Anthony said.She walked me through every step of the movement."So you can flex your foot up towards the top of the water and then push it down…and just do that a few times….you can feel the resistance of the water and that's what propels you," Anthony said. "I'm going to have you back float in the tail — I'll kind of help you float there."The lesson even included a dive completely underwater."3.2.1. breathe out — we dive down and then pop up," Anthony said. "That was so good — that was fun — and that's how we shoot video underwater."For Anthony, the joy of mermaiding as an adult goes far beyond the water itself. "I think that's what mermaiding as an adult feels like is you don't have to act like a kid but you can be an adult that plays," she said. "And that's where it can be fun or it can be more — some people just want to feel empowered. Or good in their skin and they do a photo shoot or a bucket list thing."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Hurricane Isaias continues to churn toward the Florida Panhandle, packing winds of 120 mph midday Friday as a Category 3 storm.Florida officials urged residents across the Panhandle to complete preparations immediately on Friday as Isaias moved toward an expected late-night landfall along Florida's northwest coast.During an afternoon news conference, Gov. Ron DeSantis said the hurricane is expected to make landfall around 11 p.m. and could bring sustained winds of 115 to 120 mph, dangerous storm surge, widespread power outages, flooding and tornadoes."We think it's going to land potentially as a Category 3," DeSantis said. "This is really your last chance. If you don't do it right now, then you're probably going to be running into hazardous conditions later tonight."The governor warned that storm surge would impact a large stretch of the Gulf Coast, extending well beyond the immediate landfall area.While residents in areas such as Destin and neighboring communities face the greatest surge threat, officials said coastal flooding could reach as far east as Apalachicola and potentially affect portions of the Tampa Bay region because of the storm's large size."You're going to see water across the entire region of the Florida Panhandle," DeSantis said.Officials cautioned that hazards will not be limited to communities near the eye of the storm. Tornadoes could develop far from the center, including in Tallahassee and other parts of North Florida, while heavy rain bands are expected to continue through Saturday."There will be impacts from this far, far outside the National Hurricane Center's cone," DeSantis said.State Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said dangerous conditions had already begun for some communities."The time to prepare has passed," Perdue said. "For many of you, if you're there, it's time to shelter in place and stay safe."Evacuation orders remain in effect across multiple Panhandle counties, particularly for barrier islands, low-lying areas and RV parks. Officials urged residents who are still able to leave evacuation zones to do so immediately.State crews have staged significant resources ahead of the storm, including more than 1,400 generators, fuel, food and water supplies and thousands of emergency responders.The state has also positioned 16,000 utility workers to begin restoring power once conditions are safe."We do anticipate extensive power outages here," DeSantis said.The Florida National Guard has mobilized 5,000 service members and more than 1,300 high-water vehicles. Search-and-rescue teams, helicopters, boats and other specialized equipment have been pre-positioned throughout the region.More than 6,000 linemen and restoration personnel are standing by to support power restoration efforts following Hurricane Isaias.The Florida State Guard has deployed nearly 400 soldiers to assist with pre-landfall and post-landfall efforts, including preliminary damage assessments, route clearance, points of distribution operations, and air, ground, and maritime search and rescue support.Transportation disruptions are also expected. Officials said Florida Highway Patrol may close portions of Interstate 10 and other major roadways and bridges once winds exceed 39 mph. Multiple airports, including Pensacola International Airport and airports in Destin and Fort Walton Beach, have announced closures.State officials also warned residents not to drive through flooded roadways and to stay away from downed power lines after the storm passes.Attorney General James Uthmeier warned that looting and price gouging during the emergency will be aggressively prosecuted."Don't even try it," Uthmeier said. "During emergencies, there's heightened penalties."Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia encouraged residents to document their homes and belongings before the storm by taking photos and videos and storing records digitally for insurance purposes.Officials emphasized that residents should be prepared to be self-sufficient for at least 72 hours after the storm and reminded generator users never to operate generators inside homes because of the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.As Isaias approaches, emergency managers are asking Floridians to follow local evacuation orders, monitor weather alerts, and avoid travel once conditions deteriorate."We're ready for it," DeSantis said. "We just got to get through it."Currently, 27 Florida counties are under a state of emergency.

A Hobe Sound woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she killed and buried several kittens because she believed they were possessed by demons.The Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) arrested 36-year-old Alba Chavez on Thursday after responding to reports of animal cruelty at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayAccording to MCSO Sheriff John Budensiek, three youths living in the home called 911 after they discovered several of their kittens had disappeared. The children told deputies they believed Chavez had killed two kittens earlier in the week and were worried about the remaining animals.Budensiek said the children had attempted to protect three kittens by locking them inside a bedroom before going out to dinner Thursday evening. When they returned, they found the door had been forced open and the kittens were gone."When deputies arrived, she admitted she thought the kittens had demons and said she didn't want black cats or brown cats in her residence," Budensiek said during a Friday news conference.Investigators said Chavez told deputies she had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them into the trash, later removed them and buried them in the backyard.Deputies said she then led them to a burial site behind the home and told them to bring gloves, shovels and bags if they wanted to find the missing kittens.Despite heavy rain and lightning, deputies began digging in the backyard."As they were digging, they could hear cries from the kittens," Budensiek said.Deputies rescued two kittens that were buried alive inside a plastic Publix bag. The two kittens killed earlier in the week were also recovered deceased from the burial site.A fifth kitten remains missing. Budensiek said deputies and investigators extensively searched the backyard and mobile home but have not located the animal.The two surviving kittens were rushed to a veterinary emergency clinic, where they are being treated for dehydration and monitored for potential long-term effects from being buried underground."If they survive, they'll eventually be taken to the Humane Society and go through the adoption process," Budensiek said.Chavez was arrested on four counts of animal cruelty involving torture, inflicting pain, serious injury or death to an animal. Authorities said additional charges could follow if the missing kitten is found dead.The arrest marks at least the third animal cruelty or neglect case in Martin County since late July. Asked whether the trend surprised him, Sheriff John Budensiek said reports of violence against animals often mirror broader societal problems."We've seen society kind of going downward and we see more violence with interactions with humans and then that translates into animals," Budensiek said. "In fact, a lot of times it starts with animals and then moves over to humans. So unfortunately, based on the trends and societal trends that we're seeing, it does not surprise me, but when we see it, it's extremely alarming.Budensiek said Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and is also subject to an immigration hold. The sheriff identified her as a Venezuelan national who he said is in the United States illegally.According to the sheriff, deputies had previously responded to the home for incidents involving Chavez's mental health but had never received complaints related to animal cruelty.When asked about Chavez's motive, Budensiek said investigators still aren't certain whether mental health issues played a role."She said they were demonic. She said she didn't want those cats in her house," Budensiek said. "I don't know whether it was a mental health issue or she just didn't like the cats."Budensiek said the three youths who reported the incident were emotional but showed courage by contacting law enforcement."I applaud them for reaching out, calling 911 and letting us save the two kittens," he said.The children were taken into the custody of the Florida Department of Children and Families before being turned over to their father, who lives locally, according to investigators.Other adult cats found at the home were examined by animal services and determined to be healthy.Budensiek called the case "extremely alarming" and praised the responding deputies for their efforts to rescue the buried animals."We're going to aggressively pursue criminal charges on her to make sure she pays for the damage that she did to these animals," he said.

A Martin County woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she buried several cats alive in her yard at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office arrested 37-year-old Alba Luz Chavez on four counts of aggravated animal cruelty after investigators said they discovered two live kittens and two dead kittens buried on a property in Hobe Sound. Deputies were called to the home Thursday night for what family members described as a mental health crisis. Family members told deputies Chavez believed the cats were demons and had killed several animals earlier in the week. According to the affidavit, deputies learned that Chavez had allegedly told residents of the home she killed two kittens on Monday, Oct. Three juveniles living at the residence told deputies Chavez had appeared to be experiencing a mental health episode for most of the week. The juveniles said they locked three surviving kittens inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday evening. When they returned around 6 p.m., they discovered Chavez had forced her way into the room and the kittens were gone. Investigators said Chavez initially refused to tell family members where the animals were. However, while speaking with deputies, Chavez allegedly said, “If you want the cats, you will need gloves, a red bag and a shovel,” and directed them to an area on the property. Deputies began digging and found two live kittens buried underground inside plastic Publix bags, according to the affidavit. Investigators later uncovered two deceased kittens that appeared to be in the early stages of decomposition. Detectives searched for a third missing kitten but were unable to locate it. During an interview, Chavez told investigators she had been cleaning her house and referred to the cats as “very ugly,” according to the affidavit. Investigators wrote that Chavez also made statements indicating she did not want black cats and suggested kittens of different colors “had different fates.” The affidavit states Chavez later began singing instead of answering additional questions. The two surviving kittens were taken to a pet emergency center for treatment. A veterinarian told investigators the kittens were about three weeks old and very weak. The veterinarian said it was too early to determine whether a lack of oxygen while confined inside the plastic bags had caused brain damage or other medical complications. The two deceased kittens are expected to undergo necropsies to determine their exact causes of death. Chavez was arrested and booked into the Martin County Jail on four felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty and is being held without bond.

Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest. “I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue,” Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. “That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast.” The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. “I think we’d be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don’t have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we’re at least prepared just in case these two firms aren’t available, non-responsive,” Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. “I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don’t want to delay any further.” The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30 , when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district’s own contract employees. “Since this district’s inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves,” Fowler said during that meeting. “They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves.” Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director. The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result. Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone. “It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun,” Hutchinson said. “We’re all still friends,” Boudrias said. “Us and the victims, there was no ill intent.” The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled. Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter. “That’s not a good process,” Fowler previously told WPTV. Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny. “I’m glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue,” Lee said, adding that he “welcomes any investigation from any agency.” Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a “sad day” and saying she had been a “tremendous attorney for the district.” Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee. “It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district,” Fowler previously said. “So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that’s a pretty impactful message.” Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote. “We’ll see what the men and women decide,” Lee said. “I came up on the labor side; I’ve always fought for our men and women on the line.” The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out. “I think we might actually,” Fowler said at the time. Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

Martin County’s contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution. “Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders,” Martin County officials said in the statement. Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, “we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.” Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown. “We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system,” Martin County Transit said. In an afternoon press conference, county leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday, according to the county. Jim Gordon, Martin County’s Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming. “We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today,” Gordon said. For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily. “[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food,” Joe said. Joe said he received no notice before service was cut. “No warning at all, nothing, zero.” Joe said. Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe. “I’ve had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can’t feel my feet, so I’m not getting anywhere,” Joe said. Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company’s handling of the shutdown lacked transparency. “I don’t think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans,” Argudo said. George Stokus, Martin County’s Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service. “We’re doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can,” George Stokus said. In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services. The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it. “Transportation isn’t a luxury for the people who depend on it. It’s how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn’t disappear with it,” Houwaart-Diez said. Region Martin County Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption. “This is important for people to be able to get to the doctor’s, to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there,” Houwaart-Diez said. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program’s response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY’s fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county’s transit website . A first of its kind program is coming to Boynton Beach High School. The school is launching the Palm Beach County School District’s only choice Sports Academy, giving students a chance to turn their passion for sports into a career— opportunities that go far beyond the field.WATCH BELOW: Principal Dr. Moody Fuller speaks with WPTV's Todd Wilson how the academy came to fruition “The idea came from just taking a look of our student interests,” Principal Dr. Moody Fuller said.That closer look revealed something important, Boynton Beach students have a real passion for sports and the Boynton Beach Sports Academy was born."What we wanted to do was teach them that sports are more than just being an athlete,” Fuller said.Fuller said the world of sports extends far beyond the playing field, with countless career opportunities. The academy gives students six different pathways to explore those careers."The six areas that we are focusing on, number one is going to be performance, culinary, hospitality, nutrition," he said. "We’re going to offer e-sports, photography, and broadcasting. A Hobe Sound woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she killed and buried several kittens because she believed they were possessed by demons.The Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) arrested 36-year-old Alba Chavez on Thursday after responding to reports of animal cruelty at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayAccording to MCSO Sheriff John Budensiek, three youths living in the home called 911 after they discovered several of their kittens had disappeared. The children told deputies they believed Chavez had killed two kittens earlier in the week and were worried about the remaining animals.Budensiek said the children had attempted to protect three kittens by locking them inside a bedroom before going out to dinner Thursday evening. When they returned, they found the door had been forced open and the kittens were gone."When deputies arrived, she admitted she thought the kittens had demons and said she didn't want black cats or brown cats in her residence," Budensiek said during a Friday news conference.Investigators said Chavez told deputies she had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them into the trash, later removed them and buried them in the backyard.Deputies said she then led them to a burial site behind the home and told them to bring gloves, shovels and bags if they wanted to find the missing kittens.Despite heavy rain and lightning, deputies began digging in the backyard."As they were digging, they could hear cries from the kittens," Budensiek said.Deputies rescued two kittens that were buried alive inside a plastic Publix bag. The two kittens killed earlier in the week were also recovered deceased from the burial site.A fifth kitten remains missing. Budensiek said deputies and investigators extensively searched the backyard and mobile home but have not located the animal.The two surviving kittens were rushed to a veterinary emergency clinic, where they are being treated for dehydration and monitored for potential long-term effects from being buried underground."If they survive, they'll eventually be taken to the Humane Society and go through the adoption process," Budensiek said.Chavez was arrested on four counts of animal cruelty involving torture, inflicting pain, serious injury or death to an animal. Authorities said additional charges could follow if the missing kitten is found dead.The arrest marks at least the third animal cruelty or neglect case in Martin County since late July. Asked whether the trend surprised him, Sheriff John Budensiek said reports of violence against animals often mirror broader societal problems."We've seen society kind of going downward and we see more violence with interactions with humans and then that translates into animals," Budensiek said. "In fact, a lot of times it starts with animals and then moves over to humans. So unfortunately, based on the trends and societal trends that we're seeing, it does not surprise me, but when we see it, it's extremely alarming.Budensiek said Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and is also subject to an immigration hold. The sheriff identified her as a Venezuelan national who he said is in the United States illegally.According to the sheriff, deputies had previously responded to the home for incidents involving Chavez's mental health but had never received complaints related to animal cruelty.When asked about Chavez's motive, Budensiek said investigators still aren't certain whether mental health issues played a role."She said they were demonic. She said she didn't want those cats in her house," Budensiek said. "I don't know whether it was a mental health issue or she just didn't like the cats."Budensiek said the three youths who reported the incident were emotional but showed courage by contacting law enforcement."I applaud them for reaching out, calling 911 and letting us save the two kittens," he said.The children were taken into the custody of the Florida Department of Children and Families before being turned over to their father, who lives locally, according to investigators.Other adult cats found at the home were examined by animal services and determined to be healthy.Budensiek called the case "extremely alarming" and praised the responding deputies for their efforts to rescue the buried animals."We're going to aggressively pursue criminal charges on her to make sure she pays for the damage that she did to these animals," he said.

Family and friends gathered Wednesday night at Farm and Flame restaurant in Vero Beach to remember 17-year-old Sulliman Bah, who was shot and killed last Friday during a teen party at the Garcia boat ramp in Fellsmere. Bah, known to many as Sully, had just finished his shift at the restaurant before going to the large gathering of more than 100 teens. A couple hundred people packed the restaurant, sharing stories about Bah’s kindness and the impact he had on their lives. Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described him as a loving son, brother and kind person. He was just joyful, happy all the time, Godfrey said. Godfrey said her son was the kind of person who made everyone around him feel like they mattered. "We've walked down the street, any stranger he saw, he'd greet them, 'How you doing today?' she said. "That was very important to him that he made people feel good, feel seen." Godfrey said Bah cared deeply about making people feel seen. Friends remembered him as funny and caring and kind. See also: Boynton Beach teen reunites with first responders after surviving lightning strike "He was never mean to nobody, and I hate that this happened to him because he doesn't deserve this," one friend said through tears. "Sully was a kind soul." Investigators say several fights broke out at the teen party before an 18-year-old who knew Bah shot him. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers has said he believes the shooting was in self-defense. "Getting that call on a random Friday night that one of my best friends had just gotten shot...was probably one of the hardest things I've had to go through," another friend said. One of eight children, Bah's mother said he was just a credit and a half away from graduating high school and had big plans for the future. "He wanted to travel," Godfrey said. "He wanted to spend time in a big city. wanted to be an entrepreneur." As she begins to cope with the unimaginable loss of her son, Godfrey said she wants answers about what happened that night and accountability for his death. "His life is not being valued enough, and things are not being looked at seriously enough," she said. "I believe that my son was murdered, and I believe that the shooter needs to be punished for that." The sheriff’s office says the investigation remains open. No arrests have been made, and the State Attorney will decide whether charges will be filed.

A Martin County woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she buried several cats alive in her yard at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested 37-year-old Alba Luz Chavez on four counts of aggravated animal cruelty after investigators said they discovered two live kittens and two dead kittens buried on a property in Hobe Sound.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayDeputies were called to the home Thursday night for what family members described as a mental health crisis. Family members told deputies Chavez believed the cats were demons and had killed several animals earlier in the week.According to the affidavit, deputies learned that Chavez had allegedly told residents of the home she killed two kittens on Monday, Oct. Three juveniles living at the residence told deputies Chavez had appeared to be experiencing a mental health episode for most of the week.The juveniles said they locked three surviving kittens inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday evening. When they returned around 6 p.m., they discovered Chavez had forced her way into the room and the kittens were gone.Investigators said Chavez initially refused to tell family members where the animals were. However, while speaking with deputies, Chavez allegedly said, "If you want the cats, you will need gloves, a red bag and a shovel," and directed them to an area on the property.Deputies began digging and found two live kittens buried underground inside plastic Publix bags, according to the affidavit. Investigators later uncovered two deceased kittens that appeared to be in the early stages of decomposition.Detectives searched for a third missing kitten but were unable to locate it.During an interview, Chavez told investigators she had been cleaning her house and referred to the cats as "very ugly," according to the affidavit. Investigators wrote that Chavez also made statements indicating she did not want black cats and suggested kittens of different colors "had different fates." The affidavit states Chavez later began singing instead of answering additional questions. The two surviving kittens were taken to a pet emergency center for treatment. A veterinarian told investigators the kittens were about three weeks old and very weak. The veterinarian said it was too early to determine whether a lack of oxygen while confined inside the plastic bags had caused brain damage or other medical complications. The two deceased kittens are expected to undergo necropsies to determine their exact causes of death.Chavez was arrested and booked into the Martin County Jail on four felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty and is being held without bond.

Florida Panthers forward Brad Marchand sustained a left leg injury in the second period of their 2-1 win against the Los Angeles Kings on Tuesday night.Marchand was not on the bench for the third period, and coach Paul Maurice did not have an update on his condition afterward."We'll get him looked at probably Thursday," Maurice said.Marchand was hurt after taking a stick to the face from Kings defenseman Brandt Clarke with 52.6 seconds remaining, which caused him to twist around and collide with the right post before his left leg bent back in an awkward way.Marchand was down on the ice for several minutes being examined by an athletic trainer before teammates Brady Tkachuk and Niko Mikkola helped him to the bench, with Marchand unable to put any weight on his leg. He was then helped back to the dressing room.Marchand, 38, is in his third season with the Panthers after playing his first 16 seasons with the Boston Bruins. He was traded to Florida in March 2025 and helped them win their second straight Stanley Cup that season.But the defense of those titles last season was scuttled by injuries, and now the Panthers have seen two key players injured on their four-game West Coast trip to start this season.Aleksander Barkov, one of the top two-way centers in hockey, hurt his left leg in an overtime loss at San Jose on Thursday. Maurice said earlier Tuesday that Barkov is expected to miss six to eight weeks and will not require surgery."I mean, we have a little experience with Sasha going down, so it wasn't quite as shocking the second time it happened," Maurice said. "We know we have good depth. And there's a threshold for any team, a number of injuries you just can't survive, and we passed that early last year. So, real good resolve here. The tank is deep right now. We had a big summer off, so we're strong."Clarke received a four-minute double-minor penalty. It was the second penalty of the game for Clarke, who was called for interference against Eetu Luostarinen earlier in the period. Luostarinen was shaken up on a cross-check from Clarke, sustaining a stinger, but was able to return to the game.

Florida center Aleksander Barkov is expected to miss six to eight weeks with a left leg injury and will not require surgery, Panthers coach Paul Maurice said Tuesday.Barkov was hurt in the Panthers' overtime loss at San Jose on Thursday. It appeared his left knee — not the knee that needed to be surgically rebuilt last year — buckled on the play, and the Finnish captain immediately left the ice in obvious discomfort.WATCH: Barkov won't need surgery, out 6-8 weeks, Panthers sayThe timetable would suggest that Barkov will probably be out somewhere between 20 and 25 games before he could return."That’s our best window," Maurice said. "Could be a little less, could be a little more. But we think six to eight (weeks) is the right rehab time."Florida plays at Los Angeles on Tuesday to end a season-opening four-game road trip. Maurice revealed the timetable after the Panthers' morning skate in advance of that game.The Panthers placed Barkov on long-term injured reserve over the weekend, after it became clear his absence would last longer than 10 games. The Panthers weighed multiple options on how to proceed and Barkov saw team doctors Monday before a final plan was agreed upon.Barkov was injured 20 minutes into the team’s first training camp practice for the 2025-26 season and missed the entire campaign, one of many injury issues that played a role in Florida going from a back-to-back Stanley Cup champion to a team that missed the playoffs.If there is a silver lining, it’s that Florida is well-versed in how to play without Barkov — who isn’t just the team captain, but is generally considered to be the team’s best player."If he hadn’t been injured last year we would have thought, ‘Gee, six to eight weeks is a long time,’" Maurice said. "I think last year was six to eight months, so we’re taking it."Over his most recent 10 seasons — excluding when he missed last season — Barkov had 722 points, 485 hits and 463 blocked shots. No other NHL player reached those numbers in all three categories over those years; Toronto’s Auston Matthews and Winnipeg’s Mark Scheifele were the only others with at least 700 points, 400 hits and 400 blocks in that span.And the Panthers were clearly breathing a sigh of relief knowing that he will be back this season."It's good for everything, maybe most importantly for Barky," Maurice said. "He’s our captain and we miss him and he feels it when he’s not around. So, he's probably the happiest of all of us."

While much of the attention surrounding Florida's November election has centered on Amendment 3, voters will also decide the fate of two other proposed constitutional amendments that could have significant impacts on the state's finances and agricultural industry.Amendment 1 would make major changes to Florida's Budget Stabilization Fund (Read the full text), often referred to as the state's "rainy day" fund.WATCH BELOW: Amendments 1 & 2: What to know about these lesser-known ballot measuresThe proposal would increase the maximum size of the fund from 10% to 25% of net general revenue collections. It would also require annual transfers of up to $750 million into the reserve fund and allow state lawmakers to use the money for certain critical needs.Supporters say the amendment would strengthen Florida's financial position during natural disasters, economic downturns and other emergencies by ensuring the state maintains a larger reserve of available funds.Opponents, however, argue that setting aside additional money in reserves could limit the state's ability to address immediate needs, including public services and infrastructure projects.Voters will also weigh Amendment 2, which focuses on tax relief for Florida's agriculture sector. (Read the full text)The measure would exempt agricultural equipment and certain farm-related property from property taxes. Supporters say the change would reduce costs for farmers, strengthen the agriculture industry and help preserve farming operations across the state.Those opposed to the amendment contend the tax exemptions could reduce revenue collected by local governments. Critics argue that loss of tax income could affect funding for public services and other community programs that rely on property tax dollars.Both amendments will appear on Florida's ballot this November, giving voters an opportunity to decide whether the proposed changes should be added to the state constitution. Amendment 3 increases the homestead exemption, for all non-school taxes, to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and adjusts for inflation thereafter. For this week's 'Where's Walter?', I visited Paris Ballet in Jupiter, where students are busy preparing for their upcoming performances of The Nutcracker. As soon as I walked into the studio, I knew I was stepping into a world that requires talent, discipline and plenty of hard work.Of course, I couldn't just stand on the sidelines.WATCH: The dancers and instructors invited me to join them on the floor, and after a quick warm-up, it was time to learn some ballet basics. Let's just say I quickly discovered there's a reason these students spend so much time training.I teamed up with several dancers, including Maya, who helped teach me a few of the moves from her role as the Sugar Plum Fairy. While she made everything look effortless, my legs had a different opinion.Then it was time to learn part of another routine with dancer Jay. He was kind enough to slow things down for me, but even at a beginner's pace, I realized just how much strength, balance and coordination ballet requires.I'll be honest: I'm no ballet dancer.But spending time with these young performers gave me a whole new appreciation for what they do. Every movement takes focus. Every routine requires practice. And every performance is the result of countless hours spent perfecting their craft.What impressed me most was the dedication of the students. Watching them rehearse, I saw firsthand the commitment and passion they bring to every class and every performance. Their talent shines on stage, but it's the hard work behind the scenes that truly makes it all possible.I also got a special look at preparations for this year's Nutcracker production. Seeing the dancers work together to bring the beloved holiday classic to life made me appreciate just how much effort goes into creating a ballet performance.While I don't think I'll be joining the cast anytime soon, I had an incredible time trying out a few moves and learning from some very talented young dancers.And after seeing their hard work up close, I can tell you one thing: The Nutcracker is in very good hands this holiday season.Tickets are on sale now for the Nutcracker on Nov. 21 at the Duncan Theater in Lake Worth Beach.

Videos released by the sheriff’s office show Bah opening the door of a white pickup truck, and the passenger inside the truck firing one shot, killing him. The vigil, held at the restaurant where Bah worked, began with a prayer, followed by friends sharing memories of the 17-year-old and praying for justice. "Sulli was a kind soul," said one friend, fighting to hold back tears. No arrests have been made in connection with Bah’s death. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the shooter claims he and Bah had fought before and that he fired in self-defense. Bah's mother said she doesn't think that's true. "I believe that my son was murdered. And I believe that the shooter needs to be punished for that," Godfrey said. Flowers said the investigation into the shooting is ongoing, and the state attorney will ultimately decide whether charges will be filed. Florida has reported nearly 500 dengue cases this year, including more than 250 infections acquired within the state, as new University of Florida research points to residential yards in Indian River County as a key place to understand mosquito-bite exposure. The Florida Department of Health’s latest weekly surveillance report , covering Sept. 20-26, lists 252 locally acquired dengue cases and 245 travel-associated cases statewide 497 total. The locally acquired cases were reported in Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas and Polk counties. Palm Beach County had one locally acquired case and 12 travel-associated cases; St. Lucie County had six travel-associated cases. No locally acquired dengue cases were listed for Indian River County in the report. The state’s locally acquired total includes 223 cases in Hillsborough County, the center of Florida’s outbreak. Health officials also reported 20 mosquito pools testing positive for dengue statewide. Nationally, the CDC’s most recent weekly provisional report counted 690 dengue cases among U.S. Florida accounted for 403 of those cases in the CDC reporting system, though the state’s more current surveillance report lists a higher total because reporting systems update on different schedules. Against that backdrop, researchers at UF/IFAS’ Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory in Vero Beach found a surprising mosquito pattern in suburban Indian River County. The team expected residential yards to be dominated by Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Instead, researchers found relatively high numbers of Aedes aegypti the yellow fever mosquito and one of the two species most closely associated with dengue transmission worldwide. The finding does not mean dengue is circulating in Indian River County . But it underscores why backyard mosquito control and personal bite prevention matter, researchers said. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf The first-of-its-kind study paired mosquito trapping at homes with a smartphone-based Bite Diary that let residents document when and where they were bitten. Researchers collected 3,788 female mosquitoes from 78 yards. Of 70 reported bites, nearly 93% happened outdoors and nearly 74% happened at home, according to the peer-reviewed study . The number of mosquitoes trapped in a yard was not associated with the number of bites residents reported. Instead, people who spent more time outside during the evening, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., reported more bites. Gardening and walking dogs were among activities commonly reported when bites occurred. Dengue is spread when an infected mosquito bites a person; it does not spread directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, rash, nausea and pain behind the eyes. People with symptoms should contact a health care provider, especially after travel to an area where dengue is common. Health officials urge residents to use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants when practical, repair window and door screens, and dump standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires and pool covers.

A proposed 150-unit assisted-living facility in Port St. Lucie is moving through the development process as nearby residents question whether enough is known about the environmental history of a neighboring property with petroleum contamination. The project, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF, is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development, along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard. The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component. Lucie City Council approved the project’s major site plan on Sept. Construction has not begun, and the developer must still submit construction plans for technical review and additional agency reviews. A group of residents opposes the project, citing concerns about the neighboring property’s contamination history and the potential implications for people who could eventually live at the facility. It’s not about what is being built there, resident David Lipps said, arguing that nearby businesses and other facilities could also be affected by environmental concerns. Resident Charlie D’Agata said residents have raised objections at City Council meetings for about two years. He questioned why a developer would be allowed to build near a property he described as contaminated. Residents say they have contacted outside organizations, including the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Health, in an effort to get answers about the site. An engineering letter provides some context for their concerns. In a letter discussing a March 2026 meeting with environmental officials about the neighboring property, BTEX Engineering said the proposed remediation approach should be changed because of concerns about surrounding properties, including the planned assisted-living facility. The letter said vapors would need to be captured during remediation. The environmental history of the neighboring property and the extent of any potential impact on surrounding land remain central questions for residents seeking more information. The city has approved the major site plan, but the project must clear additional steps before construction can begin. The developer is expected to submit construction plans for technical review, followed by reviews involving the South Florida Water Management District and other agencies. Residents say they want clearer answers about the neighboring property’s environmental history and how any potential risks would be addressed as the project advances.

A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school Wednesday morning, according to the Port St. Police said the crash occurred around 6 a.m. near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue. The student was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard and was near the edge of the roadway in an area marked by construction barrels when he was struck from behind. Investigators said the vehicle involved was a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. According to police, the driver initially believed he had struck a construction barrel and did not realize he had hit a person. The driver later made a U-turn at the next safe location, returned to the scene, activated his hazard lights and found the teenager unconscious on the side of the roadway. The driver has remained cooperative with investigators, and police said they have not observed any apparent signs of impairment. Authorities noted that the assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues. The student, identified only as a freshman at Treasure Coast High School, suffered life-threatening injuries and remains in critical condition, police said. The investigation is ongoing. Anyone who witnessed the crash or has dash-camera, surveillance or other video footage from the area around the time of the incident is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000. A former CIA agent convicted Tuesday of defrauding the government of $194 million reportedly used the majority of the money to acquire properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound. According to CBS Miami , court filings say 49-year-old David J. Rush of Virginia, a former high-ranking federal employee, directed $145 million to a holding company he controlled, and that $102 million was used to purchase four Florida properties: Two Palm Beach homes: $21.9 million and $27 million One Palm Beach parcel: $13.65 million One Hobe Sound parcel: $40 million Prosecutors allege Rush intended to eventually resell the properties for a profit. How the scheme unfolded According to the Department of Justice , Rush, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty Tuesday, Oct. 6, to wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia. According to prosecutors, Rush used his senior-level government position and "Top Secret" clearance to create fictitious government authorities and obtain federal money for his own benefit. Between November 2025 and March 2026, he directed approximately $145 million to a holding company established at his direction, according to court documents. The money was then used to purchase the properties. The Justice Department says Rush fraudulently obtained approximately $193.6 million in government funds. The South Florida real estate was only part of the alleged scheme. Gold bars Prosecutors say Rush separately created a fake "sensitive government activity" to justify acquiring hundreds of gold bars. On May 19, 2026, FBI agents searched Rush's Virginia home and recovered 298 gold bars, approximately $2.1 million in cash, €104,795, and numerous luxury watches. The gold had cost the government approximately $46 million, according to the Justice Department. Rush has agreed to forfeit the gold bars and cash, the Florida properties, luxury watches, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles as part of his plea agreement. What's next Rush is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. He faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison, along with possible restitution, forfeiture and a fine. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing. The Director of National Intelligence has also requested an investigation by the Intelligence Community's inspector general. The allegations and admissions are detailed in federal court documents filed as part of Rush's guilty plea.
