Isaias strengthened into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season late Wednesday as it surged towards the U.S. Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center said.Forecasters warned that it was on track to make landfall between the Mississippi coast and the Florida Panhandle late Friday or early Saturday and was expected to bring heavy rains and potentially flash flooding.The center of the cyclone was about 460 miles (745 kilometers) south-southwest of the Mississippi River, with maximum sustained winds around 75 mph (120 kph), according to an advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center.Isaias is developing more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season, tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane.According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity has been ab After Isaias (pronounced ees-ah-EE’-ahs, according to the hurricane center) became a tropical storm Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico, communities in its potential path worked quickly to prepare. Some Gulf oil wells paused production while governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties.Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that’s very familiar with major hurricanes.One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.As of Wednesday about 25% of the oil production in the region was temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated.With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.“I would characterize the oil market risk as moderate, but rising,” Burkhard said in an email.In Gulf Shores, Alabama, organizers canceled the National Shrimp Festival, which had been scheduled for Thursday through the weekend. The event drew an estimated 325,000 people last year. Gulf Shores and Orange Beach issued a statement encouraging people in low-lying areas to voluntarily evacuate.Gulf Shores resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground.Adams said she, her husband and two adult sons planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.“We’re having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don’t blow away,” Adams said. “It’s going to be noisy.”Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, saying on the social platform X that, “While I hope for minimal impacts, we must take preparations seriously.”Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The declaration activates the state's emergency management plan for hurricanes, allowing officials to deploy disaster responders and equipment. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”

Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room. As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life. Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said. Bah’s close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him. Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said. Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff’s office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense . No arrests have been made. Bah’s mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened. “I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.” During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives. Angela Sanders, one of Bah’s former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said. Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.” Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person. The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years. “He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration. Bah’s funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

Martin County's contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders.Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution."Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders." Martin County said."We understand the importance of MARTY services to our community and apologize for the disruption." Martin County said.Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, "we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.”Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown."We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system," Martin County Transit said.In an afternoon press conference County leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday.Jim Gordon, Martin County's Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming."We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today," Jim Gordon said.For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily."[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food," Joe said.Joe said he received no notice before service was cut."No warning at all, nothing, zero." Joe said.Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe."I've had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can't feel my feet, so I'm not getting anywhere," Joe said.Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company's handling of the shutdown lacked transparency."I don't think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans," Argudo said.George Stokus, Martin County's Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service."We're doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can," George Stokus said.In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services.The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need.Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it."Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it," Houwaart-Diez said.Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption."This is important for people to be able to get to the doctors to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there," Houwaart-Diez said.Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program's response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding.Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county's transit website.Residents seeking transportation assistance can call the United Way of Martin County at 772-283-4800 or click here to visit their website.Residents seeking paratransit transportation assistance can call 772-463-2822.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

MARTY public transit service in Martin County came to an abrupt halt Thursday, leaving residents who depend on the transit system without regular transportation as county officials scramble to find a solution. Martin County officials told WPBF's Caleb Califano they were given no advance warning that service would stop Thursday. According to the county, MARTY’s operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract. The company says rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs have led to significant financial losses since it began operating the service in July 2025. Despite negotiations with the county, the two sides were unable to reach an agreement. County officials said the company provided a 180-day notice to terminate its contract approximately two weeks ago. However, Thursday morning, Martin County Transit LLC notified the county that it was immediately discontinuing service. The sudden shutdown has left residents who rely on MARTY to get around the county without their regular transportation option. George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said officials are now exploring both short-term and long-term solutions to restore service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It’s just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It’s going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." In the meantime, county officials say they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents impacted by the shutdown. The county has not provided a timeline for when MARTY operations could resume. Officials say they will continue posting updates on social media and will notify residents as soon as a solution is reached. Riders react Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for the bus in Stuart on Thursday, but it never came. She was unaware that the MARTY bus had been suspended until WPBF's Jasimine Yasmine Julmisse informed her. Chaclain says she's been riding the bus for years and that it's a staple for many members of the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don’t have a driver’s license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It’s very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don’t drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don’t drive, and we go everywhere to shop." The sudden suspension of service impacted riders including Steven Godell, who said he was on his bicycle Thursday because he didn't see the MARTY bus come Thursday morning. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

For the first time, the family of a man set to be executed for the 1986 murder of an Indian River County sheriff's deputy is speaking publicly about their effort to save his life.William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for shooting and killing 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves' execution is scheduled for Oct. 20.Now, with less than two weeks remaining, Reaves' family is asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant him clemency and commute his death sentence to life in prison."I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him," Reaves' nephew, Meredith Farrington, told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey.Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of Reaves' crime or the pain Raczkowski's family has endured."I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," Farrington said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life."But Farrington added, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."That story stretches back to Sept. 23, 1986.According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County after he was unable to get a taxi.Raczkowski responded and was attempting to help Reaves call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name — a memorial to a life taken and a crime that continues to reverberate through two families four decades later."The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said.DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22, scheduling his execution for Oct. 20.Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison. Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," Farrington said.For the Raczkowski family, the case is about a life taken nearly 40 years ago.For Reaves' family, it is now about whether another life should end."But we're praying," Farrington said.Reaves has already lost his latest attempt to stop the execution in Indian River County court. He has appealed that decision to the Florida Supreme Court.For now, his execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency.If carried out, Reaves' execution will mark the 18th in Florida in 2026.

As Hurricane Isaias heads toward the Florida Panhandle, homeowners across the state will see hurricane deductibles go into effect on their insurance policies."The trigger in this case for most policies is a (hurricane) watch or (hurricane) warning anywhere in the state of Florida," Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said.WATCH BELOW: Isaias triggers Florida insurance deductibles that could cost homeowners thousandsHurricane deductibles are common in Florida and are used for hurricane-related claims. They also have a much higher deductible than the usual deductibles on insurance policies."Typically, it's 2 to 3 percent of the property's insured value — not 2 to 3 percent of the claim — so it can be pretty extensive; some people even have 5 or 10 percent deductible," Norberg said.A 2 percent deductible on a $300,000 home can run about $6,000.And that deductible applies anywhere in the state as long as a hurricane is posted somewhere in Florida."Any type of wind damage that causes a claim — say you're in Palm Beach County, those people will be subject to the wind deductible," Norberg saidThe hurricane deductible, according to state statute, expires 72 hours after the last hurricane warning is lifted.RELATED COVERAGE:

A former CIA agent convicted Tuesday of defrauding the government of $194 million reportedly used the majority of the money to acquire properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound. According to CBS Miami , court filings say 49-year-old David J. Rush of Virginia, a former high-ranking federal employee, directed $145 million to a holding company he controlled, and that $102 million was used to purchase four Florida properties: Two Palm Beach homes: $21.9 million and $27 million One Palm Beach parcel: $13.65 million One Hobe Sound parcel: $40 million Prosecutors allege Rush intended to eventually resell the properties for a profit. How the scheme unfolded According to the Department of Justice , Rush, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty Tuesday, Oct. 6, to wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia. According to prosecutors, Rush used his senior-level government position and "Top Secret" clearance to create fictitious government authorities and obtain federal money for his own benefit. Between November 2025 and March 2026, he directed approximately $145 million to a holding company established at his direction, according to court documents. The money was then used to purchase the properties. The Justice Department says Rush fraudulently obtained approximately $193.6 million in government funds. The South Florida real estate was only part of the alleged scheme. Gold bars Prosecutors say Rush separately created a fake "sensitive government activity" to justify acquiring hundreds of gold bars. On May 19, 2026, FBI agents searched Rush's Virginia home and recovered 298 gold bars, approximately $2.1 million in cash, €104,795, and numerous luxury watches. The gold had cost the government approximately $46 million, according to the Justice Department. Rush has agreed to forfeit the gold bars and cash, the Florida properties, luxury watches, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles as part of his plea agreement. What's next Rush is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. He faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison, along with possible restitution, forfeiture and a fine. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing. The Director of National Intelligence has also requested an investigation by the Intelligence Community's inspector general. The allegations and admissions are detailed in federal court documents filed as part of Rush's guilty plea.

Martin County officials are scrambling to restore public transportation service after the county's contracted transit provider abruptly canceled its services, leaving Martin County Public Transit (MARTY) riders without transportation effective immediately. In a statement Thursday, Martin County said it is aware that its contracted transit service provider has canceled service and that MARTY transit operations are currently interrupted. "Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," the county said. "Additional information will be provided as it becomes available." Officials did not immediately identify the transit provider or explain why the service was canceled. "We understand the importance of MARTY services to our community and apologize for the disruption," the statement said. In response, United Way of Martin County said it is preparing for an increase in transportation assistance requests through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents. Region Martin County "Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table," said Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County. "When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it." United Way officials said the program was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption. The organization is now anticipating an even greater need for transportation assistance. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support Ride United's response to the outage. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. WPTV reached out to Martin County Transit who responded with this statement: "We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system." Martin County Transit told WPTV that 29 employees will be losing jobs as a result of the contract termination. Residents seeking transportation assistance can call 772-283-4800 or visit https://www.unitedwaymartin.org/rideunited for more information. By: Amanda Boettcher Posted and last updated FORT PIERCE, Fla. — Jury finds former city manager Nick Mimms guilty of official misconduct, not guilty of bid tampering charge. After viewer videos showed water covering roads and vehicles struggling through several Port St. Lucie neighborhoods, the city's own budget documents show where it plans to put money to reduce flooding. The city says that work is still in its early stages. Lucie has received about 4 inches of rain over the past 48 hours , and another 2 to 4 inches could fall by the end of the week. City crews are monitoring conditions as water recedes, and officials are reminding drivers and pedestrians to stay out of flooded roads because it is hard to tell how deep the water is. Frank Camarda, who has lived in the area for more than 20 years near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into a detour. He said drivers piled in while trying to bypass flooded roads, and he believes Savona Boulevard was also underwater. Camarda said he has not seen flooding on his own street before, but he has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, and he believes that has stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said. City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain came in too fast for the system to keep up. He said the canals, swales and retention ponds were already full, which makes it harder for water to move. At one location the city monitored, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said the water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, and he described that as the stormwater system doing what it is designed to do. He said Public Works checks drainage before heavy rain and is working to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water arrives at once. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf Samples said residents who cannot get home should find other accomedations if they can, whether that be another place to stay or carpooling in vehicles that can handle minor flooding. He also said that the city is working closely with police on safety. The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, includes the Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project. It would add new retention ponds, pump systems, and upgraded valves. The plan shows $8 million in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the next two, for $30 million in all, paid for through stormwater bond financing. Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for Oak Hammock, which he placed in the California Boulevard area. He said the work will guide the design of a multi-phase project that could include new retention ponds, canal pumps, or even raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains off. He said it is hard to predict when residents will see construction or a finished project, because the city must first gather data, settle on a design, and line up funding. He called Oak Hammock a priority for the city. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said. According to the city, the project covers a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-24 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. The money would come partly from the $6 increase in the annual stormwater assessment. That went into effect Oct. 1 and raised the assessment from $189 to $195. The city says the assessment helps pay for five projects aimed at flooding and water flow: Oak Hammock, the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of swales and culverts. The city says its drainage system includes about 200 miles of canals, 1,200 miles of swales, and more than 6,000 culverts. It also notes that maintaining swales and driveway culverts, from the edge of the pavement to the property line, is the property owner's responsibility under city code.

A 17-year-old boy died after a shooting late Friday close to a boat ramp near Fellsmere and Vero Beach, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Saturday. The Indian River School District said the unnamed teen recently withdrew from Sebastian River High School to homeschool and was not enrolled in the district at the time of the shooting. "We are deeply saddened by the loss of this young person, and our hearts are with his family, friends, and the Sebastian River High School community," district spokeswoman Kyra Schafte said in a statement to WPBF. In a follow-up email she wrote: "This remains an active investigation, and we are in constant communication with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Please direct questions about the investigation to IRCSO. Our primary focus is supporting our students, staff, families, and community during this difficult time." A dance is scheduled for 7 p.m. Saturday at Sebastian River High. Read more at: https://www.miamiherald.com/news/article317482082.html#storylink=cpy At 11:24 p.m., deputies responded to reports of a juvenile shot in the area of Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512 and near the Fort Drum Marsh Conservation Area. Deputies located the teen and began lifesaving measures until Indian River County Fire Rescue arrived. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries, the sheriff's office said. "At this time, this appears to be an isolated incident, and there is no threat to the public," Lt. Kevin Jaworski wrote in an alert to the media. "This is an active investigation." He told WPBF that investigators have interviewed all parties involved in the case. Anyone with information about this incident is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office (772-569-6700) or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers (1-800-273-TIPS). Detectives from the Criminal Investigations Division and crime scene personnel were processing the scene and interviewing multiple witnesses. The area remains open to the public. The Soup Kitchen in Boynton Beach is seeing a surge in demand, with need up about 25% as residents struggle with rising gas prices, medical bills, and other monthly expenses.Marlene Mejia, CEO and executive director of The Soup Kitchen, said the need is increasing."I would say it's about 25% higher need," she said.People are telling the kitchen that tough times are getting tougher."They're telling us that the gas prices are killing them, that medication and the bills that they have to pay at the end of the month, it's not enough," Mejia said. "So, that's why we're coming in and filling in the gap." The Soup Kitchen is filling in the gap for every walk of life, including employed residents, who have homes and cars but are still not making ends meet at the end of the month."You can see people from all over and we call them the household person, which is asset limited income constrained," Mejia said. "But they're employed, so they have cars, they may have a house, they may have an apartment, and it's just not adding up at the end of the month." Yolanda Marcellus was among the dozens of people standing in a long line and walking through The Soup Kitchen for food."I just come here. They have good food every day. So, I'm thank God I'm here," Marcellus said.The kitchen is able to distribute hundreds of pounds of food every day through faithful volunteers, like Mary Webb."You just feel good helping out other people and it comes back to you," Webb said. "The goodness comes back to you." The Soup Kitchen is located at 8655 W. and they can be contacted at 561-732-7595.

Martin County officials are scrambling to restore public transportation service after the county's contracted transit provider abruptly canceled its services, leaving Martin County Public Transit (MARTY) riders without transportation effective immediately.In a statement Thursday, Martin County said it is aware that its contracted transit service provider has canceled service and that MARTY transit operations are currently interrupted."Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," the county said. "Additional information will be provided as it becomes available."Officials did not immediately identify the transit provider or explain why the service was canceled."We understand the importance of MARTY services to our community and apologize for the disruption," the statement said.In response, United Way of Martin County said it is preparing for an increase in transportation assistance requests through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents."Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table," said Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County. "When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it."United Way officials said the program was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption. The organization is now anticipating an even greater need for transportation assistance.Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support Ride United's response to the outage.Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding.WPTV reached out to Martin County Transit who responded with this statement: "We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system."Martin County Transit told WPTV that 29 employees will be losing jobs as a result of the contract termination. Residents seeking transportation assistance can call 772-283-4800 or visit https://www.unitedwaymartin.org/rideunited for more information.Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county's transit website.

Heavy rain flooded roads across Port St. Lucie Tuesday afternoon, leaving some vehicles stranded, forcing children to walk through standing water after school and prompting a response from police officers and city crews. According to the City of Port St. Lucie , a large amount of rain fell in a short period of time, leading to temporary road closures and flooding in multiple areas. Public Works crews responded to flooding near Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard, closing the roadway until it was safe for travel. The city also reported high-water conditions near Thornhill Drive and Floresta Drive, where Phase 3 construction is underway. On Southwest Thornhill Drive, school buses continued dropping off students despite flooded streets. CBS12 News saw children step off buses carrying their shoes and walk barefoot through standing water to reach home. Along Southwest Broadview Avenue near Crosstown Parkway, residents watched as water spilled across the roadway, making it difficult for drivers to tell where the street ended and floodwater began. "If you didn't see the grass here, you wouldn't know where the road is," resident Kevin Burke told CBS12 News. "It was steady sheets of rain for a good hour. Non-stop, and I mean heavy, heavy." Police officers directed traffic while Public Works crews set up barricades and monitored conditions during the evening commute. Burke said flooding in the area has become a familiar problem during heavy downpours. "When it rains heavy like it did today, it's like this all the time, from that canal coming up," he said. Burke said standing water presents concerns beyond traffic issues. "We have a pond over there by Crosstown and Bayshore. It's got signs all around it saying there are gators in it. It's a long shot, but it could happen, and that's what worries me, with kids and the animals," he said. For some residents, the flooding disrupted everyday tasks. "She has her elderly brother, who's 83 years old, and she's in her 60s, and she was going to run out and get Chinese food, and now she's still sitting here waiting because she can't get to it," Burke said. Earlier in the day, Port St. Lucie police reported flooding at several intersections, including SE Evans Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SE Eyerly Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SW Bayshore Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, and NE Floresta Drive and NE Ardsley Drive. See also: Opponents, supporters clash over Palm Beach County Israel Bonds investments City officials said Public Works crews continued monitoring conditions as water slowly receded Tuesday evening. Officials also reminded residents not to walk or drive through flooded roadways because it can be difficult to determine how deep the water is.

Jurors are deliberating in the trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms, who is accused of bid tampering and official misconduct involving city-owned properties and a nonprofit linked to his niece. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position as city manager to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit co-founded by his niece, secure a lease to develop two city-owned properties. The defense denied Mimms did anything wrong, arguing that he and his niece, Caleta Scott, have a distant relationship. The prosecution argued there was a conflict of interest, saying Scott was granted special treatment because of her relationship with Mimms. Deliberations began late yesterday after closing arguments from both sides and resumed at 9 a.m. Jurors have broken for lunch but have not yet reached a verdict. Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

A West Palm Beach woman is turning her husband’s Huntington’s disease diagnosis into a mission to raise awareness and support families affected by the progressive neurological disease.Madison Donovan says her husband, Brian, was diagnosed with Huntington's disease at age 21, just four years ago. Now, she is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk this weekend outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton.The walk is scheduled for Saturday at 9 a.m. and aims to raise both awareness and money for people and families affected by Huntington’s disease.According to Donovan, Huntington’s disease is a hereditary and progressive neurological disease that can affect movement and behavior.For Donovan, the diagnosis has become a reason to help others better understand a disease she says affects everyday families."I want to spread awareness. It’s not just a disease that goes into the rare disease book. It's something that is affecting everyday people," Donovan said.Donovan is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk as part of an effort to bring more attention to Huntington’s disease and raise funds for those affected by it.Proceeds from the event will benefit the Huntington’s Disease Society of America, Donovan said.The fundraising goal is $10,000. Donovan says organizers are already halfway to that goal.The event will take place Saturday at 9 a.m. outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton.

He returned to the area, activated his hazard lights, and found the teen unconscious on the side of the road. The driver called 911 and has remained cooperative with investigators, police said. The teen suffered life-threatening injuries and remains in critical condition. The investigation remains active. Senate candidate Angie Nixon visited Fort Pierce on Tuesday to speak with voters about reproductive health care, the economy, and other issues as part of her campaign across Florida ahead of the general election. Nixon, who represents a Jacksonville-area district in the Florida House of Representatives and describes herself as a Democratic Socialist, is holding town hall meetings across the state to connect with voters. Planned Parenthood President and CEO Alexis McGill Johnson hosted the Fort Pierce town hall, focusing on reproductive freedom and Florida's maternal mortality crisis. McGill Johnson and Nixon outlined the leadership they believe Florida families need, including protecting abortion access and expanding comprehensive health care services statewide. "Representative Nixon is a true champion for reproductive freedom," McGill Johnson said. "In the Senate, she is going to stand up for affordable health care and our right to make our own decisions about our own bodies." During the event, Nixon addressed a question about a proposed Islamic center approved for construction in Palm Beach County. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "This is a country where folks should have freedom of religion," Nixon said. "I would speak out against that type of opposition and hate if it was directed at a synagogue being built, if it was directed at a church being built, if it was directed at any other spiritual facility." Nixon also discussed the state of reproductive health care in Florida and other issues raised by voters. "Gas is high, people are struggling to get to and from work, and then they can't even afford the food anymore, let alone taking their children to the movies or out to eat, that's null and void now," one voter said. Nixon won the Democratic primary in St. Lucie County with about 54% of the vote. When asked how she plans to close the gap between herself and Republican incumbent Ashley Moody, Nixon said she intends to continue engaging with voters, including those who may disagree with her. "They have someone who is going to put them first," Nixon said when asked about the message she hopes attendees took away from Tuesday's event. She added that her campaign for U.S. Senate is focused on putting money back in people's pockets. Nixon spoke with voters for about an hour. Her next stop is in the Orlando area. Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

hero.headline: Misplaced Cellphone Sparks False Weapon Rumor at Vero Beach High School
hero.body:
A misplaced cellphone in the cafeteria at Vero Beach High School triggered a false weapon rumor on Monday morning, though school officials said there was never a credible threat to students or staff. According to the School District of Indian River County, a student had left a cellphone behind in the cafeteria and hurried back to grab it. That simple moment created confusion, and as word spread through the school, the story shifted and grew until it became a rumor that a weapon was involved.

District officials moved quickly to clarify that the alleged threat had no basis in fact. Principal Serra Finnegan sent an update to families to address the misunderstanding and set the record straight about what had actually happened. The explanation was meant to calm any fears among parents and students who may have heard the rumor before learning the full picture.

The district also publicly thanked the Indian River County Sheriff's Office for its partnership in helping address the situation as it unfolded. Officials asked families to help stop the spread of misinformation by sharing only verified details rather than passing along unconfirmed rumors, a request aimed at preventing similar confusion in the future.

The incident is a reminder of how fast rumors can travel in a school setting, especially in a crowded, fast-moving environment like a cafeteria. What began as an ordinary moment, a student rushing to retrieve a forgotten phone, spiraled into a more serious-sounding claim once inaccurate details started circulating among students. No injuries, arrests, or disciplinary actions were reported in connection with the rumor.

hero.headline: Flash Flood Warning Hits Coastal Martin County Until 7 p.m.
hero.body:
A Flash Flood Warning is in effect until 7 p.m. for northeastern Martin County, covering coastal communities including Stuart, Port Salerno, Hobe Sound, Palm City, Jupiter Island and Sewall's Point. The warning was issued as thunderstorms moved through the region, bringing heavy rainfall that has already caused flooding concerns across the area.

As of 5:23 p.m., Doppler radar showed thunderstorms producing heavy rain over the warned area. Between 2 and 3 inches of rain had already fallen, and forecasters said another 1 to 2 inches could fall before the storms clear out. Flash flooding was described as either already happening or expected to develop shortly as the rain continues to move through the area.

The warning applies to flash flooding risks in small creeks and streams, as well as urban areas, highways, streets and underpasses. Low-lying and poorly drained areas are also at risk of significant water buildup. Specific locations expected to see flash flooding include Stuart, Jupiter Island, Port Salerno, Hobe Sound, Palm City, Sewall's Point, Witham Field, Hobe Sound Beach and the Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge.

People in the affected areas are urged to stay alert and avoid driving through flooded roadways or low-lying spots where water tends to pool. Conditions can change quickly during these storms, and roads that appear passable can become dangerous within minutes as rain intensifies. The warning remains active until 7 p.m., after which conditions are expected to improve as the thunderstorms move out of the region.

hero.headline: Jupiter Nurse Arrested, Charged With Stealing Fentanyl at Tradition Hospital
hero.teaser: A Cleveland Clinic Tradition ICU nurse has been arrested on felony charges after police say she stole fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV line. Port St. Lucie police say a family member witnessed the theft before detectives confirmed it through surveillance footage.
hero.body:
A Jupiter woman who worked as an intensive care unit nurse at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital has been arrested on felony charges after Port St. Lucie police say she stole fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV infusion while on shift. Leslie Pope, 54, was taken into custody in Jupiter on Oct. 8, following a police investigation into the alleged theft.

According to investigators, a family member of the patient reported seeing Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient's fentanyl infusion line, place the syringe in her pocket and leave the room. Police said Pope was not assigned to care for the patient at the time.

Detectives said Pope returned to the patient's room the following evening and again approached the IV equipment. The family member intervened during that encounter. Investigators later reviewed surveillance footage that they say showed Pope manipulating protective caps on the IV equipment, though authorities said they could not determine whether any additional medication was removed during the second incident.

Pope now faces felony charges of grand theft of a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and fraudulently obtaining a controlled substance. The Port St. Lucie Police Department led the investigation into the alleged diversion at the hospital, located in the Tradition area of Port St. Lucie.

cards.headline: Coast Guard Tows Disabled Boat With Four Aboard Near Fort Pierce Inlet
cards.teaser: A Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce crew towed a disabled 15-foot vessel carrying four people to safety near the inlet during rainy weather Sunday.
cards.body:
A Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce boat crew assisted four people aboard a disabled 15-foot vessel near the Fort Pierce Inlet on Sunday after the boat's engine became inoperative. The incident unfolded amid rainy conditions, according to the Coast Guard.

The crew provided a manual bilge pump to the boaters as a precaution against flooding before towing the vessel safely to the Stan Blum Boat Ramp.

"Our Coast Guard crews stay prepared through continuous training, qualifications and physical fitness, ensuring they remain Semper Paratus, Always Ready, to respond to maritime emergencies across the Southeast's 1.8 million square mile area of responsibility," the agency posted Monday on Facebook.

The Fort Pierce rescue came a day after a Coast Guard Station Miami boat crew rescued one person in the water after a passing personal watercraft operator waved them down and alerted them to an overturned hydrofoil near Flagler Memorial Island.

hero.headline: Developer Sues Indiantown Over Stalled $25 Million Data Center Plat
hero.body:
Silver Fox 606 LLC has filed a lawsuit against the Village of Indiantown, its village council, planning board, and local residents, seeking emergency injunctive relief to keep its $25 million data center project moving forward. The complaint, which includes a verified petition for a writ of prohibition, accuses village officials of illegally derailing the project after a newly elected council took office in 2026.

Silver Fox bought the more than 600-acre property at 13820 SW Silver Fox Lane in 2025 after zoning verifications confirmed that computer and data processing facilities were permitted as an as-of-right use in Heavy Industrial districts. The lawsuit alleges that the new village council moved to stall or ban data center development despite earlier municipal marketing efforts that had actively recruited similar tech infrastructure to the area. Indiantown's Community and Economic Development Director administratively approved the Silver Fox plat on September 17. A local resident later filed an administrative appeal seeking to overturn that approval.

Silver Fox's legal team argues that the village's planning, zoning, and appeals board has no legal jurisdiction to review the plat approval, citing state statutes that render recorded plats unassailable without the landowner's consent. The lawsuit also points to a September 1 emergency council meeting at which the village manager and the village's long-serving village attorney were ousted. Silver Fox alleges the Village Council violated Florida's Sunshine Law during those personnel changes, raising accountability questions about how the decisions were made.

The developer is asking the court for emergency injunctive relief, a preliminary injunction blocking any stop-work orders or retroactive reviews of the project, and declaratory judgments affirming its vested development rights. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Man Fights City's 126-Camera Network in Federal Court
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie resident is representing himself in a federal lawsuit against the city, Mayor Shannon Martin and surveillance company Flock Safety, challenging a combined network of 126 license plate cameras he says violates residents' constitutional rights. Steven Greer, a former surgeon who later worked on Wall Street, filed the suit in August and has since amended it. His complaint alleges Port St. Lucie operated 53 Flock cameras along with 73 Axon license plate readers.

Greer argues the cameras, which photograph passing vehicles and record identifying information along with time and location, let police reconstruct a person's movements without a warrant. He says this violates the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures. "I was appalled at what I learned," Greer said. His complaint also cites two cases involving the cameras, including the arrest of Fort Pierce Officer Josepher Crutchfield, who was accused of searching his ex-girlfriend's vehicle 382 times, and a woman who was mistakenly jailed after her vehicle was wrongly linked to a deadly hit-and-run before charges against her were dropped. Greer contends those incidents point to a larger problem with the surveillance system itself.

The lawsuit also raises a Second Amendment argument, pointing to Flock cameras reportedly installed at the entrance to the Ocala Shooting Range in Marion County. Greer argues that recording visitors to a gun range could discourage people from exercising their right to bear arms. "When I saw that case where they have Flock cameras in gun ranges, I said, 'Whoa, that's a Second Amendment violation,'" Greer said. "The key buzzword is chilling. You know, if they scare you away from using your gun rights that's a violation." His complaint additionally challenges the city's handling of public records requests, alleging officials withheld information about camera locations and system audit logs, and raises claims under Florida's constitutional privacy protections along with questions about the legality of public spending on the network.

Port St. Lucie has already voted to remove 18 of its 53 Flock cameras, but Greer says that is not enough because a future administration could reverse a voluntary decision. "The end result is to get a consent decree, where the city and Flock agrees to pull the cameras forever," he said. His amended lawsuit seeks a court declaration that the city's surveillance program is unconstitutional, an injunction limiting the network's operation or data sharing without a warrant backed by probable cause, access to disputed public records, statutory damages and litigation costs. Greer said his main goal is a binding court order rather than money. "I'm not running for office. I'm not seeking attention," he said. "It's my way of doing something." A federal judge has not ruled on whether Port St. Lucie's camera program is unconstitutional, and the case still faces potential motions to dismiss.

"I was appalled at what I learned," Greer told the CBS12 News I-Team. Greer said he spent much of August researching Flock's technology and preparing the federal lawsuit himself. While he has no formal legal training, he says his years working as a surgeon and later on Wall Street prepared him for the technical research and writing involved in representing himself. Flock's automated license plate readers photograph passing vehicles, recording identifying information along with the time and location. His amended complaint alleges Port St. Lucie operated 53 Flock cameras and another 73 Axon license plate readers, for a combined network of 126 devices. In Fort Pierce, Officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested after investigators accused him of searching his ex-girlfriend's vehicle 382 times. In another case, a woman was arrested and jailed after investigators mistakenly linked her vehicle to a deadly hit-and-run crash. The charges against her were later dropped. Law enforcement agencies, however, defend license plate readers as valuable investigative tools, crediting the technology with helping identify suspects, recover stolen vehicles and solve crimes. "I know that police have always argued these Flock cameras really help solve crimes. What would be your response to that?" Bente asked. "That's their number one defense. It's not true," Greer said. His assertion is disputed by law enforcement agencies that have documented cases in which license plate reader information helped investigators. Whether the technology is useful in solving crimes is a separate question from whether particular searches are constitutional. Greer's lawsuit also raises an argument not typically associated with traffic cameras: the right to bear arms. He points to Flock cameras reportedly installed at the entrance to the Ocala Shooting Range, a public gun range in Marion County. Greer argues that recording who visits a shooting range could discourage people from exercising their Second Amendment rights. "When I saw that case where they have Flock cameras in gun ranges, I said, 'Whoa, that's a Second Amendment violation,'" Greer told the I-Team. The key buzzword is chilling. You know, if they scare you away from using your gun rights that's a violation." The complaint also challenges the city's handling of public records requests, alleging officials withheld information about camera locations and system audit logs. It includes claims under Florida's constitutional privacy protections and questions the legality of public spending on the network. Greer has also raised First Amendment concerns following a Sept. Lucie City Council meeting. He told the I-Team that the number of police officers present made him feel intimidated and could discourage residents from speaking out. I'm looking around, I see police officers all over the place," Greer said. Meanwhile, the legal debate over Flock is playing out across the country. In Oklahoma, a federal judge ruled Oct. 1 that a warrantless search of approximately a month of license plate location records violated the Fourth Amendment, suppressing evidence obtained following the search. The ruling concerned the specific circumstances of that case and did not establish that all Flock searches are unconstitutional. Law enforcement agencies have continued to defend the technology, while privacy advocates argue that large networks of searchable cameras allow police to monitor ordinary drivers on a scale that wasn't previously possible. Florida is already seeing changes. The Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for automated license plate readers on state highway rights-of-way, requiring their removal from those locations. Lucie also voted to remove 18 of its 53 Flock cameras. But for Greer, taking down some cameras isn't enough. When Bente pointed out that Port St. Lucie was already removing cameras, Greer argued that voluntary decisions can be reversed by future administrations. "The end result is to get a consent decree, where the city and Flock agrees to pull the cameras forever," he said. His amended lawsuit seeks a declaration that the city's surveillance program violates constitutional protections and an injunction restricting operation of the network or national data sharing without a warrant supported by probable cause. It also seeks disputed public records, statutory damages under federal privacy law and litigation costs. Greer told the I-Team that his primary goal is a binding court order, not a financial payout. hero.headline: More Than 200,000 Customers Have Power Back After Hurricane Isaias
hero.body:
More than 200,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle had their power restored as of Sunday afternoon, Gov. Ron DeSantis said, as crews continued cleanup from Hurricane Isaias. The storm made landfall Friday night near the Panhandle as a Category 2 hurricane, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of residents. About 430,000 customers remained without power as of Saturday morning, but that number has dropped sharply since then. DeSantis said Florida Power and Light is expected to largely finish restoration by Monday, while Choctawhatchee Electric Cooperative, which had about 46,000 customers still without power at the time of Sunday's press conference, is targeting Tuesday for full restoration.

"I know it's frustrating to lose power and some of you have been without it for a couple of days now," CHELCO CEO Steve Rhodes said. "Be assured we're working around the clock to recover from this devastating hurricane."

DeSantis held Sunday evening's press conference at Grayton Beach State Park in Santa Rosa Beach, one of 24 parks that have reopened since the storm. The park had been closed after a bridge washout left a 50-foot-long, 15-foot-deep gap that cut off access and threatened to harm Western Lake, according to the Florida Department of Transportation. Crews worked overnight, bringing in 600 cubic yards of sand to repair the bridge in less than 18 hours, and DeSantis said the park was expected to reopen Sunday night. The governor said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida, driven mainly by falling trees, debris and wind rather than storm surge. Two storm-related deaths have been confirmed in Escambia County.

The hardest-hit counties by power outages included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers lost power, along with Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%. DeSantis said the state plans to submit a request for a federal major disaster declaration, which requires reaching a certain damage threshold before it can be approved by the president. "I think clearly, just given the amount of trees that fell down on different things, there's going to be more than enough," he said. A major disaster declaration would open a range of federal assistance programs for individuals and public infrastructure, including funding for emergency and permanent recovery work, according to FEMA. State emergency officials said Saturday they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.

hero.headline: Church and Neighbors Rally After Port St. Lucie House Fire Injures Renter
hero.teaser: A garage fire on Carmelite Street in Port St. Lucie's Northport Village neighborhood burned renter Nigel Laidlow and displaced his family, but church members and neighbors have stepped in to help them recover.
hero.body:
A house fire in Port St. Lucie's Northport Village neighborhood injured a renter and displaced his family Friday afternoon, and members of a local church and neighbors have since rallied to help them begin cleaning up. The fire broke out on Carmelite Street near St. Lucie County Fire District crews, who responded around 1:30 p.m. and arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage.

According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading through the garage. They said a propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and impacting a neighbor's garage doors across the street. When firefighters extinguished the flames, they left behind a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot.

Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire broke out and suffered burns to his legs. He was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this."

By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through the damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, he said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. The family is now focused on recovering and determining its next steps, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation.

hero.headline: Flash Flood Warning Hits Stuart, Hobe Sound, Palm City and Coastal Martin County
hero.body:
A Flash Flood Warning is in effect for northeastern Martin County until 7 p.m. as thunderstorms continue to dump heavy rain across the coast. As of 5:23 p.m., Doppler radar showed storms producing additional heavy rainfall over the warned area. Between 2 and 3 inches of rain had already fallen, with another 1 to 2 inches possible before the storms move out.

Flash flooding is either already happening or expected to develop shortly across the warning area. Communities at risk include Stuart, Jupiter Island, Port Salerno, Hobe Sound, Palm City, Sewall's Point, Witham Field, Hobe Sound Beach and the Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge. The warning applies to small creeks and streams as well as urban areas, highways, streets, underpasses and other spots known for poor drainage or low elevation.

The threat stems from thunderstorms capable of producing intense, fast-moving rainfall. That kind of rain can quickly overwhelm drainage systems and cause water to pool or rise in places that normally handle wet weather without issue, raising the risk of sudden and dangerous flooding on roads and in neighborhoods.

Residents in and around Stuart, Port Salerno, Hobe Sound, Palm City, Sewall's Point and Jupiter Island should stay alert for rising water through the evening hours. Drivers are urged to avoid flooded roadways and underpasses, since floodwaters can be deeper and move faster than they appear. The Flash Flood Warning remains active until 7 p.m., and conditions could change quickly as the storms continue to track through the region.

hero.headline: DeSantis: Over 200,000 Customers Have Power Back After Hurricane Isaias
hero.body:
More than 200,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle had their power restored as of Sunday afternoon, Gov. Ron DeSantis said, as crews continue cleanup efforts following Hurricane Isaias. Florida Power and Light is expected to be largely finished with restoration by Monday, and CHELCO, which still had about 46,000 customers without power at the time of DeSantis's Sunday evening press conference, is targeting Tuesday to have service fully restored. The state also plans to submit a request for a federal major disaster declaration given the widespread damage.

Isaias made landfall in the Panhandle Friday night as a Category 2 hurricane. Hundreds of thousands of people lost power in the storm's aftermath, with 430,000 customers still without electricity as of Saturday morning. DeSantis said crews are making steady progress and that 24 state parks have reopened. The governor confirmed two storm-related deaths in Escambia County. State emergency officials said Saturday they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.

DeSantis said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida, mostly from falling trees, debris and wind rather than storm surge. Some of the hardest-hit counties included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers lost power, along with Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%. Because of the scale of the damage, the state intends to request a major disaster declaration from the federal government, a designation that must be approved by the president. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie House Fire Injures Renter, Displaces Family in Northport Village
hero.body:
A house fire Friday afternoon on Carmelite Street in Port St. Lucie's Northport Village neighborhood injured a renter and displaced his family, while neighbors and church members quickly stepped in to help with cleanup. St. Lucie County Fire District crews responded to the home around 1:30 p.m. and arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage.

According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading through the garage. A propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and striking a neighbor's garage doors across the street. When firefighters extinguished the flames, they left behind a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot.

Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire broke out and suffered burns to his legs. He was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this."

By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through the damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, Laidlow said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. The family is now focused on recovering and determining its next steps, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation.
