cards.headline: 2 Arrested After Woman Shot At While Fleeing Fort Pierce Attack
cards.teaser: A woman escaped an attack on South Sixth Street and was shot at as she drove away. Fort Pierce police have arrested 18-year-olds Keibin Lopez-Godoy and Kailee Yurubi in connection with the shooting.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police have arrested two 18-year-olds in connection with an attack and shooting that sent a woman fleeing for her life on South Sixth Street earlier this month. Keibin Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide, and Kailee Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.

The case began on Saturday, October 3, when Fort Pierce police officers responded to South Sixth Street at 7:12 a.m. after the victim called 911 to report that someone was shooting at her. Investigators said the woman had gone to the address to speak with her boyfriend about their relationship. When she arrived, several people ran out of the residence and began attacking her, according to police.

The victim managed to break free, get into her vehicle, and drive away from the scene, police said. As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and opened fire on her vehicle, according to investigators.

Police said a second person was arrested for allegedly driving the shooter away from the scene after the attack. Lopez-Godoy and Yurubi were both identified as the suspects taken into custody in the case.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound Woman Charged After Deputies Say She Buried Live Kittens
cards.teaser: A 37-year-old Hobe Sound woman faces four felony animal cruelty charges after deputies say she buried kittens alive in her yard during what family members described as a mental health crisis.
cards.body:
A Hobe Sound woman is facing four felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County deputies say she buried live kittens in her yard at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park. The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested 37-year-old Alba Luz Chavez on four counts of aggravated animal cruelty after investigators said they found two live kittens and two dead kittens buried on the property. Deputies were called to the home Thursday night for what family members described as a mental health crisis.

Family members told deputies Chavez believed the cats were demons and had killed several animals earlier in the week. According to the arrest affidavit, Chavez had allegedly told residents of the home she killed two kittens on Monday. Three juveniles living at the residence told deputies Chavez had appeared to be experiencing a mental health episode for most of the week. The juveniles said they locked three surviving kittens inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday evening, and when they returned around 6 p.m., they found Chavez had forced her way into the room and the kittens were gone.

Investigators said Chavez initially refused to tell family members where the animals were. While speaking with deputies, Chavez allegedly said, “If you want the cats, you will need gloves, a red bag and a shovel,” and directed them to an area on the property. Deputies dug and found two live kittens buried underground inside plastic Publix bags, according to the affidavit. They later uncovered two deceased kittens that appeared to be in the early stages of decomposition. Detectives searched for a third missing kitten but were unable to locate it.

During an interview, Chavez told investigators she had been cleaning her house and referred to the cats as “very ugly,” according to the affidavit. Investigators wrote that Chavez also made statements indicating she did not want black cats and suggested kittens of different colors “had different fates.” The affidavit states Chavez later began singing instead of answering additional questions. The two surviving kittens were taken to a pet emergency center for treatment. A veterinarian told investigators the kittens were about three weeks old and very weak, and said it was too early to determine whether a lack of oxygen while confined inside the plastic bags had caused brain damage or other medical complications. The two deceased kittens are expected to undergo necropsies to determine their exact causes of death. Chavez was booked into the Martin County Jail on the four felony counts and is being held without bond.

hero.headline: Sheriff: Deputies Heard Kittens Crying Underground in Hobe Sound Burial Case
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek on Friday gave new details on the arrest of a Hobe Sound woman accused of killing two kittens and burying two others alive, revealing that deputies heard the animals crying from beneath the ground during a backyard search. Alba Chavez, 36, faces four felony counts of animal torture after deputies said she buried kittens up to 3 feet underground at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park, with two kittens rescued alive and two found dead. A fifth kitten remains missing despite repeated searches of the property.

Deputies responded to the mobile home park Thursday night after several minors inside the home called 911 to report that Chavez had killed two kittens on Monday, placed them in the trash and later buried them in the backyard. The children, fearing for three remaining kittens, had locked them inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday night. When they returned, they found the bedroom door forced open and the kittens gone, prompting the call to law enforcement. Deputies found Chavez standing in the roadway, and she reportedly admitted to killing the two kittens, telling deputies she believed the animals had demons, calling them ugly and saying she did not want black or brown cats in the home.

Chavez then led deputies to the backyard where the kittens had been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. As deputies dug through the rain-soaked ground, they heard cries coming from underground. Two kittens were pulled out alive and rushed to an emergency veterinary facility, where they were being treated for dehydration. The sheriff said veterinarians were also concerned about possible injuries from lack of oxygen while the animals were buried, and he said the kittens could still die from their injuries despite being rescued. The two kittens killed Monday were found dead at the burial site.

Chavez was arrested and charged with four counts of animal torture involving pain, serious injury or death, corresponding to the two kittens found dead and the two found alive. She is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and also has an immigration hold. Investigators have not determined how the first two kittens died or established a motive for Chavez's actions. Budensiek said Chavez initially cooperated with deputies and led them to the burial site but later stopped answering questions about how the animals were killed. The sheriff said deputies had previously responded to calls involving Chavez's mental health but had received no prior animal cruelty complaints at the residence. Additional charges could be filed if the missing fifth kitten is found dead. The Florida Department of Children and Families became involved following the incident, and the children were released to their father, who lives locally. Officials said resources were available to help the children cope with what happened.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Man Arrested in August Shooting Death of Ex-Girlfriend
cards.teaser: Matthew Waggle was arrested Oct. 5 on a first-degree murder warrant in the death of Dawn Marie Kriskewic, who was found shot in the roadway on 1st Street in Vero Beach in August.
cards.body:
A 33-year-old Vero Beach man has been arrested on a first-degree murder charge in connection with the August shooting death of his former girlfriend, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Matthew Allen Waggle was taken into custody Oct. 5 on an active warrant accusing him of killing Dawn Marie Kriskewic. He is being held without bond at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, where he was booked.

Deputies responded to the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach in August after 911 callers reported a woman lying in the roadway. They found Kriskewic with injuries consistent with gunshot wounds and began CPR before she was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

Investigators identified Waggle as Kriskewic's former boyfriend. A coworker told detectives that Kriskewic had expressed concerns about Waggle before her death and said he had previously threatened consequences if she called police when he came to retrieve his belongings. Surveillance footage reviewed by detectives showed a person they identified as Waggle near the area around the time of the shooting, and additional footage showed him walking through the area both before and after it occurred. Investigators said the footage also captured him discarding a shirt, which they later recovered.

Near the crime scene, investigators recovered a rolling suitcase containing men's clothing and a tactical vest bearing a "security" patch. A Ruger pistol was found on a neighboring property along with a note stating that another person had given Waggle permission to use the firearm for firearm qualifications, according to the arrest affidavit. A judge signed the first-degree murder warrant for Waggle in August, and he remained at large until his arrest in October.

hero.headline: Sheriff: Deputies Heard Kittens Crying Underground in Hobe Sound Burial Case
hero.teaser: Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek revealed new details about the arrest of a Hobe Sound woman accused of burying kittens alive, saying deputies heard cries coming from the ground as they dug to rescue two surviving animals.
hero.body:
Deputies digging through a rain-soaked backyard in Martin County heard kittens crying from as deep as 3 feet underground, leading to the rescue of two animals while two others were found dead, Sheriff John Budensiek revealed Friday. The discovery came during the investigation into 36-year-old Alba Chavez of Hobe Sound, who is accused of killing two kittens earlier in the week and burying two more alive in the backyard of a mobile home park. Budensiek held a news conference to lay out new details of the case, including the frantic digging that led deputies to the surviving animals.

According to the sheriff's office, deputies were called to the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park Thursday night after several minors inside the home dialed 911, reporting that Chavez had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them in the trash and later buried them in the yard. Worried about three other kittens still in the home, the children locked them in a bedroom before leaving for dinner that evening. When they returned, Budensiek said, the bedroom door had been forced open and the kittens were gone, prompting the children to call authorities.

When deputies arrived, Chavez was standing in the roadway and admitted to killing the two kittens, the sheriff's office said. She told deputies she believed the kittens had demons, called them ugly and said she did not want black or brown cats in her home. She then led deputies to the backyard, where the animals had allegedly been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. As they dug, deputies heard crying coming from underground. Two kittens were pulled out alive, while the two Chavez allegedly killed Monday were found dead. A fifth kitten has not been located despite repeated searches of the property.

The surviving kittens were rushed to an emergency veterinary facility for treatment of dehydration, and veterinarians are also watching for possible injuries caused by oxygen deprivation while they were buried. Their survival is not guaranteed. Chavez was arrested and charged with four counts of animal torture involving pain, serious injury or death, covering the two kittens found dead and the two rescued alive. She is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and also has an immigration hold. Investigators have not determined exactly how the first two kittens died or what motivated the killings, and Budensiek said Chavez stopped answering questions about the deaths after initially cooperating. The sheriff noted deputies had responded to past calls involving Chavez's mental health but had no previous animal cruelty complaints at the home. Additional charges are possible if the missing kitten is found dead. The Department of Children and Families got involved, and the children were released to their father.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man charged with murder in August shooting death of ex-girlfriend
cards.body:
A 33-year-old Vero Beach man has been arrested on a first-degree murder charge in the August shooting death of his former girlfriend, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Matthew Allen Waggle was arrested Oct. 5 on an active warrant and is being held without bond on allegations he killed Dawn Marie Kriskewic.

Deputies responded to the 500 block of 1st Street after 911 callers reported a woman lying in the roadway. They found Kriskewic with injuries consistent with gunshot wounds and began CPR before she was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Investigators identified Waggle as Kriskewic's former boyfriend. A coworker told detectives that Kriskewic had expressed concerns about Waggle before her death and that Waggle had previously threatened consequences if Kriskewic called police when he came to retrieve his belongings.

Detectives said surveillance footage showed a person they identified as Waggle near the scene around the time of the shooting, and additional footage showed him walking through the area both before and after the shooting. Investigators said the footage also showed him discarding a shirt, which was later recovered. Near the crime scene, investigators recovered a rolling suitcase containing men's clothing and a tactical vest bearing a "security" patch. A Ruger pistol was found on a neighboring property along with a note stating that another person had given Waggle permission to use the firearm for firearm qualifications, according to the arrest affidavit.

A judge signed the first-degree murder warrant for Waggle in August. He was taken into custody at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office on Oct. 5 and remains held without bond.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Police Seek Help Identifying Critically Injured Man Found on Roadway
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police are asking the public for help identifying a man found unconscious with severe head injuries on a city roadway early Friday morning. Passing drivers discovered him around 1 a.m. near Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard. He was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where he remains in critical condition.

Police said the man suffered severe head trauma and significant bleeding and did not have identification with him. He is believed to be middle-aged or older and is known to walk in the area overnight.

Investigators described him as wearing a green, blue and white T-shirt, black shorts, multicolored Brooks athletic shoes, a gray Adidas baseball cap and Wiley X sunglasses. He was also carrying a pink umbrella with a black handle.

Police are asking anyone who recognizes the man to call 772-871-5000. Investigators also want to hear from witnesses and anyone with dashcam or security camera video from the area around the time he was found.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police Arrest Two After Woman Attacked, Shot At on South Sixth Street
cards.teaser: A woman escaped an attack outside a Fort Pierce home and was shot at as she drove away. Police have arrested two 18-year-olds, one on an attempted first-degree homicide charge.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police have arrested two 18-year-olds after a woman was attacked at a South Sixth Street home and then shot at as she fled the scene in her car. Keibin Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide, and Kailee Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact, both 18.

According to the Fort Pierce Police Department, officers responded to South Sixth Street at 7:12 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, after the victim called 911 to report that someone was shooting at her. Investigators determined the woman had gone to the address to talk with her boyfriend about their relationship. When she arrived, several people ran out of the residence and attacked her.

Police said the victim managed to break free, get into her vehicle and drive away. As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and opened fire on her car, according to police. A second suspect is accused of driving the shooter away from the scene afterward.

Lopez-Godoy was arrested on the attempted first-degree homicide charge for allegedly firing the shots at the victim's vehicle. Yurubi was arrested on the accessory after the fact charge for allegedly helping the shooter leave the area following the attack. The Fort Pierce Police Department has not released additional details on the relationship between the suspects and the victim's boyfriend or on the status of any other people who may have been involved in the initial attack at the home.

cards.headline: MARTY Bus Service Suspended Across Martin County After Contract Dispute
cards.teaser: MARTY public transit stopped running Thursday after its operator abruptly ended service amid a contract dispute with Martin County. Riders without cars were left stranded as officials scramble for a fix.
cards.body:
MARTY public transit service across Martin County came to an abrupt halt Thursday, leaving riders who depend on the buses without their regular transportation. County officials said they received no advance warning that service would stop that day. MARTY's operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract with the county, citing rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs that the company says have caused significant financial losses since it began running the service in July 2025.

Negotiations between the county and the company failed to produce an agreement. County officials said Martin County Transit LLC gave a 180-day notice to terminate its contract roughly two weeks ago, but then notified the county Thursday morning that it was discontinuing service immediately. The sudden shutdown left residents who rely on MARTY with no regular way to get around the county.

George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said the county is pursuing both short-term and long-term solutions to restore service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It's just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It's going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." County officials said they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents affected by the suspension. No timeline has been given for when MARTY operations could resume, and officials said they will post updates on social media and notify residents once a solution is reached.

The impact was immediate for riders who count on the bus daily. Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for a bus in Stuart on Thursday that never came. She said she had not known MARTY was suspended until a reporter told her. Chaclan said she has ridden the bus for years and called it essential for many in the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don't have a driver's license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It's very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don't drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don't drive, and we go everywhere to shop." Steven Godell, another rider affected by the suspension, said he rode his bicycle Thursday after the MARTY bus did not arrive that morning. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said.

hero.headline: Sheriff: Deputies Heard Kittens Crying Underground in Hobe Sound Case
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Friday that deputies digging through a rain-soaked backyard in Hobe Sound could hear kittens crying from as deep as three feet underground, a detail that emerged as he laid out new information about the arrest of 36-year-old Alba Chavez. Chavez faces four felony counts of animal torture involving pain, serious injury or death after deputies said she killed two kittens earlier in the week and later buried two more alive in the yard of her home at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park. Two kittens were pulled from the ground alive, while the two Chavez allegedly killed days earlier were recovered dead.

According to the sheriff's office, deputies were called to the mobile home park Thursday night after several minors living in the home dialed 911 to report that Chavez had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them away and then buried them in the backyard. Worried about three kittens still alive, the children locked them in a bedroom before leaving the house for dinner that evening. When they got back, Budensiek said, they found the bedroom door had been forced open and the kittens were gone, which prompted them to contact law enforcement.

Deputies found Chavez standing in the roadway when they arrived, and she admitted to killing the two kittens, according to the sheriff's office. She told deputies she thought the kittens were possessed by demons, called them ugly, and said she did not want black or brown cats in her home. She then walked deputies to the backyard, where they began searching for three kittens believed to still be alive along with the two that had already died. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. As they dug, deputies heard crying coming from beneath the ground and ultimately rescued two kittens, while the two killed earlier in the week were found dead. A fifth kitten has not been located despite multiple searches of the property.

The two kittens pulled from the ground were rushed to an emergency veterinary clinic, where they were treated for dehydration, and Budensiek said doctors are also watching for complications from lack of oxygen while buried underground. Investigators have not determined how the first two kittens died or established a motive for the killings, and Chavez stopped answering questions about the deaths after initially cooperating. The sheriff noted deputies had responded to past calls involving Chavez's mental health but had no previous animal cruelty complaints tied to the address. Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and has an immigration hold, and additional charges are possible if the missing kitten is found dead. The children involved were placed with their father following contact from child welfare officials.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Man Arrested on Murder Charge in Dawn Kriskewic Shooting Death
cards.teaser: Matthew Allen Waggle was arrested on a first-degree murder charge in the August shooting death of his former girlfriend, Dawn Marie Kriskewic, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office said.
cards.body:
A 33-year-old Vero Beach man has been arrested on a first-degree murder charge in connection with the August shooting death of a woman, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Matthew Allen Waggle was arrested Oct. 5 on an active warrant and is being held without bond at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. The warrant accuses him of killing Dawn Marie Kriskewic, whom investigators identified as his former girlfriend.

Deputies responded to the 500 block of 1st Street after 911 callers reported a woman lying in the roadway. They found Kriskewic with injuries consistent with gunshot wounds and began CPR. She was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

According to the sheriff's office, a coworker told detectives that Kriskewic had expressed concerns about Waggle before her death. The coworker also told investigators that Waggle had previously threatened consequences if Kriskewic called police when he came to retrieve his belongings. Detectives said surveillance footage showed a person they identified as Waggle near the area around the time of the shooting, and additional footage showed him walking through the area before and after the shooting. Investigators said the footage also showed him discarding a shirt, which they later recovered.

Investigators recovered a rolling suitcase containing men's clothing and a tactical vest with a "security" patch near the crime scene. A Ruger pistol was found on a neighboring property along with a note stating that another person had given Waggle permission to use the firearm for firearm qualifications, according to the affidavit. A judge signed the first-degree murder warrant for Waggle in August.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Approves Assisted-Living Project Amid Contamination Concerns
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council has approved the major site plan for a 150-unit assisted-living facility planned next to a property with a history of petroleum contamination, despite objections from nearby residents who say they still lack answers about potential risks. The project, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF, is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard. The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component.

Construction has not begun. The developer must still submit construction plans for technical review, followed by additional reviews involving the South Florida Water Management District and other agencies.

A group of residents has opposed the project, pointing to the environmental history of the neighboring contaminated property and what it could mean for future residents of the facility. Resident David Lipps said the issue is not about what is being built on the site, arguing that nearby businesses and other facilities could also be affected by environmental concerns. Resident Charlie D'Agata said residents have raised objections at City Council meetings for about two years and questioned why a developer would be allowed to build near a property he described as contaminated. Residents say they have contacted the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Health seeking more information about the site.

An engineering letter adds new weight to those concerns. The letter, from BTEX Engineering, discusses a March 2026 meeting with environmental officials about the neighboring property and states that the proposed remediation approach should be changed because of concerns about surrounding properties, including the planned assisted-living facility. The letter said vapors would need to be captured during remediation. The full environmental history of the neighboring property and the extent of any potential impact on surrounding land remain central questions for residents as the project moves toward construction review.

hero.headline: MARTY Bus Service Halted Countywide After Martin County Contract Dispute
hero.body:
MARTY public transit service across Martin County stopped abruptly Thursday after its operator, Martin County Transit LLC, notified the county it was immediately discontinuing service, leaving residents without their regular transportation. County officials said they received no advance warning that service would stop that day.

According to the county, Martin County Transit LLC had requested a significant increase in its contract, citing rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs that the company says have caused significant financial losses since it began operating MARTY in July 2025. Negotiations between the county and the company failed to produce an agreement. County officials said the company gave formal notice about two weeks ago that it would terminate its contract in 180 days, but then told the county Thursday morning that it was ending service immediately.

George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said the county is now working on both short-term and long-term solutions to restore service, though he did not offer a timeline. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It's just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It's going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." County officials said they are working with community partners, including United Way, to assist residents affected by the shutdown, and they plan to post updates on social media as a solution develops.

The suspension has already disrupted daily routines for riders who depend on MARTY. Leticia Chaclan, a Martin County resident who has ridden the bus for years, waited in Stuart on Thursday for a bus that never came and said she had not known service had been suspended. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don't have a driver's license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It's very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don't drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don't drive, and we go everywhere to shop." Another rider, Steven Godell, said he resorted to riding his bicycle Thursday after the bus failed to show up that morning. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound Woman Charged, Held Without Bond in Cat Burial Case
cards.teaser: Alba Luz Chavez faces four felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty after deputies said she buried kittens alive during a mental health crisis. A third kitten remains missing.
cards.body:
A Hobe Sound woman has been arrested and charged with four felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty after deputies said she buried kittens alive in her yard, believing they were demons. The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested 37-year-old Alba Luz Chavez this week after investigators said they dug up two live kittens and two dead kittens buried on a property at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park. Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail. Deputies had previously confirmed finding the four animals during a search that recovered two survivors alive and two dead.

Deputies were called to the home Thursday night for what family members described as a mental health crisis. Relatives told deputies Chavez believed the cats were demons and had killed several animals earlier in the week. According to the arrest affidavit, Chavez had told residents of the home she killed two kittens on Monday. Three juveniles living at the residence told deputies Chavez had appeared to be experiencing a mental health episode for most of the week. The juveniles said they locked three surviving kittens inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday evening, but when they returned around 6 p.m., they found Chavez had forced her way into the room and the kittens were gone.

Investigators said Chavez initially refused to tell family members where the animals were. While speaking with deputies, Chavez allegedly said, "If you want the cats, you will need gloves, a red bag and a shovel," and directed them to an area on the property. Deputies dug there and found two live kittens buried underground inside plastic Publix bags, according to the affidavit. They later uncovered two deceased kittens that appeared to be in the early stages of decomposition. Detectives searched for a third missing kitten but were unable to locate it.

During an interview, Chavez told investigators she had been cleaning her house and referred to the cats as "very ugly," according to the affidavit. Investigators wrote that Chavez also made statements indicating she did not want black cats and suggested kittens of different colors "had different fates." The affidavit states Chavez later began singing instead of answering additional questions. The two surviving kittens were taken to a pet emergency center for treatment. cards.headline: Vero Beach Man Charged With Murder in Ex-Girlfriend's Shooting Death
cards.teaser: Matthew Allen Waggle was arrested on a warrant in the August shooting death of Dawn Marie Kriskewic, who was found with gunshot wounds in a Vero Beach roadway. Surveillance footage and a coworker's account of prior threats helped build the case against him.
cards.body:
A 33-year-old man has been arrested on a first-degree murder charge in the August shooting death of a Vero Beach woman, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Matthew Allen Waggle was taken into custody Oct. 5 on an active warrant and is being held without bond in connection with the death of Dawn Marie Kriskewic, his former girlfriend.

Deputies responded to the 500 block of 1st Street after 911 callers reported a woman lying in the roadway. They found Kriskewic with injuries consistent with gunshot wounds and began CPR. She was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

Investigators identified Waggle as Kriskewic's former boyfriend. A coworker told detectives that Kriskewic had expressed concerns about Waggle before her death and said he had previously threatened consequences if she called police when he came to retrieve his belongings. Surveillance footage showed a person investigators identified as Waggle near the area around the time of the shooting, as well as him walking through the area both before and after it happened. Detectives said the footage also showed him discarding a shirt, which investigators later recovered.

Near the crime scene, investigators recovered a rolling suitcase containing men's clothing and a tactical vest bearing a "security" patch. A Ruger pistol was found on a neighboring property along with a note stating that another person had given Waggle permission to use the firearm for firearm qualifications, according to the affidavit. A judge signed the first-degree murder warrant for Waggle in August, and he was taken into custody at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast Kennel Club brings four days of dog sports to Fort Pierce fairgrounds
hero.teaser: The Treasure Coast Kennel Club's Pirate Cluster offers free admission to watch dock diving, FastCAT racing, agility and frisbee competitions at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds this weekend, with same-day participation available for many events.
hero.body:
The Treasure Coast Kennel Club is hosting its four-day Pirate Cluster this weekend at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds in Fort Pierce, drawing dog lovers from across South Florida for a lineup of canine sports and family activities. The event features dock diving, FastCAT racing, agility courses and UpDog frisbee competitions, with admission and parking free for spectators.

Treasure Coast Kennel Club President Lisa Root said the event covers the range of sporting activities the club organizes with dogs throughout the year. "It has to do with all kinds of sporting events that we do with our dogs, so dock diving, FastCAT, agility, UpDog (frisbee catching). It's fun," she said. Many of the events allow dog owners to sign up and have their pets try the activities the same day, though fees apply for anyone entering a dog into individual competitions.

Dock diving, one of the event's most popular draws, has dogs sprinting down a platform and leaping into a pool chasing a toy. Participants say the dogs often sense the excitement before they even reach the venue. "Once they start competing, they know what this dock means," said dock-diving participant Janet. "You'll see them when they start coming in. They just roll past the dock, and they'll start barking in the cars and stuff because they know that they get to get up here and just jump." Organizers say that enthusiasm tends to spread to the owners and spectators watching from the sidelines.

Beyond the competitions, the Pirate Cluster includes vendors and raffles, giving families a chance to spend time with other dog owners in the community. Organizers describe the weekend as an opportunity for anyone, whether they own a seasoned competitor or simply want to learn more about canine sports, to see firsthand what the activities involve. The event reflects the growing popularity of dog sports as a way for owners to stay active, strengthen their bond with their pets and connect with fellow dog lovers on the Treasure Coast.

hero.headline: MARTY Bus Service Halts Without Warning Across Martin County
hero.body:
MARTY public transit service in Martin County stopped abruptly Thursday, leaving residents who depend on the buses without their regular transportation while county officials scramble for a fix. Martin County officials said they received no advance warning that service would stop. The system's operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract with the county, citing rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs that the company says have caused significant financial losses since it began running the service in July 2025.

Negotiations between the county and the operator failed to produce an agreement. County officials said Martin County Transit LLC gave 180-day notice to terminate its contract approximately two weeks ago, but then notified the county Thursday morning that it was immediately discontinuing service, far earlier than that notice period allowed.

George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said the county is now exploring both short-term and long-term options to get buses running again. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It's just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It's going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." County officials said they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents affected by the shutdown. No timeline has been set for when MARTY operations will resume, and officials said they will post updates on social media and notify residents once a solution is reached.

The sudden suspension caught riders off guard. Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for a bus in Stuart on Thursday that never came, and said she had not known service was suspended until a reporter told her. Chaclan said she has ridden the bus for years and considers it essential for the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don't have a driver's license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It's very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don't drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don't drive, and we go everywhere to shop." Steven Godell, another rider affected by the shutdown, said he rode his bicycle Thursday after the MARTY bus failed to show up that morning. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Residents Question Contamination Near Approved Assisted-Living Site
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council approved a 150-unit assisted-living facility near a petroleum-contaminated property, but residents say they still want answers about environmental risks before construction moves forward.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council has approved the major site plan for a 150-unit assisted-living facility near a property with a history of petroleum contamination, but nearby residents say unresolved environmental questions should not be ignored as the project advances. The development, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF, is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard. The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component.

The council approved the major site plan in September. Construction has not begun, and the developer must still submit construction plans for technical review, followed by additional reviews involving the South Florida Water Management District and other agencies.

A group of residents has opposed the project, pointing to the environmental history of the neighboring contaminated property and what it could mean for the people who eventually live at the facility. Resident David Lipps said the concern isn't about what is being built on the site itself, arguing that nearby businesses and other facilities could also be affected by the contamination. Resident Charlie D'Agata said residents have raised objections at City Council meetings for about two years and has questioned why a developer would be allowed to build near a property he describes as contaminated. Residents say they have reached out to outside agencies, including the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Health, seeking more information about the site.

An engineering letter obtained by residents adds weight to their concerns. The letter, which discussed a March 2026 meeting with environmental officials about the neighboring property, was written by BTEX Engineering and recommended changing the proposed remediation approach because of concerns about surrounding properties, including the planned assisted-living facility. The letter said vapors would need to be captured during the remediation process. The environmental history of the neighboring property and the potential extent of any impact on surrounding land remain central unanswered questions for residents as the project moves toward the next stages of city and agency review.

hero.headline: MARTY Bus Service Suspended in Martin County, Riders Left Without Rides
hero.body:
MARTY public transit service in Martin County came to an abrupt halt Thursday, leaving residents who depend on the buses without their regular transportation as county officials scramble to find a solution. County officials said they received no advance warning that service would stop. MARTY's operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract with the county, citing rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs that the company says have caused significant financial losses since it began operating the service in July 2025. Negotiations between the county and the company failed to produce an agreement.

County officials said Martin County Transit LLC gave 180-day notice roughly two weeks ago that it intended to terminate its contract. But on Thursday morning, the company notified the county it was discontinuing service immediately, cutting off bus routes relied on by residents across Martin County with no transition period.

George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said officials are now exploring both short-term and long-term options to restore service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It's just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It's going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." County officials said they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents affected by the shutdown. No timeline has been given for when MARTY operations could resume, and officials said updates will be posted on social media as a solution is reached.

The sudden suspension left riders scrambling Thursday. Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for the bus in Stuart, but it never came, and she did not know service had been suspended until a reporter told her. Chaclan said she has ridden the bus for years and considers it essential for many in the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don't have a driver's license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It's very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don't drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don't drive, and we go everywhere to shop." Steven Godell said he rode his bicycle Thursday after the MARTY bus never showed up that morning. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach Man Killed in Loxahatchee Groves Motorcycle Crash
cards.teaser: A 37-year-old Jensen Beach man died Sunday night when his motorcycle slammed into the back of a van in Loxahatchee Groves, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office.
cards.body:
A 37-year-old Jensen Beach man died Sunday night when his motorcycle crashed into the back of a van in Loxahatchee Groves, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said. Derrick Teets was pronounced dead at the scene near the intersection of Southern Boulevard and D Road, close to Lion Country Safari. Deputies responded at 9:49 p.m.

According to the crash report, Teets was riding a 2021 Honda CBR600RR at high speed eastbound in the inside lane of Southern Boulevard, traveling behind a Ford Transit van driven by a 53-year-old Boca Raton woman. The motorcycle struck the back of the van. Teets was ejected from the bike, which slid into the median.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Mermaid Brandee Anthony Turns Decade-Old Hobby Into Full Business
hero.body:
Brandee Anthony, known as the Vero Beach Mermaid, has spent the past decade building a business around a childhood fantasy, offering mermaid makeovers, beach photoshoots and poolside swimming lessons to clients of all ages. Anthony is an elite level PADI dive instructor who combines her diving credentials with 15 years of experience as a professional photographer to create the underwater and beach experiences.

Anthony said the idea began with her work as a professional live streamer. "I was a professional live streamer a long time ago, so I thought it would be really cool to take all my viewers underwater, but how can I make that interesting and magical?" she said. That early curiosity turned into a career. "That was 10 years ago and I'm a little in love with mermaiding for sure," she said.

Each session starts inside what Anthony calls her magical closet, stocked with tropical-inspired tails, tops and accessories designed specifically for mermaid gear. The silicone tails each weigh about 30 to 35 pounds, and clients can choose from crowns, armbands and other embellishments to complete their look. Anthony said she helps each client pick options suited to them, pairing a tail, top, accessories and crown before heading to the beach for photos. Tail styles include designs she calls the wind trader and a leafy sea dragon pattern.

Once clients are suited up, Anthony walks them through posing on the shoreline, instructing them to move toward the water like a sea turtle and turn their fin, or fluke, toward the camera. She guides beginners through a seated pose first, telling them to relax and let the wind take their hair for what she calls a little water love. The experience then moves poolside for a basic mermaiding lesson, where Anthony teaches clients to flex their foot toward the surface and push down to feel the water's resistance, which propels the tail. She also leads clients through a back float and a brief underwater dive, counting down before they breathe out and dive down to surface again, the same technique she uses to shoot video underwater.

Anthony said clients seek out the experience for a range of reasons, from simple fun to deeper personal reasons. "I've had people come to me for fun and some for deeper reasons," she said. "Coming on a retreat or take a course really did change their lives, or changed the trajectory of their lives. I've turned a few people into pro mermaids," she said. She said mermaiding as an adult offers a chance to play without acting like a kid. "I think that's what mermaiding as an adult feels like is you don't have to act like a kid but you can be an adult that plays," she said. "And that's where it can be fun or it can be more, some people just want to feel empowered. Or good in their skin and they do a photo shoot or a bucket list thing."

hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms Convicted of Official Misconduct
hero.teaser: A St. Lucie County jury acquitted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of bid tampering but convicted him of official misconduct over a Lincoln Park nonprofit lease tied to his niece. He remains free on bond ahead of sentencing.
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors acquitted Mimms of bid tampering, the first count he faced, but found him guilty on the official-misconduct charge. They specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the city government he served.

The trial, which began Sept. 29, centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city's bidding process for two vacant lots in the Lincoln Park area. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, located near the Lincoln Theater.

During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP's evaluation criteria and committee makeup after the matter had already been referred to the city's purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP's publication and administration, and challenged the state's claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement.

Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state's request to take Mimms into custody pending sentencing. Mimms will remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. in St. Lucie County Circuit Court.

The sudden shutdown has left residents who rely on MARTY to get around the county without their regular transportation option. George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said officials are now exploring both short-term and long-term solutions to restore service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It’s just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It’s going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." In the meantime, county officials say they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents impacted by the shutdown. The county has not provided a timeline for when MARTY operations could resume. Officials say they will continue posting updates on social media and will notify residents as soon as a solution is reached. Riders react Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for the bus in Stuart on Thursday, but it never came. She was unaware that the MARTY bus had been suspended until WPBF's Jasimine Yasmine Julmisse informed her. Chaclain says she's been riding the bus for years and that it's a staple for many members of the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don’t have a driver’s license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It’s very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don’t drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don’t drive, and we go everywhere to shop." The sudden suspension of service impacted riders including Steven Godell, who said he was on his bicycle Thursday because he didn't see the MARTY bus come Thursday morning. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

cards.headline: Hobe Sound Woman Accused of Burying Cats Alive, Calling Them Demons
cards.teaser: A Hobe Sound woman is in custody after the Martin County Sheriff's Office said she buried at least four of her cats alive in her yard, believing they were demons. Deputies are still searching the property.
cards.body:
A Hobe Sound woman is in custody after the Martin County Sheriff's Office said she buried at least four cats alive in her yard because she believed they were demons. Alba Chavez, 37, was arrested following what the sheriff's office called a disturbing animal cruelty case at a home in a Hobe Sound mobile home park in the 11,000 block of Southeast Federal Highway.

Patrol deputies and investigators with MCSO Animal Services responded to the home after Chavez told them about the burials. Deputies managed to rescue two of the cats, but two others were found dead. Crews are digging up portions of the property as part of the investigation.

Chavez will face multiple counts of aggravated animal cruelty, the sheriff's office said. The agency said the investigation remains active and deputies are continuing to search the property.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police Arrest 2 After Woman Shot At on South Sixth Street
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police have arrested two people after a woman was attacked and then shot at as she fled the scene on South Sixth Street. Officers responded to the area at 7:12 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, after the victim called police to report someone was shooting at her, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department.

The investigation found the victim had gone to a residence on South Sixth Street to speak with her boyfriend about their relationship. When she arrived, several people ran out of the home and attacked her. Police said the victim managed to break free, get into her vehicle and drive away.

As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and opened fire on her vehicle, according to police. A second suspect was arrested on allegations of driving the shooter away from the scene afterward.

Police identified the suspects as 18 year old Keibin Lopez-Godoy and 18 year old Kailee Yurubi. Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Mourns Teen Sulli Bah as Family Seeks Accountability in Shooting
hero.body:
Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman "Sulli" Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office says investigators are looking into whether the shooting involved self-defense, and no arrests have been made. The celebration of life was held at the restaurant where Bah worked, and mourners described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.

As rain fell Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame as people who knew Bah gathered to honor him. Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said he left a mark on everyone around him. "He touched everybody's heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room," Rodriguez said. Friend Alex Cortez, who boxed alongside Bah and shared many memories with him, said Bah was focused on building a future for himself. "He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future," Cortez said. Another friend, Xavi Espinosa, remembered Bah's welcoming nature from the moment they met. "Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul," Espinosa said.

The sheriff's office said Bah was at the meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired, and the investigation into whether the shooting was self-defense remains open. Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his whole life ahead of him. She is calling on investigators to weigh every detail of the case. "I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right," Godfrey said. "I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail."

During the celebration, those who knew Bah took turns sharing memories of him. Angela Sanders, one of his former sixth grade teachers, recalled his personality and smile. "His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room," Sanders said. Friend Myan Agosto said Bah consistently looked out for the people around him. "He never failed to make sure everybody was okay," Agosto said. "He was just a really good friend." Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person. One speaker at the gathering reflected on the reach of Bah's short life: "He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth, look at this room." Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

cards.headline: Family of Death Row Inmate Pleads for Clemency in Deputy's 1986 Murder
cards.teaser: William Reaves is scheduled to be executed Oct. 20 for killing Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986. His family is now publicly asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to commute his sentence to life in prison.
cards.body:
William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for the 1986 murder of Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkowski, who was 29 when he was killed. With Reaves' execution scheduled for Oct. 20, his family is speaking publicly for the first time, asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant clemency and commute the death sentence to life in prison.

"I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him," said Meredith Farrington, Reaves' nephew. Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of the crime or the pain it caused Raczkowski's family. "I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," he said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life." Still, Farrington said he wants DeSantis "to look at the whole picture" before the execution proceeds.

According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County on Sept. 23, 1986, after he was unable to get a taxi. Raczkowski responded to help him call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed, and Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him. A stretch of road near the scene now bears Raczkowski's name. His brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss for nearly 40 years. "Why? Why?" he said near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody... The pain will still always be there."

DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant on Sept. 22, setting the execution for Oct. 20. Farrington is not asking for a pardon or release, but wants the sentence commuted so Reaves, now 77, spends the rest of his life in prison. Farrington points to Reaves' service as a Vietnam War veteran and decades of appeals raising questions about his mental health, substance abuse and trial representation. Court records show Reaves argued his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate evidence of his drug use and mental health. "The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case." Testimony at sentencing described Reaves as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," while later experts testified he suffered from PTSD and substance abuse.

Farrington said none of that excuses the killing. "I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," he said. "He's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life." Farrington said he understands if Raczkowski's family wants the execution to proceed. "I know that the family, the officer... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," he said. Reaves has lost his latest bid to stop the execution in Indian River County court and has appealed to the Florida Supreme Court. Unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency, the execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 and would mark Florida's 18th execution in 2026.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Mermaid Brandee Anthony Turns Diving Skills Into Magical Underwater Experiences
cards.teaser: Vero Beach-based PADI dive instructor Brandee Anthony runs a mermaid experience business offering makeovers, beach photoshoots and poolside swimming lessons for clients of all ages.
cards.body:
Brandee Anthony, known as the Vero Beach Mermaid, is an elite-level PADI dive instructor who teaches people of all ages to become mermaids. Her business offers experiences ranging from glamorous mermaid makeovers and beach photoshoots to poolside swimming lessons.

Anthony said the idea grew out of her earlier career as a professional live streamer. "I was a professional live streamer a long time ago, so I thought it would be really cool to take all my viewers underwater, but how can I make that interesting and magical?" she said. That early curiosity became a lasting passion. "That was 10 years ago and I'm a little in love with mermaiding for sure," Anthony said.

Each experience begins with a mermaid makeover inside what Anthony calls her custom fantasy closet, stocked with tropical-inspired tails, tops and accessories made specifically for mermaid gear. The closet includes silicone tails that each weigh about 30 to 35 pounds, along with crowns, armbands and other embellishments meant to complete the look. "Mermaid crowns and armbands and embellishments, kind of the final touches to help people really feel like they have a full ensemble," Anthony said. Armbands come in several styles, including options with a vibrant teal accent. After choosing a tail, top, accessories and crown, clients head to the beach for a photoshoot. Anthony, who has worked as a professional photographer for 15 years, combines elaborate costumes with beach backdrops for the shoot. She guides clients through poses on the shoreline, starting with a seated pose she describes as the easiest for beginners.

The experience also includes a poolside mermaid swimming lesson, where Anthony strips the process back from the glamour of the photoshoot to focus on technique. She teaches clients to flex and push their feet to generate the propulsion needed to swim in a tail, and helps them practice back floating before guiding them through a full underwater dive. Anthony said she tailors each session to a client's comfort level. "Once people get in a tail and they find their groove, it turns into a bunch of people just playing in a pool," she said. Clients seek out the experience for different reasons, she said, from simple fun to deeper personal milestones. "Coming on a retreat or take a course really did change their lives, or changed the trajectory of their lives. I've turned a few people into pro mermaids," Anthony said. She added that mermaiding offers adults a chance to play without losing their maturity. "I think that's what mermaiding as an adult feels like is you don't have to act like a kid but you can be an adult that plays," she said.

hero.headline: Jury Convicts Former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of Official Misconduct
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors acquitted Mimms of bid tampering, the first count he faced, but found him guilty on the official-misconduct charge, specifically determining the misconduct involved blocking communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the city government he served.

The trial, which began Sept. 29, centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city's bidding process for two vacant lots in the Lincoln Park area. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, located near the Lincoln Theater.

During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP's evaluation criteria and committee makeup after the matter had already been referred to the city's purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department, not Mimms, controlled the RFP's publication and administration, and disputed the state's claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement.

Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state's request to take Mimms into custody pending sentencing, according to court records. Mimms will remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. in St. Lucie County Circuit Court.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Women Charged After Neglected Dog Dies at Pine Creek Apartments
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police say Samya Shanice Bryant and Danielle Amanda Potts failed to get veterinary care for a severely malnourished dog that was later euthanized due to organ failure.
cards.body:
Two Fort Pierce women are facing aggravated animal cruelty charges after a severely neglected dog died from his injuries, according to arrest reports from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Samya Shanice Bryant, 25, and Danielle Amanda Potts, 28, were arrested Oct. 2 in connection with the neglect and death of a dog at Pine Creek Apartments.

Officers first found the dog on Sept. 29 lying outside an apartment. He was severely underweight with visible ribs, had infected sores on his paws, and had no access to food or water, according to police.

Bryant told officers the dog was hers and said he had been sick for weeks after another man allegedly poured boiling water on him. Police said both Bryant and Potts lived in the apartment and had control of the dog but did not get him veterinary treatment.

Animal Control took the dog for emergency care, but he had to be euthanized on Oct. 2 because of his injuries, infections and organ failure. Bryant and Potts were both arrested and charged with aggravated animal cruelty and confining or impounding an animal without sufficient food or water.

hero.headline: MARTY Bus Service Halted Across Martin County, Leaving Riders Stranded
hero.body:
MARTY public transit service across Martin County came to an abrupt stop Thursday, leaving residents who depend on the buses without their regular transportation while county officials scramble to find a fix. County officials said they received no advance warning that service would end Thursday. MARTY's operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase to its contract, saying rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs had caused significant financial losses since it took over the service in July 2025.

Negotiations between the county and the company broke down. County officials said Martin County Transit LLC gave 180-day notice to terminate its contract about two weeks ago, but then notified the county Thursday morning that it was immediately discontinuing service, catching officials off guard.

George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said the county is pursuing both short-term and long-term solutions to restore bus service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It's just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It's going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." County officials said they are working with community partners, including United Way, to assist residents affected by the shutdown. They have not given a timeline for when MARTY operations might resume, but said updates will be posted on social media as a solution is reached.

The sudden halt left riders scrambling Thursday. Leticia Chaclan waited for a bus in Stuart that never came and only learned of the suspension when a reporter told her. Chaclan said she has ridden the bus for years and called it essential for many in the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don't have a driver's license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It's very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don't drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don't drive, and we go everywhere to shop." Steven Godell said he rode his bicycle Thursday after the MARTY bus failed to show up that morning. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said.

hero.headline: Ex-Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms Convicted of Official Misconduct
hero.body:
A jury found former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms guilty Thursday of official misconduct, a third-degree felony, while acquitting him of bid tampering, a second-degree felony. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on both charges following an investigation by the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.

Investigators accused Mimms of rigging the bidding process for two vacant parcels of land along Avenue D, next to the Lincoln Theater, in favor of a local nonprofit called Lincoln Park Young Professionals. Caleta Scott, Mimms' niece and a city employee, sat on the nonprofit's board. The organization had received a $500,000 grant from Allegheny Franciscan Ministries for a community center project, but the project was never built.

Johnathan Bridges, special assistant state attorney, and Brandon White, major crimes attorney for the 19th Circuit, said prosecutors presented a mountain of evidence against Mimms, including emails and city documents. White said millions of dollars have been wasted by Fort Pierce city hall under Mimms' leadership and that the waste went unchecked for too long. He said Fort Pierce residents deserve better and that the verdict shows the corruption that occurred under Mimms, adding that it was about time someone was held accountable. Mimms was granted a pre-sentencing investigation and is scheduled to be sentenced in December at the St. Lucie County Courthouse. Prosecutors said he could face a maximum of five years in prison.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police Arrest Two After Woman Attacked, Shot At on South Sixth Street
cards.teaser: A woman escaped an attack outside a Fort Pierce home and was shot at while fleeing in her car. Police have arrested two 18-year-olds in connection with the attempted homicide.
cards.body:
A woman fled for her life after she was attacked and then shot at while driving away from a home on South Sixth Street in Fort Pierce. The Fort Pierce Police Department said officers responded to the scene at 7:12 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, after the victim called 911 to report that someone was shooting at her.

Police said the investigation showed the victim had gone to the South Sixth Street address to speak with her boyfriend about their relationship. When she arrived, several people ran out of the residence and began attacking her, according to police.

The victim managed to break free, get into her vehicle, and drive away, police said. As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and opened fire on her vehicle, according to police. A second person allegedly drove the shooter away from the scene afterward.

Fort Pierce police arrested two 18-year-olds in connection with the attack. Keibin Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. Kailee Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact for allegedly driving the shooter from the scene.

hero.headline: Hurricane Deductibles Kick In Statewide, Including Treasure Coast, as Isaias Nears Panhandle
hero.body:
Hurricane deductibles have taken effect on homeowner insurance policies across Florida, including on the Treasure Coast, because Hurricane Isaias is approaching the Panhandle. The special deductibles, which can run thousands of dollars higher than standard ones, apply to any wind-related claim statewide even in areas far from the storm's path.

Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said the trigger for most policies is a hurricane watch or warning posted anywhere in Florida. Once that happens, homeowners anywhere in the state become subject to the higher deductible for hurricane-related damage, not just those near the storm itself.

Hurricane deductibles differ sharply from standard insurance deductibles because they are calculated as a percentage of a home's total insured value rather than a percentage of the claim. Norberg said the deductible is typically 2 to 3 percent of the insured value, though some policies carry deductibles as high as 5 or 10 percent. A 2 percent deductible on a $300,000 home amounts to about $6,000 out of pocket before insurance coverage applies. Norberg said any wind damage that causes a claim, even for a homeowner in Palm Beach County, would be subject to the wind deductible while a hurricane warning or watch is in effect anywhere in Florida.

Under state statute, the hurricane deductible expires 72 hours after the last hurricane warning is lifted anywhere in Florida. Until then, Treasure Coast homeowners filing wind-related claims could face significantly higher upfront costs than they would under a standard deductible, even though Isaias itself is forecast to stay away from the region.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Shooting Suspect Charged With Attempted Homicide After Woman Fled Attack
cards.teaser: A woman escaped a group attack on South Sixth Street and was shot at while driving away. Fort Pierce police arrested two teenagers, including the alleged shooter.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police arrested two people after a woman was attacked and then shot at as she drove away from a domestic dispute on South Sixth Street. Officers responded to the scene at 7:12 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, after the victim called police and reported someone was shooting at her, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department.

Investigators said the victim had gone to the South Sixth Street address to speak with her boyfriend about their relationship. When she arrived, several people ran out of the residence and attacked her. Police said the victim managed to escape, get into her vehicle, and drive away from the property.

As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and opened fire on her vehicle, according to police. A second suspect was arrested for allegedly driving the shooter away from the scene afterward.

Police identified the suspects as Keibin Lopez-Godoy, 18, and Kailee Yurubi, 18. Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.

cards.headline: Reaves Family Pleads with DeSantis for Clemency Ahead of Oct. 20 Execution
cards.teaser: William Reaves is set to be executed Oct. 20 for killing Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986. His family is now publicly asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to commute his death sentence to life in prison.
cards.body:
William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for shooting and killing 29-year-old Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986. His execution is scheduled for Oct. 20, and with less than two weeks remaining, his family is speaking publicly for the first time to ask Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant clemency and commute his death sentence to life in prison.

"I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him," Reaves' nephew, Meredith Farrington, said. Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of Reaves' crime or the pain it has caused the Raczkowski family. "I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," he said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life." Still, he added, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."

According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County on Sept. 23, 1986, after he was unable to get a taxi. Raczkowski responded and was helping Reaves call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed, and Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him. A stretch of road near where the deputy died now bears his name. Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss for nearly 40 years. "Why? Why?" he said near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." He added, "The pain will still always be there."

DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22. Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison, but to commute his sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars. Central to the family's plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation. At sentencing, testimony described Reaves as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome" rather than post-traumatic stress disorder; later experts testified he suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments. Farrington said none of that excuses the murder. "I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," he said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."

Farrington said he understands why Raczkowski's family may want the execution to proceed. "I know that the family, the officer ... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," he said. Reaves has already lost his latest attempt to stop the execution in Indian River County court and has appealed that decision to the Florida Supreme Court. His execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency. If carried out, it will mark the 18th execution in Florida in 2026.
