cards.headline: Two Fort Pierce Women Charged After Neglected Dog Dies at Pine Creek Apartments
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police arrested two women on aggravated animal cruelty charges after a severely malnourished dog found outside their apartment had to be euthanized. Officers said the dog had infected sores, no food or water, and had gone weeks without veterinary care.
cards.body:
Two Fort Pierce women are facing aggravated animal cruelty charges after a severely neglected dog in their care died, according to arrest reports from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Samya Shanice Bryant, 25, and Danielle Amanda Potts, 28, were arrested Oct. 2 in connection with the neglect and death of a dog at Pine Creek Apartments.

Officers first found the dog on Sept. 29, lying outside an apartment at the complex. Police said the animal was severely underweight with visible ribs, had infected sores on his paws, and had no access to food or water.

Bryant told officers the dog was hers and said he had been sick for weeks after another man allegedly poured boiling water on him, according to police. Both Bryant and Potts lived in the apartment and had control of the dog, but neither got him veterinary treatment, according to Fort Pierce police.

Animal Control took the dog for emergency care following the Sept. 29 discovery, but he had to be euthanized on Oct. 2 because of his injuries, infections and organ failure, police said. Bryant and Potts are each charged with aggravated animal cruelty and confining or impounding an animal without sufficient food or water.

hero.headline: Family Asks DeSantis for Clemency Before Oct. 20 Execution in Deputy's 1986 Death
hero.body:
The family of death row inmate William Reaves is publicly asking Gov. Ron DeSantis for the first time to grant clemency before Reaves' scheduled Oct. 20 execution for the 1986 murder of Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves, now 77, has spent nearly four decades on death row after shooting Raczkowski four times in the back during a struggle outside a convenience store on Sept. 23, 1986. DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant on Sept. 22.

Farrington said he does not dispute the gravity of his uncle's crime or the pain it caused the Raczkowski family. "I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," Farrington said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life." Still, he said, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."

According to court records, Reaves called 911 from the convenience store after failing to get a taxi. Raczkowski responded and was helping Reaves arrange a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants, triggering the struggle that ended in the deputy's death. Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with that loss for nearly 40 years. "Why? Why?" he said near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name. "The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said.

Farrington is not seeking a pardon or his uncle's release, only a commutation of the death sentence to life in prison. He points to Reaves' service as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and to decades of appeals raising questions about his mental health, substance abuse and trial representation. Court records show Reaves' attorney was handling his first death row case and was accused of failing to adequately investigate Reaves' drug use and mental health. Testimony at sentencing described Reaves as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," and later experts testified he had PTSD and substance abuse impairments. "I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "He's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life." Reaves has lost his latest bid to halt the execution in Indian River County court and has appealed that ruling to the Florida Supreme Court. His execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency. If carried out, it will be Florida's 18th execution of 2026.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Mermaid Brandee Anthony Turns Diving Skills Into Underwater Magic
cards.teaser: An elite PADI dive instructor in Vero Beach has built a business transforming clients into mermaids, combining glamorous beach photoshoots with poolside swimming lessons.
cards.body:
Brandee Anthony, known as the Vero Beach Mermaid, is an elite level PADI dive instructor who teaches people of all ages to become mermaids. Her offerings range from glamorous mermaid makeovers and beach photoshoots to poolside swimming lessons. The idea grew out of her earlier career as a professional live streamer. "I was a professional live streamer a long time ago, so I thought it would be really cool to take all my viewers underwater, but how can I make that interesting and magical?" Anthony said. That curiosity took hold a decade ago and has not let go. "That was 10 years ago and I'm a little in love with mermaiding for sure," Anthony said.

Every experience starts with a mermaid makeover inside Anthony's custom fantasy closet, which is filled with tropical-inspired tails, tops and accessories made specifically for mermaid gear. "We're going to start with a mermaid makeover, which is one of my favorite parts," Anthony said. The silicone tails each weigh about 30 to 35 pounds, and Anthony rounds out the look with crowns, armbands and other embellishments. "Mermaid crowns and armbands and embellishments, kind of the final touches to help people really feel like they have a full ensemble," she said. Clients choose a tail, a top, accessories and a crown before heading to the beach. Tail styles include designs Anthony calls a "wind trader" and a leafy sea dragon pattern.

Anthony, who has also worked as a professional photographer for 15 years, pairs elaborate costumes with scenic backdrops for the beach photoshoot portion of the experience. She guides clients through their first poses on the shoreline, starting with a seated pose she calls the easiest to learn. "The seated is the easiest first pose, you can kind of just look at the ocean and relax and let the wind take your hair," she said.

After the photoshoot, clients head poolside for a basic mermaiding class, where Anthony strips the experience down to swimming fundamentals. She teaches the leg movement that propels a mermaid tail through the water and walks clients through a full underwater dive. "3.2.1. breathe out, we dive down and then pop up," Anthony said. "That was so good, that was fun, and that's how we shoot video underwater." Anthony said clients come to her for a range of reasons, from simple fun to more meaningful personal milestones. "I've had people come to me for fun and some for deeper reasons," she said. "Coming on a retreat or take a course really did change their lives, or changed the trajectory of their lives. I've turned a few people into pro mermaids." For Anthony, the appeal of mermaiding as an adult is the chance to play without judgment. "I think that's what mermaiding as an adult feels like is you don't have to act like a kid but you can be an adult that plays," she said. "And that's where it can be fun or it can be more, some people just want to feel empowered. Or good in their skin and they do a photo shoot or a bucket list thing."

hero.headline: MARTY Transit Service Halted in Martin County After Provider Cancels Contract
hero.body:
Martin County Public Transit, known as MARTY, has stopped operating after the county's contracted transit provider abruptly canceled its services, leaving riders without bus or paratransit service effective immediately. The cancellation also leaves 29 employees of Martin County Transit without jobs, according to a statement the transit provider gave in response to inquiries.

Martin County said in a statement Thursday that it is aware the contracted transit service provider has canceled service and that MARTY operations are currently interrupted. "Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," the county said. "Additional information will be provided as it becomes available." The county added, "We understand the importance of MARTY services to our community and apologize for the disruption." Martin County Transit said in its own statement, "We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system."

United Way of Martin County says it is preparing for a surge in requests through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents. The program launched in September 2022 and has provided thousands of rides to Martin County residents facing transportation barriers, but officials say it was already strained by rising demand and funding cuts before the MARTY disruption. "Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table," said Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County. "When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it." Ashley Capital has pledged an initial $2,500 donation to help support Ride United's response to the outage. United Way stressed that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its help is only a temporary measure depending on available funding.

Residents who need transportation assistance can call 772-283-4800 or visit unitedwaymartin.org/rideunited for more information. Martin County said it will provide updates as it works to restore public transit service, with details available on the county's transit website.

hero.headline: Reaves Family Pleads for Clemency Before Oct. 20 Execution in Deputy's Death
hero.body:
The family of death row inmate William Reaves is publicly asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant him clemency before his scheduled Oct. 20 execution for the 1986 murder of Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves, now 77, has spent nearly four decades on death row after fatally shooting the 29-year-old deputy four times in the back during a struggle at a convenience store.

Farrington said he does not dispute the gravity of his uncle's crime or the pain it caused the Raczkowski family. "I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," Farrington said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life." Still, he said, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."

According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County on Sept. 23, 1986, after he could not get a taxi. Raczkowski responded and was helping Reaves arrange a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants, leading to a struggle in which Reaves shot and killed the deputy. DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant on Sept. 22, setting the execution for Oct. 20. Farrington is not seeking a pardon or release for his uncle, but wants the sentence commuted to life in prison, pointing to Reaves' record as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and decades of appeals raising questions about his mental health, substance abuse and trial representation. Testimony at sentencing described Reaves as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," and experts later testified he had PTSD and substance abuse issues. Court records show Reaves argued his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate that evidence. "The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case." Farrington said none of it excuses the killing. "I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," he said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."

For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has grieved near his brother's gravesite. "Why? Why?" he said. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now carries his name. "The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said. Farrington said he understands the Raczkowski family's position. "I know that the family, the officer ... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," he said. Reaves has already lost his latest bid to stop the execution in Indian River County court and has appealed that ruling to the Florida Supreme Court. His execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency. If carried out, it would be Florida's 18th execution in 2026.

cards.teaser: A woman escaped an attack outside a Fort Pierce home and was shot at as she drove away. Two 18-year-olds now face charges in the case.
cards.body:

Fort Pierce police identified the suspects as Keibin Lopez-Godoy, 18, and Kailee Yurubi, 18. Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.

hero.headline: Family Demands Charges in Fellsmere Teen Party Shooting Death
hero.body:
Family and friends of 17-year-old Sulliman Bah gathered Wednesday night at Farm and Flame restaurant in Vero Beach to remember the teenager, who was shot and killed last Friday at a party attended by more than 100 teens at the Garcia boat ramp in Fellsmere. Bah, known to many as Sully, had just finished his shift at the restaurant before heading to the gathering. A couple hundred people packed the restaurant to share memories of his kindness and the impact he had on their lives.

Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving son, brother and kind person who was joyful and happy all the time. She said he made a point of greeting strangers on the street and asking how they were doing. "That was very important to him that he made people feel good, feel seen," she said. Friends remembered him as funny, caring and kind. "He was never mean to nobody, and I hate that this happened to him because he doesn't deserve this," one friend said through tears. "Sully was a kind soul." Another friend said learning Bah had been shot was one of the hardest things she has had to go through.

Investigators say several fights broke out at the party before an 18-year-old who knew Bah shot him. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers has said he believes the shooting was in self-defense. The sheriff's office says its investigation remains open and no arrests have been made. The State Attorney will decide whether charges will be filed.

Godfrey said she does not accept the self-defense characterization and wants accountability for her son's death. One of eight children, Bah was just a credit and a half away from graduating high school and had plans to travel, live in a big city and become an entrepreneur, his mother said. "His life is not being valued enough, and things are not being looked at seriously enough," Godfrey said. "I believe that my son was murdered, and I believe that the shooter needs to be punished for that."

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire District's Search for Outside Law Firm Stalls Amid Hazing Fallout
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District's effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders has stalled after one law firm contacted by the board disclosed a potential conflict of interest and another never responded. The board had hoped to hear from outside law firms during a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning about drafting the policy, but instead found itself without outside legal help lined up before its next meeting on Oct. 21.

St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one firm never returned her calls, while another disclosed the conflict. "I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." Board members discussed contacting additional firms in case the original two are unavailable. "I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," said Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and I don't want to delay any further."

The push for a new complaint policy follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they called a significant gap in district policy: there is no clear, independent process for handling complaints against certain contract employees, including the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said at that meeting. "They, being those positions, have essentially been able to investigate themselves."

The policy gap has drawn scrutiny following a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters, Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, after a third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Baldwin and Hutchinson had filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025 that was ultimately denied, and they later filed an amended complaint alleging the hazing investigation and their terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, effective 90 days later, just minutes after the special board meeting. Lee has said he welcomes outside scrutiny of the district's complaint process, while firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in his leadership. The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin. Board members are expected to keep searching for an outside law firm ahead of the Oct. 21 meeting.

hero.headline: Florida Amendments 1 and 2 Would Boost State Reserves, Cut Farm Taxes
hero.body:
Florida voters in November will decide two lower-profile constitutional amendments covering the state's reserve fund and property tax breaks for farmers, alongside a higher-profile measure on the ballot. Amendment 1 would increase the maximum size of Florida's Budget Stabilization Fund, commonly called the rainy day fund, from 10% to 25% of net general revenue collections. Amendment 2 would exempt agricultural equipment and certain farm-related property from property taxes.

Under Amendment 1, the state would be required to make annual transfers of up to $750 million into the reserve fund, and lawmakers would be allowed to use that money for certain critical needs. Supporters say the change would strengthen Florida's financial footing during natural disasters, economic downturns and other emergencies by ensuring a larger pool of reserve funds is available. Opponents argue that setting aside additional money in reserves could limit the state's ability to address immediate needs, including public services and infrastructure projects.

Amendment 2 targets tax relief for Florida's agriculture industry by exempting farm equipment and related property from property taxes. Supporters say the exemption would lower costs for farmers, strengthen the agriculture sector and help preserve farming operations across the state. Opponents contend the tax break could reduce revenue for local governments, which rely on property tax dollars to fund public services and community programs.

Both measures require voter approval to be added to the Florida Constitution. They appear on the same November ballot as Amendment 3, which would raise the homestead exemption for non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. Voters can find information on vote-by-mail options and early voting locations through county election offices ahead of the November election.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Mourns Sulli Bah as Family Presses for Arrest in Fatal Shooting
hero.body:
Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman "Sulli" Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said no arrests have been made and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while those who knew the Sebastian River High School student described him as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room. Isaac Rodriguez said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. "He touched everybody's heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room," Rodriguez said. Friend Alex Cortez, who boxed with Bah and spent time with him outside the gym, remembered him as driven. "He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future," Cortez said. Another friend, Xavi Espinosa, recalled feeling instantly welcomed by Bah. "Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul," Espinosa said.

The sheriff's office said Bah was at the Friday meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp when shots were fired. Investigators are reviewing whether the shooting was self-defense, and no arrests have been announced. Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his whole life ahead of him and called on investigators to weigh every detail of the case. "I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right," Godfrey said. "I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail."

During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the mark he left on their lives. Angela Sanders, one of his former sixth grade teachers, recalled his personality and smile. "His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room," Sanders said. Myan Agosto described Bah as a friend who constantly checked in on others. "He never failed to make sure everybody was okay," Agosto said. "He was just a really good friend." Friend Zani Zoutten remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person. Another speaker at the gathering reflected on the reach of Bah's short life. "He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth, look at this room," the speaker said.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Police Arrest Two After Woman Attacked, Shot At on South Sixth Street
hero.teaser: A woman escaped an attack at a South Sixth Street home and was shot at while driving away. Fort Pierce police arrested two 18-year-olds in connection with the shooting.
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police arrested two 18-year-olds after a woman was attacked at a South Sixth Street home and shot at as she fled in her vehicle. The Fort Pierce Police Department said officers responded to South Sixth Street at 7:12 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, after the victim called 911 to report someone was shooting at her.

The investigation found the victim had gone to the South Sixth Street address to speak with her boyfriend about their relationship. When she arrived, several people ran out of the residence and began attacking her, according to police. The victim managed to break free, get into her vehicle and drive away.

As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and opened fire on her vehicle, police said. A second suspect was arrested on allegations of driving the shooter away from the scene afterward.

Police identified the two people arrested as Keibin Lopez-Godoy, 18, and Kailee Yurubi, 18. Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Eyes $30M Oak Hammock Drainage Fix After California Boulevard Flooding
cards.teaser: City budget documents outline a multi-year, $30 million stormwater project near California and Savona boulevards along with a proposed $6 increase to the annual stormwater assessment.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031 includes a $30 million Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project, and city officials are also proposing a $6 increase to the annual stormwater assessment, raising it from $183 to $189. The plans come after viewer videos showed roads covered in water and vehicles struggling through several city neighborhoods this week. The city has received about 4 inches of rain over the past 48 hours, with another 2 to 4 inches possible by the end of the week.

Frank Camarda, who has lived near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace for more than 20 years, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into a detour as drivers piled in trying to bypass flooded roads. He believes Savona Boulevard was also underwater that night. Camarda said he had not seen flooding on his own street before, though he has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, but he believes that has stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said.

City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain came in too fast for the stormwater system to keep up, since canals, swales and retention ponds were already full. At one location the city monitored, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said the water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, which he described as the stormwater system doing what it is designed to do. He said Public Works checks drainage before heavy rain and works to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water arrives at once. He said residents who cannot get home should find another place to stay if possible, and that the city is working closely with police on safety.

The capital plan, submitted to City Council on April 13, would fund the Oak Hammock project through stormwater bond financing, with $8 million budgeted in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the following two years. The project would add new retention ponds, pump systems and upgraded valves, covering a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-23 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for Oak Hammock, which will guide the design of a multi-phase project that could include new retention ponds, canal pumps, or raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains off. He said it is hard to predict when residents will see construction or a finished project, since the city must first gather data, settle on a design and line up funding, but he called Oak Hammock a priority. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said.

The proposed $6 assessment increase would help fund five projects targeting flooding and water flow, including Oak Hammock, the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of swales and culverts citywide. The city's drainage system includes about 200 miles of canals, 1,200 miles of swales and more than 6,000 culverts. City code makes property owners responsible for maintaining swales and driveway culverts from the edge of the pavement to the property line.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Board Hits Snag Finding Law Firm for Complaint Policy
cards.teaser: One law firm never returned calls and another cited a conflict of interest, stalling the St. Lucie County Fire District Board's effort to draft a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders, with board members hoping to hear from outside law firms during a workshop Wednesday morning instead learning that one firm never returned calls and another disclosed a potential conflict of interest. St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said she appreciated the second attorney's honesty, noting the attorney provided two references, both on the West Coast. The board discussed reaching out to additional law firms ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21. Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said the board owes it to itself to have a courtesy conversation with other firms in case the first two are not available. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and I don't want to delay any further," Johnson said.

The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: there is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees, including the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said at that meeting. "They, being those positions, have essentially been able to investigate themselves."

The issue has drawn scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters, Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, who were fired after a third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Baldwin and Hutchinson had filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025, which district officials ultimately denied. They later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint alleging the hazing investigation and their terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. The district has said it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in the matter. Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, effective 90 days from her notice, and the district said she will continue providing services during that period. Lee has said he welcomes outside scrutiny of the district's complaint process and called Sabol a "tremendous attorney for the district."

Firefighters have also been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee, a result Fowler said would carry significant weight if a majority of firefighters say they can no longer serve under him. Lee said he would wait for the results before commenting further, adding that he has always fought for the men and women on the line. The union is continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin, and Fowler has questioned whether the fire board itself may have authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for arbitration to play out. Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new complaint policy before the board meets again Oct. 21.

hero.headline: New Ikonick Energetics Primer Plant in Indiantown Adds 100-Plus Jobs to Martin County
hero.body:
Ikonick Energetics has opened a new primer manufacturing facility in Indiantown, expanding its ammunition production operation in Martin County and adding more than 100 jobs across its two local sites. The expansion comes as Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties continue to report unemployment rates above the statewide average.

The Indiantown facility makes primers, one of four components used to build ammunition. Richard Rhatigan, vice president of law enforcement and government sales at Ikonick USA, said the plant has significant production capacity. "At full capacity you're looking at a billion primers per year," Rhatigan said. He explained the role primers play in the finished product: "It is one of the four components that go into building ammunition, so the primer actually ignites the powder which is incased within the brass."

Cameras were not permitted inside the Indiantown primer facility, but Ikonick gave a look at its ammunition manufacturing operation in Stuart, where workers combine the primer, brass casing and projectile to produce finished rounds. With the addition of the Indiantown plant, the company says about 75% of each piece of ammunition is now produced in Martin County. The new hires are expected to include both entry-level and specialized manufacturing positions. "When you talk about American manufacturing what that really means is, the people who work in our facilities, they live in our community," Rhatigan said.

Rhatigan said the company sees room for more growth in the area. "The opportunity for expansion is here and it is part of supporting the community in Martin County," he said. The Indiantown Chamber of Commerce said the new facility represents a significant investment in advanced manufacturing for the region. Ikonick also said its Martin County operations will help meet ammunition needs for law enforcement training. "We can support the state and local law enforcement training needs with our ammo with our facility in Stuart and here in Indiantown," Rhatigan said. For Indiantown, the facility adds to the community's manufacturing sector and could bring further employment opportunities as Ikonick continues to expand.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Police Arrest Two After Woman Attacked, Shot At on South 6th Street
hero.body:
Fort Pierce Police have arrested two 18-year-olds after a domestic dispute on South 6th Street turned into a shooting over the weekend, with a woman shot at as she fled the scene in her vehicle. Officers responded to South 6th Street at 7:12 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, after the victim called police to report that someone was shooting at her.

According to the Fort Pierce Police Department, the investigation found the victim had gone to South 6th Street to talk with her boyfriend about their relationship. When she arrived, several people ran out of the residence and began attacking her. Police said the victim managed to escape, get into her vehicle, and drive away.

As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and began shooting at her, according to police. A second suspect was arrested for allegedly driving the shooter away from the scene afterward.

Police identified the suspects as Keibin Lopez-Godoy, 18, and Kailee Yurubi, 18. Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.

hero.headline: UF Study Finds Dengue-Linked Mosquito Common in Indian River County Yards
hero.body:
A new University of Florida study has found that Aedes aegypti, the mosquito species most closely linked to dengue transmission worldwide, is surprisingly common in residential yards across Indian River County, even though no locally acquired dengue cases have been reported in the county. The finding comes as Florida has reported nearly 500 dengue cases this year, including more than 250 infections acquired within the state.

Researchers at UF/IFAS' Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory in Vero Beach conducted the first-of-its-kind study by trapping mosquitoes at homes and having residents log their bites using a smartphone-based Bite Diary. The team expected yards to be dominated by Aedes albopictus, the Asian tiger mosquito, but instead found relatively high numbers of Aedes aegypti, the yellow fever mosquito. Researchers collected 3,788 female mosquitoes from 78 yards during the study, which was peer-reviewed.

Of 70 bites residents reported, nearly 93% happened outdoors and nearly 74% happened at home. The number of mosquitoes trapped in a yard did not predict how many bites a resident reported. Instead, people who spent more time outside in the evening, between 5 p.m. and 9 p.m., reported more bites, with gardening and dog walking among the most common activities linked to bites. Researchers emphasized that the finding does not mean dengue is circulating in Indian River County, but said it shows why backyard mosquito control and personal bite prevention still matter.

The Florida Department of Health's weekly surveillance report covering Sept. 20-26 listed 252 locally acquired dengue cases and 245 travel-associated cases statewide, for a total of 497. Locally acquired cases were reported in Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas and Polk counties, with Hillsborough County accounting for 223 of them as the center of the state's outbreak. No locally acquired cases were listed for Indian River County. Palm Beach County reported one locally acquired case and 12 travel-associated cases, and St. Lucie County reported six travel-associated cases. State health officials also reported 20 mosquito pools testing positive for dengue statewide. Dengue spreads only through mosquito bites, not person to person, and symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, rash, nausea and pain behind the eyes. Health officials urge residents to use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants when practical, repair window and door screens, and dump standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires and pool covers. People with symptoms should contact a health care provider, especially after travel to an area where dengue is common.

The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, sets aside $8 million in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the next two for the Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project, funded through stormwater bond financing.

Samples said water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday and called that the stormwater system doing what it was designed to do. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Residents Still Dealing With Flooding From Tuesday's Storm
cards.teaser: Barricades remain up and city crews are on standby after heavy rain flooded roads and swales across Port St. Lucie, with one resident reporting two feet of water on California Boulevard.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents are still dealing with the aftermath of heavy rain that flooded roads and swales Tuesday, stranding vehicles and prompting city officials to leave barricades up as crews prepare for more possible rainfall. City officials said most of the floodwater had receded by 8 p.m., but some residents say problems with standing water and damaged swales remain.

Resident Tommy Fry shared video of his flooded driveway on California Boulevard. "This is the end of the driveway and, you know, two plus feet of water," Fry said. "It poured, you know, it came down pretty quick, probably 45 minutes of rain," he said, describing how fast the water rose.

"Just insanity, you know, it's just water two feet deep in the middle of California Boulevard and a waterline 15 feet up my driveway from the street and, of course, the swale over here that's been like that. I can't mow it," Fry said. Drone footage showed severe flooding near Savona and California boulevards, with streets covered in water after the afternoon storm and some vehicles stranded as drivers tried to get through.

Scott Samples, the city's strategic communications team leader, acknowledged residents' frustration with the swale system. "We're responsible for a very wide network of swales, right, so we try to get to as much as we can," Samples said. He said public works crews check drains before storms hit, but added that heavy rainfall can overwhelm the system. "We try to do as much as we can. We know that Mother Nature sometimes is going to win, and we try to do the best that we can to make sure that first of all, people are safe and the inconvenience lasts as little as possible," Samples said. He said the city is also looking at longer-term fixes. "So, we're looking at how can we change some of the stormwater management across the city. These are longer-term projects that, you know, I know people would like to have solutions right now. But again, our goal is to try to do this as well as we possibly can for the long term," Samples said. City officials said crews and equipment remain on standby in case more heavy rain hits the area.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Fire District's Search for Complaint-Policy Law Firm Hits Snags
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Fire District Board's effort to hire an outside law firm to draft a new complaint policy stalled this week after one firm stopped responding and another cited a conflict of interest.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board is struggling to find an outside law firm to help draft a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders, as fallout continues from a hazing investigation that led to three firefighter firings and a no-confidence vote against Fire Chief Jeff Lee. During a board workshop Wednesday morning, members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about taking on the work, but instead learned the search had stalled. St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one firm never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest. "I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast."

Board members discussed reaching out to additional firms ahead of their next meeting Oct. 21. Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said the board should not wait on the two firms already contacted. "I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and I don't want to delay any further."

The push for a new policy follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members acknowledged a significant gap: the district has no clear process for independently handling complaints against some of its own contract employees, including the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said at that meeting. "They, being those positions, have essentially been able to investigate themselves."

The scrutiny intensified after a third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters, Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, were fired as a result. Baldwin and Hutchinson had filed a complaint against Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025 that was later denied, and they filed additional complaints alleging their terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days later. Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee, and the union is continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin. Board members are expected to keep searching for an outside law firm before the board's Oct. 21 meeting.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police Arrest Two After Woman Attacked, Shot At on South Sixth Street
cards.teaser: An 18-year-old man faces an attempted homicide charge after Fort Pierce police say he opened fire on a woman fleeing an attack, and a second suspect is accused of driving him away from the scene.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police have arrested two people after a woman was attacked and shot at while fleeing a domestic dispute on South Sixth Street. According to the Fort Pierce Police Department, officers responded to South Sixth Street at 7:12 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, after the victim called 911 to report that someone was shooting at her.

Investigators said the victim had gone to the South Sixth Street address to talk to her boyfriend about their relationship. When she arrived, several people ran out of the residence and attacked her. Police said she managed to break free, get into her vehicle, and drive away. As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and opened fire on her vehicle, according to police.

Fort Pierce police arrested Keibin Lopez-Godoy, 18, in connection with the shooting. Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. A second suspect, 18-year-old Kailee Yurubi, was arrested on a charge of accessory after the fact for allegedly driving the shooter away from the scene.

The investigation into the attack and shooting remains active. Fort Pierce police have not released additional information about the relationship between the victim and the other people who confronted her at the residence.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie's $30M Oak Hammock Flood Fix Still Years Off as More Rain Looms
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie's long-term plan to fix chronic flooding around Oak Hammock remains in its early stages even as residents report standing water in their neighborhoods and the city braces for another 2 to 4 inches of rain by the end of the week, on top of the roughly 4 inches that have already fallen over the past 48 hours. The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, sets aside $30 million for the Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project, with $8 million budgeted in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the following two, funded through stormwater bond financing. The city is also proposing to raise its annual stormwater assessment by $6, from $183 to $189, to help pay for that project along with four others targeting the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of aging swales and culverts.

The renewed attention follows viewer videos showing water covering roads and vehicles struggling through several Port St. Lucie neighborhoods this week. Frank Camarda, who has lived near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace for more than 20 years, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into an impromptu detour as drivers piled in trying to bypass flooded roads, including what he believes was Savona Boulevard. Camarda said he had never seen flooding on his own street before, though he has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times in the past. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, but that maintenance appears to have stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said.

City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain simply came in too fast for the stormwater system to keep pace, with canals, swales and retention ponds already full before the latest downpours hit. At one monitored location, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, which he described as the system working as designed. He said Public Works checks drainage ahead of heavy rain and works to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water falls at once. He advised residents who cannot get home to find another place to stay if possible.

Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for the Oak Hammock project, which covers a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-23 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. That analysis will guide a multi-phase design that could include new retention ponds, canal pumps, or raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains more effectively. He said it is too early to predict when construction might begin, since the city must still finalize data, design and funding, but called Oak Hammock a city priority. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said.

cards.headline: Driver Describes Hitting Treasure Coast HS Student in PSL as Neighbors Cite Dark Road
cards.teaser: A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student remains in critical condition after being struck by an SUV while walking to school in Port St. Lucie. The driver told police he thought he had hit a construction barrel, and neighbors are raising concerns about the lack of streetlights on the road.
cards.body:
A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student remains hospitalized in critical condition after being struck by an SUV while walking to school Wednesday morning in Port St. Lucie, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. New details released by police show the driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person until he turned back to check.

Police said the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue. Investigators said the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway, alongside construction barrels in the area, when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man.

According to police, the driver made a U-turn at the next location where it was safe to do so and returned to the scene. Once back in the area, he activated his hazard lights and found the teen unconscious on the side of the roadway. Police said he immediately called 911 and has remained cooperative throughout the investigation. Investigators said there were no apparent signs of impairment involving the driver, though they noted the assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues. The crash remains under investigation, and police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident or who has dash camera, surveillance or other video footage from the area to come forward. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

Howard Shapiro, who lives across the street from where the crash occurred, said this stretch of Port St. Lucie Boulevard can be dangerous. "I don't walk around here is no lighting outside at nighttime," Shapiro said. "Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there." Shapiro said crews are currently improving the roadway, but lights are still needed. "They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's going to be helpful. But streetlights need to follow," he said. Celine Gabriel, who lives off nearby Becker Road, said she avoids Port St. Lucie Boulevard altogether. "I don't even come down this road no more," Gabriel said. "I go all the way down to I-95, come up on Gatlin to take my child to school."

cards.headline: St. Lucie Fire District's Search for Law Firm to Draft Complaint Policy Stalls
cards.teaser: One law firm went silent and another flagged a conflict of interest, slowing the St. Lucie County Fire District's effort to create a policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders before the board meets again Oct. 21.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District's search for an outside law firm to help draft a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders has stalled, delaying reform efforts sparked by a hazing scandal involving three fired firefighters. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping write the policy. Instead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one firm never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest. "I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast."

Board members discussed reaching out to additional law firms ahead of the board's next meeting Oct. 21. "I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," said Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further."

The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: there is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees, including the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said at that meeting. "They, being those positions, have essentially been able to investigate themselves."

The push for a new policy comes amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters, Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, who were fired after a third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson had filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025, which district officials ultimately denied. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint alleging the hazing investigation and their terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, effective 90 days from her notice, and the district said she will continue providing services during that period. Board members are expected to keep searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the board meets again Oct. 21.

"I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie's $30 Million Oak Hammock Flood Project Still Years Out
cards.teaser: After viral videos showed flooded streets near SW California Boulevard, city budget documents reveal a $30 million stormwater plan for the Oak Hammock area, funded partly by a proposed $6 assessment hike, though officials say construction remains years away.
cards.body:
Videos showing flooded roads and vehicles struggling through standing water in several Port St. Lucie neighborhoods have renewed attention on the city's stormwater spending, including a $30 million Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project that remains in its early planning stages. The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, includes $8 million in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the next two for the project, paid for through stormwater bond financing. Part of that money would come from a proposed $6 increase in the annual stormwater assessment, raising it from $183 to $189, according to the city's website.

Port St. Lucie has received about 4 inches of rain over the past 48 hours, with another 2 to 4 inches possible by the end of the week. Frank Camarda, who has lived near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace for more than 20 years, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into a detour as drivers tried to bypass flooded roads, including what he believes was Savona Boulevard. Camarda said he had not seen flooding on his own street before but has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, but he believes that has stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said.

City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain came in too fast for the stormwater system to keep up, with canals, swales and retention ponds already full before the latest downpours hit. At one location the city monitored, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, which he described as the system doing what it was designed to do. He said Public Works checks drainage before heavy rain and works to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water arrives at once. He said residents who cannot get home should find another place to stay if possible, and that the city is working closely with police on safety.

Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for Oak Hammock, which he placed in the California Boulevard area. That work will guide the design of a multi-phase project that could include new retention ponds, pumps for canals, or raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains off. He said it is hard to predict when residents will see construction or a finished project because the city must first gather data, settle on a design and line up funding. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said. The project covers a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-23 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. The stormwater assessment also helps fund four other projects, the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of swales and culverts, across a drainage system that includes about 200 miles of canals, 1,200 miles of swales and more than 6,000 culverts. The city notes that maintaining swales and driveway culverts between the edge of the pavement and the property line is the property owner's responsibility under city code.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Woman Shot At While Fleeing South Sixth Street Attack
cards.teaser: A woman escaped by car after being attacked and shot at during a domestic dispute on South Sixth Street in Fort Pierce. Two 18-year-olds now face attempted homicide and accessory charges.
cards.body:
A woman fled for her life on South Sixth Street in Fort Pierce after she was attacked and then shot at while driving away, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department. Two 18-year-olds have since been arrested in connection with the attack.

Police responded to South Sixth Street at 7:12 a.m. Saturday, October 3, after the victim called 911 to report that someone was shooting at her. Investigators determined the woman had gone to the address to speak with her boyfriend about their relationship. When she arrived, several people ran out of the residence and began attacking her.

The victim managed to break free, get into her vehicle, and drive away, police said. As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and opened fire on her vehicle. A second person then allegedly drove the shooter away from the scene.

Police identified the suspects as Keibin Lopez-Godoy, 18, and Kailee Yurubi, 18. Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide, while Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Moves Precincts 39, 52 Polling Site for Nov. 3 Election
cards.teaser: Voters in two St. Lucie County precincts will cast ballots at a new location after renovations closed their usual polling place. Election officials are encouraging early voting to help ease the transition.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County voters assigned to Precincts 39 and 52 will vote at a temporary polling location for the Nov. 3 general election because of renovations at their regular site. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker announced Tuesday that the two precincts will move from the Spanish Lakes Country Club clubhouse to Lakewood Park Church, 5405 Turnpike Feeder Road in Fort Pierce.

Walker encouraged affected voters, and voters countywide, to consider casting ballots early to avoid lines on Election Day. The county's newest early voting site, Lakewood Park Branch Library at 7605 Santa Barbara Drive in Fort Pierce, is now open for the first time for a general election. Other early voting locations include the Renaissance Business Park at 4132 Okeechobee Road in Fort Pierce, the Zora Neale Hurston Library at 3008 Avenue D in Fort Pierce, the MIDFlorida Credit Union Event Center at 9221 SE Event Center Place in Port St. Lucie, the Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. in Port St. Lucie, the Lewis Library at 2950 Rosser Blvd. in Port St. Lucie, the Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence at 500 NW California Blvd. in Port St. Lucie, and Minsky Gym at 750 SW Darwin Blvd. in Port St. Lucie. Early voting runs daily until 6 p.m.

Voters who plan to cast a vote-by-mail ballot are reminded that a deadline applies to request one. Those returning ballots by mail are encouraged to do so at least seven days before Election Day to ensure timely delivery. Vote-by-mail ballots can also be dropped off in person at any early voting site or at designated Supervisor of Elections offices, including the Renaissance Business Park at 4132 Okeechobee Road in Fort Pierce, the St. Lucie West South County Annex at 250 NW Country Club Drive in Port St. Lucie, the Havert L. Fenn Center, and the Tradition Tax Collector office at 10264 SW Village Parkway.

Walker's office is urging residents in Precincts 39 and 52 to note the change ahead of time so they know where to go on Election Day. Voters with questions about their assigned precinct or early voting options can confirm details through the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections office.
